                  ... and then the Dragons came

THE EVENTS OF THAT DAY SHATTERED HER UTTERLY, FRAGMENTED HER SO
that it took her a year to emerge from a feral struggle of daily survival to
finally bury the dead, to speak the rites, and to lift her eyes from the bloody
ground and see the forest beyond. The dragons had come upon her life with
fire and steel in the dead of night, laid waste with the purposeful savagery
one only sees from the world of men and left. The dragons took the heads
of some of their victims, they had raped others, but in the end they had
killed almost everyone. Everyone but her and her brother, whose body she
never found. She had somehow sensed their presence and fled, screaming
for people to run and hide, but no one else was awake and when they were,
it was already too late.
   They were just men, dressed in heraldic armor emblazoned with
dragons. They stank of evil and death. She was 14 years old, alone in the
forest, surrounded by the bodies of her loved ones and she survived. The
wolves came but did not feast, the crows descended on the grove but left the
bodies intact. The ground itself gave up fruit and food to her and she
survived.
   Years later, the elven druid, Gleinanion Othal, came to the ruined grove,
and saw her there. He marveled at how this place sang for her. The old ways
had witnessed the barbarity of men there, and had somehow remade a


                             Made in Highland
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                       1                                     2

sacred space amid the ghosts and wounds on its fabric. The cause of that
restiching and that reconstruction was Gardwen.
   For her, though, the space provided the channel for the old ways
blessings, but also wove into her a mourning and a loss.
   It was therefore, a shock, when a decade later, Gardwen saw a retinue of
soldiers, dressed as dragons, walk by on the road.




                                     2

                   The Voice of Death Herself.

MAGDA HAD BEEN HAPPY, BEFORE THE DREAMS BEGAN. SHE WAS OLD, AFTER
all, and appreciated the quiet life. She had crops to tend, pigs to feed, work
to do. It wasn’t complicated and didn’t involve killing anyone.
   The dreams were all nightmares, as these messages always were – one
does not find oneself beholden to the Goddess of Death without the jarring
terror of the dark looking over you at each contact, no matter how brief.
   As visions went, these seemed simple enough: a brother and sister
clutching each other in a desperate embrace only to the boy torn away by
reptilian talons whilst she stood over the quiet, resolute girl. Two identical
men, doppelgängers of each other, standing back to back with blades drawn,
ringed by fire with dragons swooping around them. As she stepped forward
to help, they were all engulfed in flame. True to form, the dreams always
ended in her own violent death so that she’d wake abruptly, muttering
irreverent curses at her patroness. The backdrop of the dreamscape was


                             Made in Highland
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                       1                                  3

always the same: Vacarus’ Square in Zorastor.
   Her most recent audience with Hel was just marginally calmer –
thankfully. The goddess stood stark against a blasted sky with dire wolves
howling and her voice coarse and cracked in the wind. “Save these children
– lay the dragon warrior to rest – kill these spirit sucking miasmic shit
eating little fucks. Unleash your fury on them!”
   She woke in her berserk rage, screaming with fury and wrecking
everything in her immediate vicinity. As the anger passed, panting with
sudden exhaustion, and looking around her beloved, utterly thrashed home.
She threw up her hands in frustration and screamed “who are you even
talking about?” – and sat heavily back on the bed amid the ruin of her
home.




                                     3

     Warriors, Knights, Murderers, and the Damned

THERE WERE BETWEEN TWENTY AND THIRTY ARMED, ARMORED MEN,
traipsing forward with some degree of military discipline. It seemed a long
march, since they had the look of men who had been walking for many
days, and as before, likenesses of dragons shone from shoulder guards,
breastplates and shields.
   With an almost strange sense of detachment, Gardwen felt a beat of calm
before her pulse jumped and her adrenaline rose in a crescendo. Crouching,
only a moment of fear passed before her jawline hardened and she fell into


                             Made in Highland
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                       1                                      4

a crouch to pursue them.
   The men walked until dusk, set up camp, cooked, set their guards and
bedded down. Hours later, long past midnight, she crept, wolflike and
stealthy as a ghost, to hide beneath a thick patch of gorse at the heart of
their camp. Her heart still racing, she willed it with quiet breaths and silent
prayer into such a quiet and stillness that no living thing observed her
presence.
   Hours after, a voice muttered out of the darkness, ‘So, let me get this
straight: we’re walking the length and breadth of Mystamyr so that his
Lordship can do what?”. A second, raspier voice answered “Win the fucking
tourney at Zorastor.” The first speaker shot back “With what? None of us
are good enough to stand a blind fart’s chance of winning.”, to which the
final rasping rejoinder came: “The boy, he’s going to use the boy to win”.
   This revelation was met with a silent moment of comprehension,
realization, and derision. “We’re walking hundreds of miles through kritch,
swamps, and shit so that the illustrious Lord Baron Hanzo di Teufel himself,
can show off his new secret weapon in a fucking archery tournament? Why?
What the fuck? Why?”
   Another beat.
   “Politics, Tat, you should know, it’s all politics nowadays” a conciliatory
rasp whispered, as the two men sauntered over to another part of the camp,
now out of earshot.
   Seeking answers, Gardwen harnessed the magic she had learned to reach
out through rivulets of energy to see the speakers’ souls and found only a
blankness from the two men – casting her viewpoint more broadly, she was
immediately overwhelmed by an ocean of evil radiating from the men
around them. These were the men who massacred her family and countless
others through the borderlands in raids, pogroms, and reprisals over the last
30 years. These were hardened, damned, murderers who thrived in
slaughter and exulted in pain. She stifled a gasp and stayed very still until
they had decamped and moved on.

                             Made in Highland
   Not understanding deeply, but knowing enough. Gardwen set herself to
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                       1                                    5

travel to Zorastor and find this Baron. She returned to the grove to leave it
in good order with Gleinanion before calling her wolf companion, Ruhi, and
embarking on a cross-country trek to Zorastor.
   As one blessed and held by the Old Ones, her footfalls through the
wilderness were silent and easy. She made good time through forests and
over the plains until she arrived, within sight of the city following a road
replete with travelers. She stayed off the road, suddenly aware of how
otherworldly she looked to the merchants, soldiers, and farmers traveling on
the road.
   As she reached a ford leading to the town, she stopped. This threshold
left her suddenly unsure as she now had to join the flow of travelers on the
road. She looked around at people walking by. She could see how the
majority of them averted their eyes and muttered comments, but there was
one pair of bright blue eyes that watched her piercingly.
   On the other side of the road, an ancient, tiny grandmother straightened
up from the sort of deep crouch old peasant women rest in. Leaning her
tiny, cloaked frame on a staff, the old woman walked over, her face deeply
wrinkled and mottled with the passage of time. There was a deep-seated
strength and seriousness to her demeanor as she came and Gardwen sensed
a fluidity and ease in the old woman’s movement that belied her apparently
ancient age. She reached out with her magic to sense the woman’s heart and
soul in a casting that was batted away by the steel trap of the woman’s
mind.
   As she arrived, the crone’s face narrowed in focus as she looked straight
into Gardwen’s eyes.
   “Who are you?” she asked, as if striving to solve a deep personal mystery
that had bothered her for years.




                             Made in Highland
                                      1                                     6




                                     4

                The Lord Baron’s Grand Entrance

RANDALL KNEW ZORASTOR AS ONLY AN EX-STREET-URCHIN CAN. HE KNOW
the smells and feel of the streets so well, he could likely run over the
rooftops blindfolded and find his way without falling. He had grown up
here, stealing, begging, cajoling. He had never known his mother, who he
heard referred to as ‘a sad story’ and left well alone. Taken in by some of
the working women of the Street of Red Lanterns, he had managed to make
himself both useful and funny enough to survive the crime lords and street
gangs. Now, he lived well as a professional thief on the streets of the city.
He was an accomplished liar, a skillful picker of both locks, pockets, and
misplaced trust. He could even cross blades with city guards, city heavies,
and even the occasional over-confident nobleman if the situation warranted.
Randall was well-known for imaginative problem-solving on the streets. If
something really, really needed to get done, 8 times out of 10, he’d get it
done for you.
   The upcoming tourney was proving to be quite the thing. He’d never
seen so many strange and wonderful people on the streets of his town. As
he watched the comings and goings at the Gate of Triumph to the west of
the city, he marveled at the steady drip drip drip of new adventurers,
mercenaries, and fresh meat to his town.
   Randall was wafting around Caravan Square, looking for all the world


                            Made in Highland
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                       1                                    7

like a man gainfully employed by a merchant to run odd-jobs and wrangle
customers, but was in reality scouting for potential marks. His eye was
drawn to the unmistakable figure of a high-ranking noble clearly attempting
to blend in whilst doing absolutely the opposite. He was flanked by two
footsoldiers, wearing a long woven woolen cloak that only partially covered
the silk and ermine of an astonishingly expensive outfit. Any Zorastan with
an eye for such things would immediately recognize such attire as that
befitting a Duke or a Baron. A ruby-encrusted amulet flashed at the man’s
neckline and a gem-inlaid rapier dangled at the man’s belt.
   Aha, thought Randall. Potentially dangerous, but a possibly huge payday.
   He made his way forward as the Baron gestured to one of his guards to
scout ahead. “One less sword in the way” he thought and was about to make
his introductions when the second guard saw him and blanched white with
recognition, shock, and the sort of fear you rarely see in the eyes of men
who are paid to fight and kill. As if guided by the spirit of Nilo Valis
himself, he reflexively put a finger to his lips and winked at the man. There
was no reason for anyone to have that kind of reaction to him, unless…
   “My lord Santo!” the guard blurted in a whisper, “ we thought that you
were to stay at the citadel for at least another week. Your father….”
   “I came ahead” Randall interrupted, improvising madly, “My father is
not to be disturbed by my presence here. I came to scout for him.” and with
that, turned on his heel to duck away from the Baron’s gaze as he turned
around to view the scene.
   Now, that has to be worth something, Randall schemed. If I resemble
this man’s son enough to spark recognition (and terror, apparently) in his
guards, there might be some angle ripe for some thievery.
   He followed the man’s little retinue through the bazaar, observing his
showmanship and obvious charisma. Perhaps the merchants simply smelt
the wealth and pandered to the nobles conversation, or perhaps the guffaws
and laughter Randall heard from the people he spoke to were genuine.
   Randall felt a pair of eyes following his and turned to see Nus Rutas. A

                             Made in Highland
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                          1                                    8

thief, like himself, but more of a pickpocket and less of a burglar
(professionally speaking). “What do you make of that?” Randall said by way
of an icebreaker.”I don’t like it, he’s got be some sort of spell caster if he’s
not just pitifully careless. I’d be wary, if I were you.”
   “Really? A mage? How come?”
   “No one is that confident without having some kind of ace up their
sleeve”
   Randall laughed but secretly registered his own caution based on what
he had seen.
   “You gonna tell Saliman? Jubal would pay to know about this guy.”
   “Reckon, good to see you Nus – stay out of the stocks now”
   “you too”
   and with that the cutpurse slid away. Randall tailed the Baron for a little
while longer until he inevitably sauntered into the most expensive brothel in
town. The thief pondered his fortunes and began to think of some sort of
plan.




                                        5

                         The Lakelady’s Javelin

AS THE SON OF A MILITIAMAN FROM ANMINSTER, HE NEVER WOULD HAVE
imagined that he, Conall Bjornlash, would be a traveling companion to (and
confederate of) an illustrious knight of the realm. The fact that she was
heart-stoppingly beautiful, an elf, and more lethal with a bow than perhaps


                               Made in Highland
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                              1                            9

anyone in Mystamyr made even more astounding to him, and yet, here he
was, chatting about the weather to the knight’s squire and keeping careful
watch for bandits hiding up amongst the brush on the road up ahead.
   Her name was Temerach Nebulo, also widely known to the people of
Mystamyr as ‘the Lakelady’s Javelin’. It was largely a mystery how a elven
female rose to greatness in the close knit community of knights known as
the Swords of the Lake. These were soldiers, sworn to a code of honor
beyond any other and held to account by the Goddess Nimue herself.
Temerach’s skill with a bow was legendary and her abilities with the spears
she fought with were prestigious also. As an order, they were sworn to the
safety of the realm and operated at a level elevated from that of the city
watch or even the King’s army. They held battle honors from the uprising
against the Dragonkings and led austere, disciplined lives of service and
honor.
   Conall had travelled to Mystamyr’s capital, Sharna, two years before and
had found work as a sell-sword. His sharp wit and sense of decency had
riled up the wrong people. He only narrowly escaped an ignominious
murder at the hands of his colleagues, through the chance intervention of an
old friend who happened to be passing. He was collapsed on the ground,
bleeding badly from a leg wound, and Old Johz, a wizard of the Order of
the Blue Star, squatted down in front of him with a sardonic smile and said
‘Still getting yourself in scrapes I see’.

A Slow Start to the Day

WAKING EARLY, CONALL DRESSED AND STEPPED OUT OF THE ROOM. HE
muttered an incantation and gestured surreptitiously so that his features and
clothes shifted into a new, unrecognizable configuration as he walked
through the brothel’s narrow corridors, turning corners, and descending the
stairs to leave. He was now someone else, a nameless Zorastorian man with
dark clothes and a large felt hat. He walked briskly to his prearranged dead-
drop location with Temerach’s agents. He slipped a coded note behind a
brick in a wall of an inn, turned on his heel and walked to the Bazaar.
   Zorastor was waking up. Hawkers were selling all manner of food, some
delicious smelling, some more esoteric. There were pastries, cooked birds,
drinks, fried fruit, and all manner of breakfast. He grabbed a selection for
his newfound friends and headed back to the Sylph’s embrace, watching for
signs that the spell he had cast to change his appearance was about to
expire. As he walked up the front steps, he released the spell and smiled at
the open-mouthed bouncer as he entered.
   He jauntily walked to the rooms and found everyone awake. He had
sweet meats for the wolf and pastries for everyone else.
   They chatted more about their plans for the day – who would talk to


                            Made in Highland
&2345678901234567890123456789&
                                         1                                  34

whom and what might be next for them. Conall would talk to his contacts –
Gardwen insisted that she should come and look out for them, and Randall
resolved to find out more from his local contacts about the comings and
goings at the Baron’s manor.
    As everyone was eating, Randall left to cross the street to the brothel
known as the ‘Promise of Heaven’. This was where he grew up and it was
always strangely pleasant and familiar to visit. The thought that someone
who looked like him had tricked any of the girls into thinking that he had
almost killed one of them lit a fury deep in his bones that still ate away at
him. He walked in and asked for Asphodel.
    As soon the message was delivered to her room, she emerged, robed,
half-dressed and rushing. As she saw him in the hallway, her face gave way
to relief and came up to him, chattering “I knew it couldn’t be true, I knew
it. What happened? They said that you killed Emmerelda.”
    “She didn’t die, she’s all cut up but she’ll live. Of course it wasn’t me,
just a bastard nobleman’s son who looks like me.” He seethed as he spoke.
“I’ve got to clear my name”
    He reached out to her shoulder in an unconscious seeking of contact, he
and Asphodel had known each other for years and trusted each other as
brother and sister. “I heard that a bunch of the girls are working up at the
Dragonshits’ manor, anyone from here?”
    “A few girls went. I didn’t, they didn’t want any elves.” That caught
Randall’s attention, partly from relief, but also registering the underlying
prejudice.
    “Exactly. Seemed a little odd to us too, but that’s what borderlanders are
like.”
    “Can I talk to one of the girls who did go?”
    Asphodel called for Moriata, an older woman with the calm intelligence
of someone who can survive and make the most of almost any situation
involving men. She walked up with a friendly nod to Randall born of a
lifelong acquaintance.

Purewater is built on water and admits it.

There is no ground. There are buildings, and there is water, and between them
there are ledges a yard wide with no rail. The traffic that matters goes
underneath, poled and rowed and shouting. The city drinks from a channel that
runs down out of the lake and through the temple on Temple Isle, and the
priestesses of the Lake Lady say the water is the goddess and mean it plainly.

Once there were Dragon Kings. They are gone and every child knows it. What is
left of them is armour on the border lords, a name on a barony, and men who
would like the old power back badly enough to pay for it.

The Lake Lady's Tourney comes once a year. Archery, single combat, and a
scramble through the canals. It is older than the Governor's office. For three
days the city fills with strangers and nobody looks closely at anybody.

This is what happened in those three days.

Purewater is built on water and admits it.

There is no ground. There are buildings, and there is water, and between them
there are ledges a yard wide with no rail. The traffic that matters goes
underneath, poled and rowed and shouting. The city drinks from a channel that
runs down out of the lake and through the temple on Temple Isle, and the
priestesses of the Lake Lady say the water is the goddess and mean it plainly.

Once there were Dragon Kings. They are gone and every child knows it. What is
left of them is armour on the border lords, a name on a barony, and men who
would like the old power back badly enough to pay for it.

The Lake Lady's Tourney comes once a year. Archery, single combat, and a
scramble through the canals. It is older than the Governor's office. For three
days the city fills with strangers and nobody looks closely at anybody.

This is what happened in those three days.

=== style ===
# Style Card: Hemingway

## Sentence rhythm
Short declarative sentences. Compound sentences joined with "and," rarely
subordinate clauses. Paragraphs of two to five sentences. Repetition of key
nouns instead of pronoun variety.

## Diction
Plain Anglo-Saxon vocabulary. Concrete nouns: things you can touch, drink,
carry. No abstractions unless a character speaks them. Numbers stated plainly.

## Dialogue
Untagged or "said" only. Long exchanges with no attribution once the rhythm
is set. Characters talk past each other; the real subject is never named.

## Description density
Sparse. One or two physical details per scene, chosen for weight. Weather
and terrain matter. Interior states shown only through action and omission.

## POV and tense
Close third person, past tense. The narrator never explains feelings; the
iceberg stays underwater.

## Signature moves
- The true sentence: open a scene with one flat factual statement.
- Ritual detail: hands doing work (rigging, cleaning, cooking) described step by step.
- The unsaid: end scenes one beat before the emotional payoff.

## Never do
No adverbs of manner. No semicolons. No similes longer than four words.
Never describe a character's emotion by naming it.

# Chapter 1 — The Ford

The mist did not lift. It was the same temperature as the air and it stood
waist-high over the river and the queue stood in it.

Magda had walked three hundred miles. She had a quarterstaff and a staff sling
and a purse with very little in it, and she was seventy years old and did not
look it, which was the goddess's doing and not hers.

For eleven nights she had dreamed the same three things. A young woman with a
wolf. A burning house. A knight in dragon-scale who was dead and had not been
told. Hel did not explain. Hel pointed.

The woman from the dream was thirty feet up the queue.

She was younger than Magda had thought. Her cloak had been mended by someone
with no gift for it. She was not looking at the city like the others. She was
looking north up the road where the last of the dragon-scale was going away at
a trot, and there was a grey wolf sitting against her leg, and nobody in the
queue stood within eight feet of her.

Magda went up the outside of the line on the wolf's side, which is the wrong
side.

At twelve feet the wolf stood up. It did not growl. A carter behind her said
*oh* very quietly and found something to do with his hands.

She put her hand into the fur at the base of its neck where the ruff is
thickest and a hand goes in to the wrist. The animal locked. Its head came
round and its jaw was four inches from her forearm and its breath was hot on
the inside of her wrist.

She scratched. Down, once, the way you work out a burr.

The animal came apart in the shoulders first and then the back.

=== NOVELIZATION.md ===
# Novelization Workflow

Turn a campaign's journal into a typeset novel. You (Claude) are the author;
`novelist.py` is the extractor and the press. Canon flows one way: nothing
you write here goes back into TypeDB.

## CLI

```bash
NOV="${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/mythras-gm/novelist.py"
PRJ="${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/mythras-gm"
uv run --project "$PRJ" python "$NOV" <command> [args] 2>/dev/null
```

Requires `pandoc` and `typst` for `build` (`brew install pandoc typst`).

## Workflow

1. **Extract.** `extract --campaign <id> [--out <dir>]`. Default output is
   `./novels/<campaign-slug>/` -- run it from the campaign's exported repo so
   the manuscript lives alongside `journal/` and `lore/`. Read the produced
   `source.md` end to end before writing anything.

2. **Pin the style.** If the user names a shipped style, read
   `styles/<name>.md`. If they give a freeform description, write a one-off
   card in the same format (use `styles/_template.md`). Either way, copy the
   card to `<manuscript>/style.md` and set `style:` in `book.yaml` -- the
   style must be reproducible in a later session.

3. **Outline.** Basic rule: **one session = one chapter.** Each chapter
   covers a full play session's events in order; narrative beats within the
   session become scene breaks, not separate chapters. One line per chapter:
   working title + session number + which journal events it covers (cite
   event ids from the source.md comments). Present it to the user and wait
   for approval before drafting.

4. **Draft.** One chapter at a time to `chapters/NN-<slug>.md`, starting each
   file with `# Chapter N — Title`. Scene breaks within a chapter are a line
   containing only `---` (typeset as ⁂). Set `status: drafted` in `book.yaml`
   when the outline is fully drafted.

   *Front matter (optional):* a `front-matter.md` in the manuscript root is
   built in before chapter one -- use it for a prelude/preface that orients a
   reader to the world. Give it its own page and title with a raw `{=typst}`
   block (e.g. `#pagebreak(weak: true)` + a centered `smallcaps[Prelude]`),
   **not** a `# heading`, so it does not register as a chapter (keeps chapter
   numbering and figure placement intact). Player-visible lore only.

5. **Canon rules.** Journal events are plot truth -- never contradict them.
   Characters, locations, factions, and player-visible lore give texture.
   You may invent connective tissue: interiority, transitions, minor sensory
   detail, unnamed bystanders. Invention flows one way only: embellishments
   created for the novel must never be written back into the journal, lore,
   or any game record. GM-only lore is excluded from `source.md` and
   must never leak into the prose. Leave `[TODO: ...]` markers for anything
   you need the user to decide; `build` refuses to run until they're resolved.

6. **Illustrate (optional).** Add engraving-style plates (or any look) to the
   book. Like prose styles, art styles are reproducible cards in
   `styles/art/`. The CLI is plumbing -- you write the prompts.

PRJ=/Users/gullyburns/mythras-gm/skills/mythras-gm
M=/Users/gullyburns/purewater-campaign-v2/novels/and-then-the-dragons-came-purewater-authors-cut
cat > "$PRJ/styles/gully-burns.md" <<'EOF'
# Style Card: Gully Burns (the author's own hand)

Derived from *... and then the Dragons came*, the 16-chapter Zorastor draft
(13,177 words, Oct 2023). That is a **different campaign** — Zorastor, Myrtis,
Lythande, Hakiem, Jubal, the Vulgar Unicorn. Take the voice, never the nouns.

## Sentence rhythm
Long accumulating openers that state the whole emotional situation up front
and then unpack it in clauses hung off commas — "shattered her utterly,
fragmented her so that it took her a year to emerge from a feral struggle of
daily survival to finally bury the dead, to speak the rites, and to lift her
eyes from the bloody ground." Then the paragraph shortens as it goes. Triads
everywhere: *stealing, begging, cajoling*; *raids, pogroms, and reprisals*;
*hardened, damned, murderers who thrived in slaughter and exulted in pain*.
Paragraphs run four to eight sentences and are broken by one-line paragraphs
used as drumbeats.

## Diction
Modern, warm, unembarrassed. Latinate where it earns weight (*sonorous*,
*deniability*, *incandescent*), Anglo-Saxon and profane where it earns speed.
Swearing is native to the narration as well as the dialogue — *fucking*,
*shitkickers*, *a nasty little shit*. Occupations and competence get named
precisely: a picker of locks, pockets, and misplaced trust.

## Dialogue
Loose tags, often none. In group scenes, deliberately anonymous — *"What now?"
Someone asked. "Justice." someone else said.* People interrupt, talk over each
other, and change the subject. Characters swear at each other affectionately.
Long speeches are allowed when a character is explaining the world; they are
not trimmed for realism.

## Description density
Bursts, not sweeps. One or two exact details and move on — a staff *burnished
for combat, not long walks by the sea*; an innkeeper's bow *conspicuously
missing his thumb*. Smell and noise before sight. Rooms get a sentence;
people get a paragraph.

## POV and tense
Close third, past tense, **one head per chapter**, named in the opening line.
Rotate freely between chapters — protagonists, allies, and at least once the
enemy. Free indirect discourse throughout: the narration slides into the
character's own words without quotation. *Fuck. Just the sort of thing you
don't need.*

## Signature moves
- **Small-caps lead-in.** Every chapter opens with its first clause in caps
  running straight into lowercase: `AS THE HOOD WAS RIPPED FROM HIS HEAD,
  RANDALL SUDDENLY realized where he was.`
- **"A beat."** Used bare, as its own paragraph, to mark timing. Also
  *Another beat.* / *There was a beat, and then her composure shattered.*
- **The aphoristic aside to the reader**, usually second person or general:
  *It is never wise to appear distracted on the open streets.*
- **The hard chapter button** — a short flat line that closes the chapter and
  often reverses it: *This was a mistake.* / *These were the catacombs, after
  all.* / *But even thieves had lines that could not be crossed.*
- **Comic undercut after intensity.** A goddess delivers a prophecy and then
  swears like a docker; a woman wakes from a holy vision and shouts *who are
  you even talking about?* at her wrecked bedroom.
- **Epithets** conferred in dialogue and then adopted by the narration — the
  Lakelady's Javelin, the woman from the woods, the pig woman.

## Never do
Never be cold. Never withhold interiority — this narrator tells you what
people feel and why, and is fond of them. No iceberg theory, no clipped
minimalism, no refusing the emotional payoff. Don't sanitise the sex work or
the violence, and don't leer at either. Never use the Zorastor nouns.
EOF

Purewater is built on water and has never pretended otherwise. There is no
ground in it worth the name. There are buildings, and there is water, and
between the two there are ledges a yard wide with no rail and a drop into
traffic that is poled and rowed and shouting at you. Children learn the ledges
before they learn their letters. Visitors learn them by falling in.

The city drinks from a channel that comes down out of the lake and runs through
the temple on Temple Isle before it runs anywhere else, and the priestesses of
the Lake Lady will tell you that the water *is* the goddess, and they do not
mean it as a figure of speech, and if you push them on it they will look at you
with the particular patience of people who have had this conversation with
merchants before.

Once there were Dragon Kings. Everybody knows they are gone. What is left of
them is scale-pattern armour on a few border lords, a name on a barony out past
the marshes, and a small number of extremely wealthy people who would like the
old power back and are prepared to be patient and expensive about getting it.

The Lake Lady's Tourney comes once a year — archery, single combat, and a
scramble through the canals for whoever can swim and climb and doesn't mind
being laughed at. It is older than the Governor's office and everyone knows
that too. For three days the city fills up with strangers and nobody looks
closely at anybody, which is very good for trade and has historically been very
bad for one or two individual people.

This is an account of three of those days, and a fourth that nobody had
planned for.
EOF

# Chapter 1 — The Woman on the Other Side of the Road

THE MEN CAME IN THE NIGHT WITH FIRE AND STEEL AND THEY DID IT WITH THE
particular unhurried savagery that you only ever see from the world of men,
and when they had finished they went away again, and Gardwen was eleven years
old and alive in a wood with nine people to bury and no one to help her do it.

She counted them in the morning. That is the part she has never told anyone
properly, because it does not sound like grief when you say it out loud, it
sounds like bookkeeping. But she counted them, all of them, going along the
line of what the fire had left, and she counted eight and she counted them
again and there were still eight.

Her brother was seven. They had taken him alive and they had taken only him,
out of nine people, and they had burned the rest so that nobody would ever be
able to do what she had just done and arrive at the number.

She spent a decade after that being the person who hid. That is how she thinks
of it. Not the survivor, not the last of them — the one who was small enough to
get into a hollow and stay there while it happened. The old ways came to her in
that wood and blessed her and taught her to close a wound and read a track and
walk through a forest without moving a leaf, and none of it ever once addressed
itself to the question of the boy.

Ten years of that colour of scale. She picked it up in four different
territories and lost it again every time.

And then, three days ago, she found a column of them on the north road going
somewhere at last instead of nowhere, twenty-odd men and a covered litter, and
she had followed it here, eating their dust, sleeping when they slept, and she
had come out of the trees at the last to find that the road went into a ford
and the ford went into a queue and the queue was full of people.

That stopped her.

Ten years in the wilderness will do that. She stood at the edge of the churned
mud and looked at forty strangers standing in it, farmers and carters and a
family with a goat and three nuns and a troupe of tumblers, and understood with
a lurch that she was going to have to stand among them.

She could see how it landed on them. The eyes going and coming back. The
mutters. The way the whole queue had quietly arranged itself into a shape with
a hole in it where she and the wolf were standing, an eight-foot circle of very
polite terror that moved when she moved.

Fine. Let them.

She put her hand into Ruhi's ruff and looked north up the road, where the last
of the dragon-scale was going away at a trot, and she made herself think about
the litter and not about the people.

Which is when she noticed that one pair of eyes had not gone away.

On the other side of the road, an ancient, tiny woman was straightening up out
of the sort of deep crouch that old peasant women rest in. She was cloaked and
mud-hemmed and leaning on a staff, and her face was so deeply wrinkled and
mottled by the passage of time that it was hard to put a number on her, and she
was looking at Gardwen the way you look at a word you know you have read
somewhere before.

Gardwen reached out. It cost nothing and she did it without thinking, a small
casting she had used a thousand times, a flick of attention at the shape of a
stranger's heart —

— and it went into the old woman and hit something like a steel trap and came
straight back at her.

She had never had that happen. Not once, in ten years.

The crone was already walking. She came across the mud on the wolf's side,
which is the wrong side, which is the side nobody uses, and she did not slow
down at twelve feet when Ruhi rose off her haunches and turned to face her
square and every conversation within thirty feet stopped.

Gardwen's hand went inside her cloak. Not fast. The way you put a hand on a
door latch in a house you don't trust.

The old woman stopped at an arm's length outside what the wolf considered hers.
She nodded, once — the nod you'd give a neighbour over a fence — and looked
Gardwen straight in the eye, and asked her question like a woman finally
getting to the end of something that had been bothering her for years.

"Who are you?"

And Gardwen, who had answers ready for *what do you want* and for *get that
animal away from me* and for four or five other things besides, found that she
had nothing prepared for that at all.
EOF

# Chapter 2 — The Voice of Death Herself

MAGDA HAD BEEN PERFECTLY HAPPY BEFORE THE DREAMS STARTED, THANK YOU
very much. She was old. She had crops and pigs and a roof that mostly kept the
weather where it belonged, and a life that did not, on the whole, involve
killing anyone, which after a certain age is the sort of arrangement a woman
comes to appreciate.

The dreams were nightmares. They always are. One does not enter into an
understanding with the Goddess of Death and then get pleasant dreams about
orchards; there is a price for the contact and the price is that some part of
the dark is always looking back at you, however brief the visit.

There were three things in it and there were three things every night.

A young woman with a wolf.

A house on fire.

And a knight in dragon-scale who was dead, and walking, and had not been told.

Eleven nights of that, and always the same instruction at the end of it, in a
voice like a rusted hinge, under a blasted sky, with dire wolves howling
somewhere off in the dark where she couldn't see them:

*Lay the dragon warrior to rest.*

Not kill. Hel is specific by being unspecific. Hel points, and does not explain,
and expects you to do the arithmetic yourself, and if you get it wrong that is
apparently also part of the lesson.

Magda had turned it over for three hundred miles and it still would not come
apart in her hands.

And there was the other thing, which she would not have admitted to anyone: she
was seventy years old and she did not look it, and had not looked it for a very
long time, and that was the goddess's doing and not hers. It is a strange kind
of blessing that mostly means you outlive everybody you were fond of. She had
buried enough people to be extremely clear-eyed about the terms.

So. Three hundred miles, a quarterstaff, a staff sling, fourteen stones and a
purse with very little in it, and here she was at a ford outside a city she had
last seen twenty years ago, standing in a queue, with no further instructions
whatsoever.

And then a young woman came out of the treeline with a wolf.

---

Up close, the girl was worse than the dream had suggested. Road-grime worked
into the seams of the knuckles and none at all under the nails, which means she
washes what she can and has given up on the rest. Thin in the way of someone
who eats when there is food rather than when there is hunger. And young — much
too young for the flat, patient watchfulness in her face, which is not a thing
anybody is born with. Somebody put that there.

"Gardwen," she said, when she was asked. And then, in the voice of a woman who
has had this conversation before and expects nothing at all to come of it:
"You'll want to be somewhere else, mother. People who stand near me have a poor
time of it."

Magda grunted at her. It is not a word. It is the noise you make at a gate
that has swollen shut, and it carries about the same amount of argument.

"I've been dreaming of you, girl."

Then she walked past her — past, not at, on the wolf's side — and put her hand
into the fur at the base of the animal's neck, where the ruff is thickest and a
hand goes in to the wrist.

The wolf locked. The whole animal, shoulder to haunch, one decision made at
once, and its head came round and its jaw was four inches from Magda's forearm
and its breath was hot on the inside of her wrist.

She did not move her hand. She scratched, down, once, the way you work a burr
out.

The rigidity came out of the shoulders first and then the back, and the head
turned away, and the animal made a low sound in its chest that no townsman
would recognise as anything at all. Up north they would have known it. Up north
they would have said the dog had decided you were furniture, and furniture is
the highest rank a stranger gets.

"—*don't*," Gardwen said, three seconds too late, her hand half out and
stopping. "Ruhi doesn't let people do that."

"My goddess tells me you're someone I need to help," Magda said. "Don't know
why. That's what she told me."

"Your goddess." Slowly. "*Which* one."

And Magda could hear exactly what the question was. The girl was asking whether
this was one of the singing ones. Whether she was about to be told that it had
all been for the best.

"Hel," she said. "Death." The wolf's weight settled against her shin. "Not
death in battle." She said it the way you would correct someone about which
field the boundary stone is in. "The other kind. Everywhere else. In the bed,
in the byre, in the bad winter. The ones nobody sings about."

Gardwen went very still.

Magda has seen that look before, on people who came expecting to be sold
something. It is the look of a bucket that has had the bottom go out of it.

"No," Gardwen said quietly. "No, that's — that's an honest god."

Then, fast, like a woman pulling a splinter: "Does she show you a boy?"

Her hand had gone into the wolf's ruff beside Magda's. She did not appear to
have noticed doing it. Her knuckles were white.

There was a beat.

"No," said Magda. "Not a boy."

And she did not dress it, because she had delivered enough bad news across
enough gates to know that softening it only makes people hear it twice. A
knight. Dragon-scale. Dead and standing up and walking and nobody had told him.

She watched the girl's face do the arithmetic and arrive somewhere else
entirely from where it had been sent.

"Dragon Knights," Gardwen said. Flat. "It's Dragon Knights you dream of."

And then Magda knelt down in the mud.

It made a sound like a boot coming out of a bog. It was cold, and it went
straight through the wool, and she was seventy years old on the outside and
there was nothing dignified about any part of it. Behind her one of the
tumblers said something and another one laughed and was hit.

She held the staff out crosswise in both hands, the way it is done, the way her
grandmother had done it once to a man who died the following spring.

"I'm to fight for you, girl. Protect you and yours, however you'd ask it. Die
for you, if it comes to that."

Gardwen did not take the staff.

She stood there with her hand in her wolf's fur next to a stranger's hand and
her mouth doing something unsteady, and she looked hard at the middle distance,
the way people do when they will not do the other thing in public.

"Get up," she said. It came out wrong. "Get *up*. You'll — the ground's
freezing, you'll ruin your knees, get up—"

And she was reaching down and hauling, one hand under Magda's arm, and her grip
was a great deal stronger than it looked and not steady at all.

"Ten years," she said, very low, for nobody else. "Ten years and not one
person. Not one. And a pig-farmer kneels in the *mud* at a *ford*—"

She stopped. Swallowed it. Put the flat watchfulness back on like a hat, and it
did not sit right any more, and she knew it did not.

"I don't know what to do with you," she said.

Then she offered her forearm, wrist to wrist, the woodland version of the way
soldiers do it.

"Gardwen. My brother was taken by men in that armour. Ten years ago. He's the
only thing I have left to look for, and I'm three days behind that column, and
if your god has business with a dead man in dragon-scale then Hel and I want
the same road for a while."

Neither of them, standing in the mud at the ford with their hands in a wolf,
had the least idea that they had just described the same person.
EOF

# Chapter 3 — A City With No Ground

THE CUSTOMS MAN AT THE WATER-GATE HAD A SYSTEM AND HE WAS PROUD OF IT,
and it had worked all morning, and it was about to stop working.

Carts and cargo paid by the wheel. Foot traffic paid a tourney-week head-toll,
or produced something that made it not worth his morning to argue, and he had
already turned two people back and waved three nuns through without looking up.
He had a tally-board under his arm. He had put a lot of himself into that board.

Magda did not wait to be got to. She went to him — straight up the outside of
the line past the fishmonger and the family with the goat, which is wrong, and
everyone in that queue knew it was wrong, and she could feel forty people
deciding at once not to be involved.

He turned round with his mouth already open. Something practised. *Back in
line, mother.*

She looked at him.

She has put her hand over the eyes of men who were shouting an hour before, and
gone out afterwards and fed the pigs, because the pigs do not care. Whatever
that does to a face, it has had fifty years to do it to hers. She let him have
all of it.

"We're going in."

The mouth closed.

He looked at the staff, which is not a walking stick and has never once
pretended to be. He looked at the wet grey animal watching him with the total,
patient attention of something that has never in its life been told it is a
good girl. He looked back at her face and did not find anything there that was
negotiating.

She could see him reaching for the words — *toll*, *licence*, *by order of the
Harbor Masters* — and she could see each one arrive, look at the situation, and
decide against it.

"There's a fee," he said. It came out with no starch in it at all.

"There is."

She let the pause go long enough for him to understand that she was not going
to fill it.

He looked down at his board. "Two on foot," he told it. "And a *dog*." He wrote
*dog*. Then he underlined *dog*, as though the underlining were a form of
protest that history would one day recognise. "Muzzled inside the Merchant's
Quarter, that's not me, that's the Guild, and if it goes for anyone it's your
neck not mine—"

"Understood."

"—and I never saw it."

"You never did."

He stepped aside. He did it small, so it wouldn't look like stepping aside.

And as she went under the chain-boom he said it, not quite to her, in the
flattened voice of a man reasserting something to himself: "Everyone's mad this
week. It's the Tourney." And then, because he could not help it, because the
thing had been sitting in the top of his head since dawn:

"Third lot today gone through with something they won't show me."

---

The noise arrived first. It comes up off the water and off the stone at the
same time and hits you from underneath. Then the smell: salt, tar, fish, hot
oil, wet rope, and under all of it the sweetish standing note of a city that
sits in its own water and has made its peace with the arrangement.

Gardwen got six feet inside the gate and stopped dead with her back against a
wall and her hand knotted in the wolf's fur, breathing like somebody who has
just been put down somewhere with no trees in it.

"There's no *ground*," she said.

"Aye. It's all boats and barges and slipways here, lass."

She learned it the way woodland people learn things, which is badly for ten
minutes and then all at once. Magda kept her on the inside with a hand flat to
the wall, and after the third bridge she stopped looking at her feet, and after
the fifth she was reading the water — which boat has right of way, which shout
means *move*, which of the poled barges will take a passenger and which one is
somebody's home. Ruhi hated every part of it and did it anyway, low and close,
ears flat, a wet grey misery at heel.

The ferryman across the Lullwater charged them for the wolf and did not charge
them for Gardwen, and would not explain why.

Bunting everywhere. Bad wine on trestles. Somebody's cousin selling favours in
di Teufel colours off a tray, dragon-scale green, three for a copper, and doing
extremely well out of it.

Away over the roofs a bell started up, and then another one, ragged and out of
time with the first. Then they stopped. Nobody they passed seemed to know what
they had been for.

---

The Pearl is an island and it is the loudest quiet place in the city. Narrow,
tall, swept, scrubbed, and lamplit at three in the afternoon because the alleys
there never really get daylight. Music from somewhere above. Two women on a
balcony watching the street the way farmers watch weather.

Halfway along a canal-side row there is a green door under a carved lintel — a
sylph with her wings folded, worn nearly smooth by two hundred years of hands.

Magda knocked the way she had knocked twenty years ago, and the woman who
opened it was a great deal older than that knock remembered.

"*Magda.*"

"Constantine."

"You're not dead." Said with genuine delight, one professional to another.

"Not yet. It keeps being suggested."

Constantine took in the rest of it in a single pass — the young woman standing
much too straight, the staff, the wolf — and to her enormous credit the only
thing that moved was one eyebrow, and only slightly.

"Beds," she said. It was not a question. "It's Tourney week, I've got the city
and half the border in my lap and every room's spoken for—" She stepped back
and held the door wide. "—so you'll have the top back room over the water, and
it's cold, and the shutter sticks, and I'll bring a brazier up. Bring the dog.
If it eats a client I'll take it out of your purse."

The hall smelled of beeswax and orange peel and, underneath, the honest fug of
a house where a great many people sleep. A girl of about thirteen came past the
foot of the stairs with an armful of linen twice her size, saw the wolf, stopped
dead, and dropped the entire load.

"*Ila*," Constantine said, without heat.

The girl was not listening. She was looking at Ruhi with her mouth open and her
whole face lit up like a feast-day.

And on the landing above, leaning on the rail with her hair down and a cup of
something in one hand, was a woman who did not appear to be in a hurry about
anything, ever.

"Constantine," she said down the stairwell, amused. "You've brought home a
*wolf*."

"I've brought home a *friend*, Emmeralda. The wolf is incidental."

Emmeralda came down the stairs the way water comes down stairs, took Magda's
chin in two fingers and turned it, unhurried and professional and examining.

"Not one day. Not *one*. You were a hard old woman when I was a young one and
you're the same hard old woman now, and I've had two decades of people telling
me *my* face is unnatural."

"Mine's a curse."

"Mine's an *asset*."

Then, later, at the bottom of the stairs, with something under the brightness
for just a moment: "You didn't come for the Tourney."

"No."

"No." She accepted it, and filed it, and did not push. Which was, in the event,
the last decision anybody in that house made freely for some time.
EOF

# Chapter 4 — Not My Business

THE KNOCK CAME AT THE HOUR WHEN A BROTHEL STOPS BEING A HOUSE AND STARTS
being a business, and it was the kind of knock a young man gives a door when he
is entirely certain of his welcome. Three, brisk.

Magda was three floors up with a brazier going and a shutter that stuck, and
Gardwen was sitting with her back against the bed-frame cleaning mud off her
boots with a knife, and Ruhi was asleep across the door, and none of them had
any business with whoever that was.

Then a second voice in the hall. Young. Male. Well-bred. Border vowels.

And a name, clear enough through the floor to be certain of it: *Emmeralda.*

Magda stepped over the wolf and got the door shut without letting the latch
speak, and went down as far as the turn above the second landing, where the
overhang puts you in shadow and the hall lamp does not reach.

She has spent most of seventy years moving quietly around animals. She got
where she was going and nobody marked it.

From up there she could see most of the hall. Constantine with her back turned.
The young man facing her, hood back, dark clothes, road-dust still on the hem —
he had not changed since he rode in. Nothing in his hands. Talking quickly.
Constantine nodding in the way she nods.

Then Emmeralda came in from the parlour door, changed since the afternoon —
hair up, something green. She said something. The young man laughed.

Then she went up the near stair, the one that comes past the second landing,
twelve feet from where Magda was standing.

He followed her.

They would pass below her in a few seconds. The shadow was good. It was not a
wall. Staying put was about to become a contested thing, and there was no
particular reason to be found on a stair in a house that was not hers.

She withdrew.

*Not my business.*

And it *wasn't*. That is the thing to hold on to, afterwards, and she did hold
on to it, and it did not help at all. Constantine had run that house for thirty
years. Emmeralda was not a girl. Hel had not walked her three hundred miles to
mind a brothel door, and a woman who came in through the water-gate that
morning without paying does not go and tell a nobleman that she does not care
for his face.

She went back up. Gardwen did not ask, which was a thing Magda filed away about
her. Ruhi resettled across the door and the house carried on being a house —
the stringed instrument, someone laughing on the second landing, water working
at the stone under the window.

She lay on the bed with her boots off and her staff under her hand where it
always is, and looked at the ceiling, and after a while she went under.

---

Somewhere below, an hour later, a young man who was not nearly as good at this
as he believed attempted something he had never been trusted with, and — against
every expectation of his father's, and of his father's men, and very probably
of his own — he got it right.

Then he tried to leave, and made a comprehensive disaster of it.

---

There was no scream. That was the first thing, and it was worse than a scream.

There was a crash — something big going over, a table or a chest, and glass
after it — and then a man's voice, high and completely undone, saying *no no no
no* very fast. Then a door hitting a wall hard enough to shake the frame two
floors up.

Running feet on the canal-side stair. A slip. A worse noise: a body hitting a
landing full length, and something metal skittering away across boards.

More running. A shutter thrown.

And a splash in the canal below that was far too big to be a man getting neatly
into a boat.

Magda came up out of sleep on animal reflex because Ruhi was already standing.
Then the house began shouting at itself all at once — Constantine bellowing
with no words in it, a woman crying on the second floor, somebody hammering on
a door.

Gardwen was on her feet with the boot-knife held low and reversed, looking at
Magda, waiting to follow her lead.

The metal thing that skittered across the boards had not gone into the water.

And from the room the two of them had gone into: nothing at all.

# Chapter 5 — Shrieks of the Sylph

CONSTANTINE HAD RUN THE SYLPH'S EMBRACE FOR THIRTY YEARS AND HAD BURIED
two of her women and married off four more and had never once, in all that
time, had to stand in a doorway of her own house and refuse to go into a room.

There were twenty-two people under her roof that night. Nineteen upstairs and
three in the kitchen, and she could have told you every name and what each of
them was owed and who was sending money home to whom.

She had been in the hall when he came. She had done the warm professional thing
she does. She had thought, in passing, *this one is very bright tonight*, and
had not made anything of it, because a young man with border money going up her
stairs with his heart going is not a phenomenon, it is a Tuesday.

Now she was standing in a doorway with a bar in her hand and her people crowded
in the passage behind her, and the smell that was coming out of that room was
scorched hair and something sweetish underneath it, like fat gone over in a
pan, and something else beneath *that* with no name she had for it, and the
back of her throat kept closing on its own.

The wolf would not go through the door. That was the detail that finished her.
The animal was braced in the doorway with its legs locked and its head low,
snarling at a room with nothing in it.

Chalk on her floorboards. A worked figure, a big one, with corners on it,
scuffed through at the foot where somebody standing inside it had gone
backwards out in a hurry.

The shutter was off its latch and swinging and there was cold canal air coming
in.

And Emmeralda was sitting up in the bed.

She was opened from the hollow of her throat to her hip. One long deliberate
cut. Not a slash and not a stab — somebody had *drawn* it, slowly, with
something barbed, and the edges of it were wrong, and it was still bleeding,
and it was not being held closed by anything at all.

She had her head tilted slightly. She was looking at the door. She was smiling
at Constantine.

"You needn't crowd," she said. Her own voice, perfectly level, pleasant. "It
doesn't hurt at all."

---

The druid girl had got there first and had been on the bed with both hands in
it to the wrists, head down, saying something low and fast in no language
anybody knew, and every hair on Constantine's arms had gone up.

She had watched the flesh come together under the girl's palms. She wants that
on record. She *saw it close*.

And then she saw it open again from the inside, deliberately, the way a hand
pulls a curtain back.

The girl came out into the passage afterwards with blood to both elbows that
was not hers and her hands hanging at her sides, and stood against the wall,
and said, "I closed it. Magda, I *closed it*. Both hands, everything I had, and
it went in and it *took* — and then it opened again. On its own. Not tore.
*Opened*. Like a mouth."

Inside the room, quite clearly, in a warm and perfectly ordinary voice,
Emmeralda was telling Constantine that he was fussing and that she would like
her green shawl, the one with the birds on it, because it was cold with the
shutter open.

Constantine has been called by every name a woman in her trade gets called and
has answered to most of them cheerfully. Nobody in that house had ever called
her *he* in her life. She did not correct it. She stood in the doorway with the
bar in her hand and she did not correct it, because the thing in the bed was
using Emmeralda's mouth to be charming at her, and there did not seem to be a
polite way to raise the matter.

---

Then the old woman came up the stairs.

She had gone *down*, apparently, while everyone else in the house was going up,
and she came back with a soaking cloak over her arm and a lamp in her hand and
the entirely settled expression of a woman who has been outside dealing with
something.

She went into the room. She sat on the bed when she was asked to. She let the
thing pat the coverlet at her with a bloody hand.

And then, in the voice of a woman asking after a neighbour's roof, she asked it
who the young gentleman had been, so that they would know how to greet him on
his return.

It brightened at being consulted about hospitality.

"Santo," it said. "Just Santo — he didn't give me the rest, they never do, they
think it's clever." A little conspiratorial lean, and the wound gaped with the
movement. "He'll want the green room, I should think. He liked the birds on my
shawl."

And then, thoughtfully, arranging the coverlet over the ruin of itself,
house-proud:

"He said he'd come back for the others. Four more, he said, and then his father
would *have* to see. He was quite emotional about it." A small indulgent laugh.
"Men and their fathers, Magda."

Constantine got both hands flat on the doorframe and held herself up with them.

"*Santo*," she said. "He said *Santo*."

Because there is exactly one Santo who comes into this city in the week of the
Lady's Tourney with border vowels and a cloak that cost more than her front
door, and he is the son and heir of Baron Hanzo di Teufel, who rode in through
Caravan Square that same morning with twenty-odd Dragon Knights at his back and
who was at that moment being toasted by half the men on the Governor's council.

Twenty-two people under her roof.

A priest meant a report, and a report meant the Watch, and the Watch that week
meant the Governor, and the Governor was drinking with that man's father.

She got them into her counting room and put her back against the door and said,
"What do we do?" — and understood, as she said it, that she was asking a
pig-farmer from the north whom she had not seen in twenty years, and that she
was going to do whatever the answer was.
EOF

# Chapter 6 — And Then the Water Closed

GOING DOWN THREE FLIGHTS IN THE DARK AT SPEED AT SEVENTY IS NOT A HEROIC
act and Magda has never once pretended otherwise. Nothing dramatic happened.
She did not fall. She simply took the stairs at the pace a body takes them at
the end of a long life, one hand hauling on the rail, with the lamp on the
second landing gone out and the turns tight and every second of it audible to
her as *not fast enough*.

She met Ila coming up. The girl hit her rather than stopped — two fistfuls of
skirt, barefoot, white to the lips.

"She won't *open* it—" hauling, trying to turn her round, back up the way she
had come. "The door's shut and she won't open it and Constantine's got the bar
out and Emmeralda *won't answer*—"

Gardwen went past both of them toward that door without breaking stride.

And Magda stood there for exactly as long as it took to notice that the
canal-side stair kept going *down* — past the boot room, to the water door and
the slipway — and that not one person in that house was going that way. Every
soul under that roof was going up. Down there in the dark it was quiet, and the
water was still moving from whatever had gone into it.

She took the girl's hands off her skirt.

She loaded as she went. Stone in the pouch, cord round the knuckles, staff
cocked back along the forearm.

---

The water door was unbarred and standing half open and swinging. Whoever came
through it had left it that way.

Four stone steps going down into black water, green and slick below the third.
A skiff moored to the ring at the bottom, riding oddly — the painter still tied
but the boat shoved out and drifted back, rocking harder than the canal
warranted.

The water directly off the slipway was still working. Not ripples. The deep,
slow turnover of something that went in heavy and recently.

One lamp on the far bank, forty feet off, its light lying flat on the surface.
Under that surface, nothing at all.

There was a shape on the second step down, right at the waterline, that was not
stone. She got a hand on it and hauled it up: a cloak, heavy with canal, dark,
good cloth, expensive, the hem still carrying road-dust under the wet. It had
caught on the mooring ring. It had not come off a man who was being careful.

Then she looked out across the water and found something to shoot at.

Thirty feet out and moving left, upstream: the fast ugly chop of somebody
swimming badly and in a hurry. A head. The pale smear of a face turning back
toward the house. Then just the shoulders working.

He was making for the far ledge where the lamp was, where there was a set of
iron rungs up the wall. Forty feet of open water between him and them, and he
had covered maybe a third of it.

He had not seen her. She was a shape in a dark doorway and he was looking at
the upper windows, where all the noise was.

---

Here is the whole of the reasoning, and it took about a second and a half.

She did not know his name. She did not know he was a baron's heir, or that the
house would be turned upside down for him inside a day, or that a man with no
colour in his face at all would spend three days walking this city with her
description in his mouth. She knew that somebody had gone into a room in a
house where she was a guest and done something to a woman in it that made a
wolf refuse a doorway, and that he was now thirty feet away and getting further,
and that she had a sling.

Backlit against the far lamp. Dark water. A moving target.

The staff came over and the stone went out flat across the water with that low
buzzing note they make.

She did not hear it hit. She *saw* it — the head snapped sideways, hard, wrong,
the way a head does when it has stopped being steered from inside. The working
shoulders stopped working.

He went under without a sound. No thrashing, no cry. The chop where he had been
smoothed out into ordinary canal, and the wake he had been dragging caught up
with the place he was not any more, and there was one hand above the surface for
a moment, open, not grasping at anything.

And then that was gone too.

Forty feet away the lamp on the far bank went on being a lamp. The iron rungs he
had been making for went on being empty.

The water closed and kept moving.

Behind her, up in the house, a woman began screaming and this one did not stop.

---

She went at the cloak there and then, on the slipway, in the dark, with feet
already coming down the boot-room stair — and did not finish. Outer pockets
first, because that is where a hurrying man puts things: a few coins, a folded
scrap gone to pulp, a lump of resin or wax. Then her hands found weight.
Something small and hard sewn in behind the lining at the breast, with no seam
to it on the outside, needing a knife and a minute and a light.

She had none of the three. Not yet.

Later, two doors down from a room she could not stay in, with a lamp off a
linen-closet bracket and the cloak opened flat on the floor and the stitching
arguing with the thumb-edge of her belt knife, she took the thing apart
properly.

A ring. Heavy gold, a man's, big enough to want a knuckle, with a beast cut
into the face — long, coiled round on itself, its tail through its own jaws.
Good work. Old work. Sewn into a cloak by somebody who did not want it on his
hand that night.

A twist of oiled silk, still dry inside. A few long hairs bound at one end with
fine copper wire, and a flake of something brown and hard that was not wax.

The hairs were dark red.

Emmeralda's are black to the root.

Eleven border coins, heavier and older and off a different mint, unchanged
since he arrived. A tailor's mark stitched inside the collar where the wearer
never looks — a little tower with three windows, embroidered rather than
stamped, which is a mark for somebody whose custom is worth the extra work. A
pulped letter dried flat against the hot lamp glass, of which two things
survived: part of a line in a fine clerk's hand, *—ee days before the Lady's
Tourney, at the hou—*, and the bottom half of a broken seal with the same beast
on it.

And in the left cuff, folded twice and stitched flat so it would not rattle, a
second twist of oiled silk.

Empty. Used.

There were three more like the first, wrapped in the same bundle. All full. All
hair.

None of it black.

Whatever he had come to that house to do, he had the makings for four more.
EOF

# Chapter 7 — The Girl Who Dives for Oars

ILA WAS FROM THE SHOALS AND SHE HAD BEEN IN THE WATER BEFORE SHE COULD
walk, which is the ordinary condition of tide-flat children and not, as
Constantine kept insisting to people, some sort of accomplishment.

She dived for lost oars for a copper. She had once gone under the Lullwater
bridge on a bet and come up the other side, and Constantine had taken the skin
off her for it, and she had done it again the following week to establish the
principle.

She was thirteen. She had been in that house for two years. Emmeralda had
taught her to read the price list and then, when that turned out to be dull,
had taught her to read properly, and had been extremely rude about her
handwriting, and had given her a hair ribbon at midwinter that Ila kept in a
tin.

That night two of the women were holding her by the arms in the kitchen so that
she would not go upstairs and sit with Emmeralda, and she was fighting them
silently, which is a great deal worse to watch than shouting.

---

Constantine came down for her herself. She did not explain much on the way. She
said there was a thing that had to be done in the canal and that only Ila could
do it, and that she could say no, and that Constantine would not think less of
her, and that this was not Constantine's asking.

Ila was in the boat before anybody offered her a hand.

"I can go deeper than nine feet," she said immediately. "I can go under the
*Lullwater*. Constantine, tell her—"

"I told her."

There was the wild woman with the wolf, soaked and grey and shivering in the
bilge with a line still round her waist, and Ila felt a small unworthy stab of
pity for a grown adult who evidently could not swim, and was too well brought up
to say so.

And there was the old grandmother from the afternoon, sitting in the stern with
a staff across her knees.

"What am I looking for?"

---

The old woman did not soften it. That is the thing Ila has thought about most
since.

"Look here love. The man who hurt Em is down there, dead and drowned with a
caved in skull. You've got to go down and hook his body so I can drag him out
and put him somewhere so we don't get in trouble."

Ila went completely still.

Not the fear. That came later. First there was just the arithmetic of it. *The
man who hurt Em. Down there. Dead.*

"—caved in," she said.

"Aye."

"Who—" She stopped. She looked at the boathook lying in the bilge. She looked
at the old woman. And she worked out, in about two seconds, that nobody in that
boat was surprised, and that the woman who had come in that morning with a wolf
was the one giving the instructions.

"*You* did it."

"Aye."

And then the old woman said, "I know it's hard but you're all we've got to make
it right," and then, to the shivering wolf-woman, with something close to
desperation in it: "Gardwen — fuck, help me explain. I'm no good at this."

Which is when Gardwen got up out of the bilge water.

She was still shaking and her lips were blue and she did it anyway. She came
forward on her knees so that she was down at Ila's level and not looming over
her, and she took the shawl the girl had already half shed and put it back round
her shoulders, and her voice went quiet and completely steady, which it had not
been all night.

"Ila. Look at me. When I was your age, men came to my house at night and killed
my family. Every one of them. And I hid, because I was small and there was
nothing else I could do, and I have spent ten years being the person who hid."

Ila stared at her.

"Nobody's asking you to hide. There's a job, and you're the only one in this
boat who can do it, and it's a *filthy* job. You'll touch him. It'll be cold
and it'll be dark and he'll be heavier than you think and you will not like any
part of it, and it will be over in a minute, and then Emmeralda's house stays
standing and everyone in it goes on living here."

She put the end of the line into Ila's hands.

"That's the whole of it. You can say no. I'd not think less of you, and neither
would she."

Somewhere off toward the Lullwater a dog was barking. The canal moved under the
boat.

Ila's fingers closed on the line.

"Two tugs if I've got him," she said. Her voice cracked in the middle of it and
she carried on anyway. "Three if I need to come up."

---

She went in without a sound. No splash worth the name — she tipped backwards
off the thwart and the water took her and closed over, and the line paid out
smooth and steady and not in jerks, which is the difference between a swimmer
and everybody else.

It went out a long way. It stopped.

Nothing for a count of ten. Nothing for a count of twenty.

Then two tugs. Firm. Deliberate. Then two more, and the line went heavy —
properly heavy, dead-weight heavy, coming taut across the gunwale — and two
pairs of hands got onto it and hauled.

She came up beside the boat with her arms wrapped round the line, gasping, hair
plastered flat, not looking at anything at all except the sky.

"His face is *up*," she said.

She said the right thing first. That is what the old woman told her afterwards
and it turned out to be the thing she needed said.

---

They took the wet shawl off her and dropped it in the bilge and put the old
woman's own cloak on her instead, which swamped her entirely and smelled of
three weeks of road and pig and was dry. Then the old woman rubbed her arms
hard, the way you bring a lamb round, brisk enough to hurt a bit.

"You went into black water on the word of an old woman you met this morning,
and you found what you were sent for, and you came back up and you said the
right thing first. That's what you gave us. That's the whole job. I've stood
beside grown men in worse than this who did none of it."

"I touched his—"

"Aye. You did. That'll come back on you tonight and probably tomorrow and then
less after that." She pulled the cloak closed under Ila's chin and held it
there a moment. "It doesn't mean anything's wrong with you. It means you did a
hard thing. There's a difference, and nobody tells you, so I'm telling you."

Ila made a sound and folded forward against her, and was allowed to, and cried
properly for about a minute with her fists in the old woman's shirt.

Then she stopped, because she was thirteen and mortified, and pulled back and
scrubbed her face with the heel of her hand.

"Emmeralda's still up there," she said.

"She is."

"Is she going to be all right?"

Behind them, Gardwen did not say anything at all.
EOF
