# Chapter 8 — A City That Dredges Itself

MAGDA'S FIRST PLAN WAS THE OBVIOUS ONE AND SHE PUT IT ON THE TABLE
straight away, because it had the advantage of being what actually happens to
rich fools in this city about twice a month. Put him somewhere on the approach.
Leave the gold on him. Purewater thieves will kill a wealthy idiot for his rings
quite happily, and everybody knows it, and the Watch will write it down without
looking up.

Constantine did not hesitate. "Yes. God help me, yes. It's the only story that
holds. A rich border boy comes to the Pearl with his father's gold on him and
doesn't know the water, and he's found in the morning face-down off the Shoals
with his purse cut and his rings gone." A glance at the ring on the table.
"You've already done the hard part of that."

Then she stopped, and did the thing she is actually good at, which is finding
the hole.

"But the body's in *my* canal. Behind *my* water door. And it went in heavy and
it didn't come up. The outflow runs west past the Lullwater on the ebb — that's
two hours off yet, and until then he's on the bottom in about nine feet of
water more or less where you put him. After the ebb he could be anywhere, and
'anywhere' includes the grating at the Shoals, which they clear every morning
with a *crowd* watching."

Which is how they came to be out on a canal in the dark with a boathook and a
line and a thirteen-year-old, and how they came, after the girl had been taken
back up the slipway wrapped in Magda's cloak, to be sitting in a skiff with a
sack in the bottom of it and a decision still to make.

---

There were two ways and Constantine laid them both out like a woman reading a
ledger.

Leave the ring on him. Then whoever finds him strips him, and inside a day
there is a Pearl thief trying to sell a di Teufel signet to a fence, and
Crowbill's people hand that boy to the Dragon Knights themselves rather than
have the trouble, and it is finished, and it was never here.

"But the moment that ring turns up, the Baron knows his son is dead. And a
father who knows tears the city apart looking for the *why*."

Keep it. Then he is a drowned foreigner with his purse cut, and he stays
nameless for two days, maybe three, while the Baron is still expecting him at
supper.

"That's time. But there's no thief in the story, and 'nameless drowned man' is
a story the Watch stops believing the moment somebody comes asking after a
missing lord."

As for where — the Lullwater. Past the bridge on the north side there is a
stretch of bad water and worse people, and men wash up there twice a month with
their boots gone and nobody asks a single question. Two hours' poling. And two
hours out on the canals with him in the bottom of the boat the whole way.

Magda shrugged.

"Keep the ring. Keep the clothes and the cloak. How about we do this — he's
never found?"

Constantine looked at the sack for a while.

"Never found is harder than it sounds in a city that dredges itself," she said.
"You weight a man and drop him in a canal, and in six or seven days the gas
brings him up with the weights still on him, and then it isn't a drowning any
more — it's a *murder*, and the Watch works murders."

She counted it off on her fingers, in the dark, in a boat.

"So it's one of two. **Burn him** — and the only fires hot enough are the Forge
Quarter's, which means a guild furnace, which means a guildsman who saw you and
wants paying every year for the rest of his life." She shook her head slowly.
"I've watched a man be bled that way. It doesn't end.

"Or **the deep channel**, past the Shoals, where the harbour drops off into the
sea. Opened so he doesn't float. Weighted. On the ebb, so what's left goes out
and not back in. The ebb starts in an hour and a half and runs about four.
That's the window, and there isn't another one before it's light.

"That's an hour's poling to the harbour mouth in a boat with no light on it,
past the Harbor Masters' pontoon, and out into open water in a skiff that is
not built for it. If a patrol stops us we are three people and a corpse and
there's no story that survives it."

She stood up and took the pole.

A beat.

And Magda, sitting in the stern of a boat she did not own, listening to a
madame with thirty years of running a house on the Pearl explain the tidal
constraints on the disposal of a nobleman, smiled to herself.

*Amateurs.*

"Do you know anyone who keeps pigs?"

Constantine stared at her.

"Give me twenty minutes with a saw and I'll have little old Santo here as a
nice pile of butchered meat we just feed to the pigs. Then he's shit and no
one's the wiser."

It took her a moment to be sure Magda was serious, and then a moment longer to
get past being sure.

"You're—" She stopped. Started again. "In my *house*."

"You've a boot room with a stone floor and a drain that goes straight into that
canal. I saw it on the way down."

She opened her mouth and shut it, because that is exactly what she has.

She turned and looked at the water for a long time. When she spoke again her
voice had gone somewhere flat and far away.

"There's a hog-yard on the edge of the Shoals. Man called Renko — he takes the
kitchen waste off four houses on the Pearl, mine included. Two carts a week,
before dawn, and one of them's tomorrow. He doesn't ask what's in the barrels.
He never has. He's not a good man and he's not a talker, and he'd take coin to
go on not being one."

She rubbed her face with both hands.

"It's *better*," she admitted, and hated it. "No boat. No Harbor Masters. No
four-hour ebb window and no Lullwater. It's all *inside*, and it's done before
the house wakes.

"But it's hours, Magda. It's hours of it, in my scullery, with twenty-two
people asleep over your head and a demon in my green room asking for her shawl.
And in the morning I have to stand in that room and take delivery of my own
bread."

From the stern, quietly: "I'll help."

Constantine laughed. One, with no humour in it at all.

"Of course you will."

She put the pole in and brought the skiff round to the slipway.

"There's a saw and a cleaver in the scullery," she said. "And a bone-tub. Don't
ask me why I know where they are."

---

It is not fast and it is not hard. It is the same job it always is. You find
the joint, you go through the joint, you do not fight the bone. The trick with
a big carcass is patience and a sharp edge and Magda has had fifty years of
both.

Gardwen held what needed holding and turned what needed turning and did not
flinch once, which surprised Magda not at all.

The drain did its work. The canal took the rest.

They talked, because you do. Magda said something about having killed one of
the enemy tonight, which was meant as encouragement, and Gardwen stopped with
her hands on the table and looked down at the work.

"He's the right age to be one of their sons. Not one of the men." She turned a
piece over without being asked. "Ten years ago he'd have been twelve. Sat at
somebody's table while it happened. Getting told the story after, probably, and
being proud of it." Her jaw set. "So no. Not one of the ones who came. But he
grew up into exactly what they wanted him to grow into, and he did *that* to
Emmeralda with four more women's hair in his cloak, and I'd have put the stone
through his head myself."

She wiped her wrist across her forehead and left a mark there she did not know
about.

"It's a start. It's not the one I came for."

The saw went on. Somewhere over their heads a floorboard settled and both of
them stopped, and it did not come again.

Then Gardwen said, not looking up: "Magda. That thing upstairs said *his father
would have to see*. See what?"

"I've no idea. Nothing good."

It took until the small hours. They scalded the slate and the floor and the
drain with three kettles, and Gardwen put the saw and the cleaver back on their
hooks exactly where they had been, which was somehow the worst part of the
entire night.

Four barrels, with Constantine's own house-mark burned into the ends.

Renko's cart came at the fifth bell and Constantine walked it down herself,
because it is not the sort of thing you send a boy with.

Above them, faintly, through three floors, a woman was laughing. Warm and easy
and delighted.

Neither of them said anything about it.

# Chapter 9 — Twenty Minutes

MARISETTE RULES THE PEARL AND SHE DOES IT WITH LEDGERS, WHICH IS A THING
people find disappointing when they finally get into the room and discover a
woman in a plain grey wrap doing sums at four in the morning with her hair down
and no jewellery on at all.

She had been up since the third bell, and she had not been up because she was
worried. She had been up because her man on the bridge had come and told her
something and then she had sat with it for an hour and a half, deciding whether
to send men, and had decided to give them until dawn.

This is what he had told her. Noise at Constantine's, at about the third bell.
A woman screaming, and then not screaming, which is worse. The water door open
and a light on the slipway. The skiff out on the canal twice — once with three
people in it, and once with four.

And that on the second trip one of the four had been Ila. That she had gone
into the water. And that she had come out of it crying.

He had come and told her that last part because he knows Marisette likes Ila.

So when the black door opened at four in the morning and Constantine came in
with a wet bundle and two strangers, Marisette had already done most of the
work.

She poured coffee into three cups without asking whether anyone wanted it, and
pushed them across, and sat back.

"Right. Before you start."

She laid it out — the noise, the light, the two trips, the girl — flatly, in
order, without any pleasure in it.

"You've got twenty minutes before I have to be someone else. Tell me what's in
my island."

---

The old woman was not, by her own admission, one for talking, and then talked
anyway, and did it in about six sentences with no shape to them at all, which
is a delivery Marisette has learned to trust more than eloquence.

One of Emmeralda's clients had cut her open and put something in her. He had
been swimming away. She had killed him with a sling. They had got him out of
the water afterwards and turned him into pigment for disposal.

And then, in exactly the tone of a woman getting to the point at last:

*It was Hanzo di Teufel's son. He was planning on doing this to four more girls
and he wanted to show his dad.*

Marisette did not move at all while she talked.

When she stopped, Marisette reached out and turned one of the coffee cups a
quarter-turn on its saucer, and that was the only thing that happened for about
five seconds.

"Say the last part again."

"Hanzo di Teufel's son."

"Santo." Flatly, like checking a figure. "Twenty-two, black hair, very
handsome, laughs before the end of the joke."

"That's him."

"He came to my house three days ago asking after Asphodel and I turned him away
because I didn't like his hands."

She is completely still when she says this and her voice does not change at
all, which anybody who knows her would find alarming.

"I sent him to *Constantine's*."

Constantine said, "Marisette—"

"Don't." Not sharp. Just closed.

---

She went through the evidence the way she goes through stock. The ring she
barely glanced at — turned it once, set it down. The letter she read twice. The
coins she pushed aside.

Then she came to the four twists of oiled silk and opened the first one with
her thumbnail, and the copper wire and the long dark red hairs came out into
the lamplight.

And Marisette stopped.

She sat looking at it for a great deal longer than she had looked at anything
else.

"Constantine. Who at your house has red hair?"

"Nobody."

"No." She laid the hairs flat on the desk and separated them with one
fingernail, four or five strands, precisely, the way you lay out evidence. "
Nobody at mine either."

She looked up, and for the first time since they had come in she was not
running the room.

"There are two women on this island with hair that colour, and I know them
both, and neither of them works. One of them is a Watercrafter's daughter."

Her jaw tightened.

"The other is the High Priestess of the Lake Lady's own niece."

---

The girl told her tale then, because the old woman nodded at her, and told it
the way you would give a report — no shape to it, nothing arranged, which is
somehow the worst possible way to hear it.

Nine of them. Eleven years old. She went back in the morning and counted them
all and her brother was not there. He was seven. They had taken him alive and
taken only him and burned the rest so nobody would count.

"That boy in the canal said his father would *have to see*. See what he'd made.
That means his father makes things too. And his father has had my brother for
ten years."

Marisette sat back.

"A litter," she said slowly. "Curtains sewn shut. Guards facing inward."

"Aye."

"He entered a champion for the Single Combat. Nobody has seen the man. It's
been the joke of the week — the Baron's mystery swordsman. Not one soul in this
city has laid eyes on him."

She picked up the ring, finally, and turned it over.

"But a champion nobody has seen is not a champion. It's a *thing being kept*.
Men who are proud of a swordsman show him off. You parade him at the Siren's
Call, you let the odds move, you take money off the Guilds — that is the entire
point of entering one." She set it down. "Hanzo di Teufel has not let a living
soul look at his. He has him behind a wall and a litter with the curtains
stitched, and his guards face inward, and you don't face inward to keep people
out. You face inward to keep something *in*.

"How old would your brother be now?"

"Seventeen," Gardwen said.

It came out flat and immediate, the way a number does when you have counted it
every year for ten years.

"He'd be seventeen. Santo was twenty-two." Her hands had gone white on her
knees. "It's not him."

"No," Marisette agreed. "It isn't."

She let that sit exactly long enough.

"Seventeen is young for the Single Combat. It is not too young. I have seen
younger die in it."

The clock behind them went on being expensive.

"I'm not telling you it's your brother, girl. I've no idea and neither have you
and I'd not have you break yourself on a hope." Said almost gently, which from
her appeared to cost something. "I'm telling you that the thing in that estate
is being hidden, and the boy who came out of it was carving women up to impress
his father, and that his father is at this moment three streets from the
Governor with a demon-worker's blood in him and an entry in the Lady's own
Tourney."

She stood.

"Which makes it my island's business now, and I don't have twenty minutes any
more."

---

She looked at the old woman properly then, the way she had looked at the hair.

"Who are you?"

"Magda. I keep pigs."

"Mm." She did not smile. "You killed the Baron's heir with a sling from a
doorway in the dark, at what — thirty feet? — and then took him apart in a
scullery and had him in barrels before the fifth bell." A beat. "You keep pigs."

"Aye. And other things."

She accepted that. She wrote one line in the ledger and blotted it.

Then she gave them the only job in Purewater that nobody else could do, and she
was honest about why.

"Every face I own is known on this island. My people can't get within a street
of that estate without it being reported to somebody by noon. You two walked
through the water-gate yesterday morning. Nobody in this city knows your names.

"That is worth more than anything else you've brought me tonight."

She sat back down and picked up her pen.

"So: sleep. Eat. And this afternoon I want to know what is behind that wall.
Not a rescue. Not a fight. *Looking.*"

And then, without looking up:

"And when you find out whether that boy in the litter is seventeen, Gardwen —
you come to me before you do anything about it. Not after."

# Chapter 10 — One Bag a Day

YOU CAN SEE THE SHIP FROM THE SECOND BRIDGE, WHICH IS THE FIRST THING
wrong with it, because a ship you can see from two districts away is not a ship
anybody is hiding.

Above the roofs of the Forge Quarter there was the usual column of dark furnace
smoke, and standing separate from it, lower down at the waterline, a long flat
streak of white.

Steam. A hundred feet of it, coming off the water in a continuous sheet along a
private pier, not stopping, with no fire under it.

The thing at that pier was a deep-water vessel, dragon-prowed, black-hulled,
high out of the water and entirely out of scale with the canal traffic around
it. Moored bow-in with her stern to the open channel and the Mouth beyond,
which means she can leave at any hour without turning.

Where the hull met the water, the water was boiling. Gulls would not go near
it. There was a dead-water slick round the stern with things floating in it
belly-up.

Magda and Gardwen came at it along the working yards, which were working —
coopers, a rope-walk, a chandler, men moving timber — and nobody stopped them,
because two women walking through a working yard in the afternoon are
furniture. Which is a fact about the world that Magda has spent seventy years
being grateful for.

---

She stood in the lee of the last cooperage for the better part of an hour and
watched what a ship actually needs.

Not much went *on*. That was the first thing. No provisioning carts, no
chandler's boy, no water butts — which is strange for a vessel that size at a
pier, until you notice the covered gangway aft with the canvas laced down both
sides, and understand that they are bringing everything aboard where nobody can
see it, in their own hands, from their own boat.

Things came off, though.

Slops. Twice, a knight carried a covered pail down the ramp and emptied it into
the dead water at the stern. Nobody collecting it. Nobody being paid to.

Laundry. A woman came at the second bell with a barrow and took a bagged load
from the *pier head* — not from the deck; handed down to her by a knight who
did not let her past the bollards — and went away again toward the rope-walk.

Ash and clinker, in barrows, from somewhere below decks, tipped on a spoil heap
at the end of the yard. Far more of it than a galley fire makes.

And a cooper's boy delivered four new barrels to the pier head, left them, and
was waved off. The knights carried them aboard themselves.

Nobody who was not a Dragon Knight had been past those bollards all afternoon.

---

There was also, at the far end of the yard, a hog-man's cart with an old nag
and two barrels and a lad who was not paying attention to anything, and who was
making an enormous mess of backing the horse round.

Magda went over to help, because she knows all about hogs.

The horse was not impressed by her either. It laid its ears flat and swung its
quarters and the offside wheel went into the spoil heap and the cart tipped far
enough to put one of the barrels over on its side. The lid stayed on. Mostly.

The lad said a word she would have clipped him for.

Then they spent a couple of minutes getting the wheel out, and she got her
shoulder under the barrel while he righted it, and by the end of it they were
both filthy and he had stopped being embarrassed.

"She does that," he said, glaring at the horse. "Every time. Every single time,
right at the end."

"She's testing whether you've noticed her."

"I've *noticed* her—"

"No, lad. She wants you to go to her head *before* she starts, not after."

He considered this with the deep suspicion of a fifteen-year-old being told
something obviously true.

His name was Pell. He did the Forge Quarter yards on alternate days for Renko
out on the Shoals, which Magda kept her face entirely still about.

She had failed at the only thing she had set out to do, which was impress a boy
with a horse, and had acquired a friend instead. This happens more often than
anybody admits.

---

He complained about the rope-walk, who had put nails in their waste last month.
Then he jerked his chin down the pier at the steaming black hull.

"Not that lot, though. *They* don't give us nothing."

"Tight bunch, are they?"

"Tight? They're *unnatural*, is what they are."

And he counted it off, aggrieved, the way you complain about a bad customer,
and handed her the entire shape of the thing without the least idea he was
doing it.

Every yard on that side gave their waste to Renko. Cooperage, rope-walk,
chandler; even the furnace lads gave up their bones. That is how it works. That
lot tipped it in the water. In the *water*, right off the stern, good scraps,
meat and all. Renko went down there himself on the first day and offered to take
it for nothing — for *nothing* — and they walked him back up the pier by his
elbows and told him not to come again.

And the ash. Barrows of it, off that ship, since the day she tied up. Show me
the galley fire that makes that much clinker in a week.

"Only one that gets anything off them is the laundry woman. Yannick's wife. Bag
down at the bollards, coin in her hand, off you go. She's not allowed past
neither. She won't talk about it, though. Went right off, she has. Which is a
shame, 'cause she'll talk about anything."

Magda thought about that for a moment.

"How big is the bag? Is there a lot of laundry?"

Pell stopped, and actually thought about it, which he clearly never had.

"Not big. One bag. She carries it on the barrow but she could carry it on her
hip if she wanted — I've seen her lift it one-handed off the bollard."

He frowned.

"Every day, though. That's the thing, now you say it. Rope-walk's forty men and
they send out twice a week. That ship sends out *every day* and it's one bag."

He clicked at the horse.

"And it's all the same, she said once before she went quiet on it. Not shirts
and hose and what-have-you like a normal house. All the one thing. Sheets, I
suppose. Bedding."

He got the nag moving, and said the rest over his shoulder, cheerfully, with no
idea at all what he was handing her:

"She had a right go at Renko about it in the tavern, first week. Said she'd take
their coin but she'd not take it long, and if they wanted that much *boiling*
every day they could get a woman with a stronger stomach."

He raised a hand. "Alternate days, missus! Tell Renko I said you know your
horses!"

And the cart lurched away up the yard, and the nag did the thing with her
quarters again exactly as predicted.

---

Magda went back to counting.

Eight. That was all of them. Two at the pier head, two at the top of the ramp,
three working on deck — one of whom did nothing at all but walk the same twenty
feet over and over and look at the shore — and one who came up out of the aft
hatch with a barrow of clinker, went down the ramp, tipped it, and went back.

Eight men. In scale, all of them, on a hot afternoon, aboard a moored ship.
Nobody in shirtsleeves. Nobody idle. Nobody talking.

No banner at the masthead. For a nobleman in residence there would be colours
flying; every other hull in that harbour with anybody aboard had something up.
That mast was bare.

No Baron. Nothing in anything but scale and livery. No servants, no clerk, no
valet, nothing that looked like a household. The good clothes and the gold were
somewhere else — north-west round the point, where the boat went.

And the shutters amidships had not opened once all afternoon. It was a warm
bright day and every port on every hull on that water was open to air the ship
out, and those were closed, and — now that she looked at them properly — they
were closed from the *outside*. There was a bar across.

Gardwen had gone very quiet beside her.

"Magda," she said. "Sheets. Every day. Boiled."

# Chapter 11 — Boiled Blood

ANN YANNICK HAD WASHED FOR THIS QUARTER FOR TWENTY-TWO YEARS AND IN THAT
time she had done a house with a consumptive in it, a birth-bed that went
wrong, and a man who lost a hand at the rope-walk, and she could tell you the
difference between all three by the shape of the stain.

That is not a boast. It is simply what the work is. You get a shape to it —
where it came from, how it lay, whether he thrashed. Blood is a language and
she has been reading it since she was nineteen.

For four mornings she had been washing something she could not read at all, and
her husband did not want to hear about it, and there was nobody else.

She was up to her forearms when the shadow fell across the door.

"If it's for the rope-walk you're a day early."

Behind her, on the end copper — the one furthest from the door, on its own —
there was a load going that was not like the others, with the lid half over it.
The water in it had been changed recently; there was a grey slick round the rim
where it had been tipped out and the drain channel by her feet ran the wrong
colour and had not been sluiced. And there was a stack of clean folded sheets
by the door with a cloth over them, and the cloth did not quite cover the
corner of the top one, and that corner had a stain in it that had been boiled at
and had not come out. It had gone the brown that blood goes when you cook it
into cloth.

The old woman in the doorway was looking at it.

Then she came in out of the sun, took the bench by the door where the draught
is, and sat down the way a woman of seventy sits down — all at once, with a
noise.

And then she did not say anything.

She looked at her boots. She rubbed her knee. She observed, once, to nobody in
particular, that the steam was pleasant on the joints.

The young one who had come with her stayed outside in the yard with her back to
the wall, which Ann noted and did not comment on.

Copper. Lift. Turn. Copper.

Four days of it, with a husband who says take the coin.

It took a long while. The old woman got most of the way through not asking.

Then Ann lifted a load, dropped it, wiped her forehead with the back of her
wrist, and said it to the copper rather than to her:

"Do you know what boiled blood smells like?"

The old woman said nothing.

"'Course you do. You've a face like you've buried people."

And out it came.

"Four days I've had that. Every morning. One bag, and it's all sheets, and every
one of them's the same.

"It's not a wound. This is the *same shape* every day. Same place on the sheet.
Same size. Like it's been let out of him careful, in the same spot, and mopped,
and put back.

"And there's something else in it that doesn't come out. Not blood. Blood boils
out with lye and time. That doesn't. It goes *grey*, and it smells like the
forge, and my hands were numb to the elbow the first day and I've worn gloves
since."

She put the paddle down.

"They pay double. My man says take it. And I lie there at night thinking —
whoever's in that ship, he's still bleeding tomorrow. Four days. Somebody's
keeping him alive to do it again."

---

And then the old woman made a joke about it.

She meant well. Ann is prepared to say that now, at a distance. She arranged her
face into something sympathetic first, which was worse than not trying — her
face does not know how to be that, and what it produced was closer to
indigestion — and then she said something about honest work, and how most folk
pay double to keep blood *off* their sheets, not on.

It is the sort of thing that is funny in a byre at four in the morning with
people who have been up all night with a bad calving.

It is not funny in a wash-house.

It landed in the steam and died there.

Ann Yannick's face closed like a door. She picked the paddle back up and the
rhythm changed — shorter, harder, the movements of a woman who has remembered
she is working.

"You're not from the yards," she said.

Not hostile. Worse: careful.

"You came in with a young one who's stood outside my door instead of coming in,
and you sat down and let me talk, and you've asked me nothing, which is how the
Watch does it and how Crowbill's do it and how a certain sort of woman from the
Pearl does it. And now you've made a joke about blood.

"So I'll ask, since you won't. Who are you, and why do you care what's in my
coppers?"

---

Here is what saved it, and Ann has thought about this since.

The old woman did not try the joke again, and she did not try charm, which she
has none of. She told the truth, flatly, and let Ann decide about it.

North. Cold winds and sharp ice. *I joke about blood because I've seen and
cleaned up my fair share.* And: *the men on that boat are up to some evil shit
that might need stopping. Sounds like you're thinking the same way.*

Ann looked at her for a long moment through the steam. She has been lied to by
better liars than that, and she did not find what she was checking for.

"North," she said. "Aye. I thought there was something in the vowels."

She worked for a bit.

"Evil shit that might need stopping," she repeated, and something that was not
quite a laugh came out of her. "My man says I'm being a woman about it."

She lifted a sheet out, wrung it, dropped it into the rinse.

"Three things, then. And I'll deny every one of them if you ever say I said it.

"**One.** It's not a sick lad. Sick men sweat, and they piss the bed, and they
stink of the sickness. There's none of that. Whoever's in that bed isn't ill
and isn't dying and isn't getting better. He's being *kept*.

"**Two.** Second morning, the bag came down heavier and there was a shirt in it.
Not linen — a fighting man's under-shirt, quilted, for wearing under scale." She
paused. "The arming-points were cut. Not untied. *Cut*, all of them, front and
back, the way you do when you're getting something off a man who isn't helping
you.

"**Three.**"

She stopped paddling.

"The knight who hands the bag down. Big fellow, white eyebrows, no colour in him
at all — he's the one that walked Renko off the pier. Yesterday he asks me, all
friendly, whether I ever wash for the houses on the Pearl. Whether I know
anyone that does."

She looked straight at her.

"I said no. But he wasn't asking about laundry, was he."

---

The old woman asked her about Marisette then, which Ann thought was a strange
turn until she understood that it was not.

"Everyone knows Marisette. She's not on this side of the water but she doesn't
need to be." She turned a load. "What do I think of her. She's not *kind*. Don't
let anyone tell you she is. She'll take a girl's whole life apart to keep her
house standing and she'll do the sums out loud while she does it.

"But she's straight. That's rarer. She says a price and it's the price. And when
Ganny Corliss's daughter got herself in trouble with a Watercrafter's son two
winters back — a Forge Quarter girl, mind, nothing of hers, no reason at all —
Marisette had the Guild sat down and settled inside a fortnight, and the girl
kept the child and the money, and the boy's father still can't say her name
without going purple."

She wrung out the sheet.

"So. She's a hard woman who looks after women. There's worse to be."

Then her hands went still in the water, and she arrived at it.

"You *are* off the Pearl."

She looked at the door, at the young one standing in the yard.

"And that white-haired bastard was asking me yesterday about women who do
laundry for the Pearl houses. He wasn't hunting a washerwoman. He's hunting
something that went *from* here *to* there. Or from there to here."

She pulled her hands out of the copper and dried them on her apron, and she was
not calm any more.

"What did you people *do?*"

---

The old woman told her that too, more or less, and then said the thing that
made up her mind for her, which was that at some point you have to choose sides.

And then she asked which part of the boy they were bleeding.

Ann took a clean sheet off the folded stack and shook it out flat across the
bench between them and put her hand down on it.

"Sheet goes on the bed this way — hem to the head, you can tell from the wear
where a man's heels go. So." She laid her palm high on it, a little left of the
middle. "It's *here*. Every morning, four days. About the size of my two hands
together."

She spread her fingers.

"Upper body. Left side. Chest, or just under the arm — high enough that if he
was on his back it ran sideways, because the edge of it's always feathered
toward the outside. Same spot, same size, and it's *sharp*-edged, not spread.
That's not a wound that's healing and breaking open. A healing wound weeps
different every day, wider then narrower, and the shape wanders. This doesn't
wander.

"Somebody opens the same place, the same way, every morning. And then somebody
else changes the bed.

"And the grey. That's not in the blood. It's *round* it — you get the red out
and the grey stays behind in a ring, like a scorch. That's what numbs your
hands."

She folded the sheet and squared it off on the stack and stood there with both
hands on it.

"You said choose sides."

She went to the end copper and lifted the lid off and started fishing the load
out into a basket with the paddle, and slapped it down wet.

"They're due at the sixth bell for that. They'll get it. I'll smile at the
white-haired bastard and take his coin."

She looked up.

"But you tell Marisette that Ann Yannick washes for that ship every morning,
and she'll go on doing it, and she'll go on *looking*. And if that boy's still
bleeding on the day of the Tourney, I want somebody to have done something
about it."

The old woman put a hand on her shoulder on the way out. Not a pat. She took
the weight of it, once, the way you grip a man's arm before he goes over a
wall.

Ann reached up and put her wet hand over it and held it there a moment, and
neither of them said anything, because there was nothing that would have
improved it.

# Chapter 12 — A Thing Being Kept

HESPER HAD SPENT THIRTY HOURS IN A GREEN ROOM ON THE PEARL WITH A DEMON
that would not stop talking to him, and he had come away with a notebook full
of very small handwriting and the settled conviction that boredom is the most
underrated interrogation technique in the profession.

He is an unremarkable man. That is deliberate and it has taken work. Plain dark
coat, physician's bag, a voice that does nothing at all, and thirty years of
being the person nobody in a room afterwards can describe.

He was in the corner of Marisette's counting room when the two of them came
back from the Forge Quarter at dusk, and he had been sitting there with a cup
of something going cold since before they arrived, and neither of them had
noticed him on the way in, which he permitted himself a small private pleasure
about.

Marisette listened to the whole of the recon without interrupting once. Eight
men. No banner. No Baron. The boat from the north-west. The barred shutter. The
barrows of clinker. One bag a day. The same place on the sheet. The cut
arming-points. And the laundress's name and the laundress's message.

At the end she said, "Eight." And then, differently, "*Eight*."

And then: "Ann Yannick will not lose that work, and she will not be alone in
that wash-house again after tomorrow. I'll see to it."

Hesper put his cup down.

"Your friend asked after the courtesan. She's alive. She'll stay alive. It's got
no interest in killing her — quite the reverse, it likes the house and it likes
being fussed over and it has been extremely helpful all afternoon, which is the
part I want to talk to you about.

"But I'd rather start with what you just said. Because a wound in the same
place, opened every morning, with a grey scorch round it that numbs the hands—"

He stopped.

"How long has that ship been at that pier?"

---

This is the part that Hesper has taught for years and never once had to use.

The Baron rode in through Caravan Square yesterday at midday. Marisette had it
from three people within the hour.

But the ship came before him. She came by sea, round the Mouth, and tied up at
that pier five days ago — Marisette knows because the Harbor Masters made a
noise about the berth and were made to stop making a noise about it.

Five days. And the laundress has been washing that bed for four.

"Then it started the day *after* the ship tied up, and the Baron was still
three days up the road when it did."

He sat forward.

"Do you see what that means? Nobody started anything here. That is a *routine*.
That is a thing that has been done to somebody every morning for however long,
in whatever house it was done in before, and they carried on doing it at sea,
and they carried on doing it here."

He picked the cup up, found it cold, put it down again.

"And they brought him by *water*. Twenty-odd knights ride three days up the
road in the open, and the thing in the litter goes round by sea in a hull that
steams. You don't do that for a champion. You do that because a road has
villages on it, and villages have people in them, and whatever is in that cabin
cannot be taken past people for three days."

Marisette said quietly: "Hesper."

"I know."

"Tell them what it said."

He was silent for a moment.

"The thing in Emmeralda spent the afternoon complaining. It's bored, it's fond
of the girl's memories, and it will talk about anything to anyone who'll sit
with it. And what it complained about, at some length, was that it had been
promised something better than a courtesan.

"It said its master's father keeps a *proper* one. And that his is 'the old
kind, the kind that remembers being a person.'"

---

The old woman grunted at that. *Like a ghost? Like a dead knight?*

And then she told him about her goddess.

Eleven nights. A woman with a wolf. A burning house. A knight in dragon-scale
who is dead and has not been told.

And the instruction.

*Lay the dragon warrior to rest.*

Hesper did not say anything for a long time. When he did, the unremarkableness
had gone out of his voice, which is a thing that happens to him perhaps twice a
decade.

"Say the last part again."

"Lay the dragon warrior to rest."

"*Rest*," he repeated. "Not destroy. Not banish. **Rest.**" He put both hands
flat on his knees. "Madam, you don't lay a demon to rest. There's nothing in a
demon to rest. You bind it or you break it and either way you may as well be
arguing with a fire.

"You lay a *dead man* to rest."

He stood up and took two steps and stopped, because it is a small room.

"'The old kind. The kind that remembers being a person.'" He turned round.
"That is a **shade**. A person who died and did not go where the dead go — kept,
and bound, and put somewhere. And you cannot keep a shade in a jar or a stone
for long; it wears through. You keep it in a *living body*, because a living
body renews itself, and the wearing-through goes into the flesh instead of the
vessel.

"Which is why somebody opens the same place on that boy's chest every single
morning. It is not torture and it is not a ritual scar. It's *maintenance*. You
bleed the host to keep the seat clean. The grey your laundress can't boil out
is what comes off the seam — that's the shade's wear coming out of him with the
blood, and it's numbing her hands through a copper of lye."

The druid girl had not moved at all.

"How long," she said, "can they keep a person like that?"

"Years," said Hesper. "If they start young enough that the body grows around
it."

She sat down.

---

He watched the old woman go over to her afterwards and put a hand on the back
of her neck, and it was not a gentle gesture, and it was exactly the right one.

"Seventeen," the girl said. "*If they start young enough.*"

"Aye."

"He was seven, Magda. I've spent ten years hoping he was alive." Her voice was
very steady and very small. "I never once thought about what for."

"I'm all right."

"You're not."

"No." A pause. "But I'll do."

---

And then the old woman asked about the bells.

Hesper had not thought about the bells. He is prepared to admit that. He had
been in a room with a demon for thirty hours and had not once considered that
anything was happening outside it.

Marisette set her cup down.

"Yes. Yesterday, just after midday. Everyone assumed it was for the Baron's
entry, because it started while the column was in Caravan Square and this city
will assume anything."

"It wasn't?"

"It was the Lady's temple on Temple Isle. And that wasn't a welcome peal, it was
ragged and out of order and it came from the water-tower, not the campanile."
Her mouth thinned. "That's the *fouling* alarm. They ring it when something goes
wrong with the sacred channel — a dead beast in the intake, a spill, a body.
It's been rung four times in my life."

Hesper said quietly: "And they stopped it inside a quarter of an hour."

"They did. Which they don't do unless somebody senior tells them to."

She looked at the old woman.

"The High Priestess Nerissa rang the alarm on the day Hanzo di Teufel entered
this city, and then somebody had it silenced before the third peal, and nobody
has said a word about it since."

She picked the pen up and put it down again.

"And her niece has red hair."

---

The old woman's face went hard at that, and she squared off at Marisette and
said the obvious thing, which is that there are only eight of them on that boat
and with enough men you could simply go and take him. She was honest that it
was not the smartest way. She said it was her way.

Marisette did not flinch and she did not laugh.

"Eight is eight. I can put twenty men at that pier before the sixth bell
tomorrow. Crowbill can put forty, and he'd do it for what's in your purse.

"And then I have twenty men against eight Dragon Knights in scale, on a deck,
at night, and I lose eleven of them and it's still even money. And by dawn every
one of them has a name and a mother on this island, and Hanzo di Teufel — who is
at this moment eating supper with the Governor's brother — knows to the hour who
came for his ship."

She spread her hands.

"It's not that it's stupid, Magda. It's that it's *last*. You only get to do it
once, and after you've done it there is nothing else you can do."

Which was correct, and Hesper let it stand, and then said the part that
actually frightened him.

"There's a worse problem. You'd be stealing a lit lamp."

He leaned forward.

"Whatever is seated in that boy is held there by something, and it is not the
ship and it is not those eight men. Take the body out and you have not freed
anyone — you have carried a bound shade into the middle of the Pearl with its
keepers coming after it, and the first thing that happens when the maintenance
stops is that the wearing-through goes somewhere else."

He looked at Marisette, then at the old woman.

"You cannot rescue him until you know what the anchor is. Otherwise you're not
rescuing a boy. You're moving a problem into a house full of women."
EOF

# Chapter 13 — Four Minutes After Noon

NERISSA HAS SERVED IN THAT TEMPLE SINCE SHE WAS NINETEEN AND IN
forty-two years the channel has never once done what it did at four minutes
after noon on the day Hanzo di Teufel entered the city.

Not fouled. She has had fouled. Fouled is a dead ox in the intake and a week of
prayers and a great deal of tedious correspondence with the Harbor Masters.

This went *thin*.

The Lady's presence in her own water went thin, the way a voice goes thin at a
distance, in the space of about ten heartbeats, and Nerissa was standing in the
tank with her sleeves rolled when it happened and she felt it go out from
underneath her hands.

So she rang the tower.

And by the third peal there was a boy from the Governor's household at her gate
with a written instruction to cease, on the grounds that the city was welcoming
a distinguished guest and the bells were causing alarm during a formal entry.

Written and sealed by Prince Emeric. Who is twenty-four years old, and
well-meaning, and who has been told by three separate men on his council this
fortnight that his uncle would like the Tourney to go smoothly.

And she stopped.

She has been furious about that for a day and a half, and the fury has nowhere
to go, because she was also right to stop. She is the High Priestess of a
temple paid for by that city's Guilds and she had *nothing* — a thin feeling in
the water and no cause she could name in front of a magistrate. If she had rung
on she would have been removed by Thursday and replaced by somebody who would
not ring at all.

She had not slept since.

---

She was sitting on the step of the great tank at midnight with her feet in the
water and her sleeves pushed up, doing nothing at all, when Lilura came down
the colonnade at a pace that was not quite running with a note in her hand and a
wolf at the gate.

Marisette does not send people to her. Ever. That was the first thing.

The second thing was that the wolf sat down in the middle of the gateway and
looked at one of the Swords until he moved his feet, and that half the watch had
made a sign at it, which is the oldest shape their faith has and Marisette knew
exactly what she was doing when she sent it.

They came in through the colonnade past the tank where the channel runs through
the temple itself, and the sound in that room is enormous, water on stone,
everywhere, no other noise at all.

Nerissa did not get up.

"Leave the wolf. It can drink. Nothing in this water will mind."

And then, with no ceremony left in her whatsoever:

"Marisette does not send people to me. Ever. So say the worst of it first and
we'll work backwards."

---

The old woman said the worst of it first.

That she had killed Hanzo's son after he bound a demon into one of the girls at
the Sylph's Embrace, and then fed his body to pigs. That working backwards from
there, they thought he had been planning to do the same thing to Nerissa's
niece. And that they thought the Dragon Knights had taken the young one's
brother ten years ago and were hosting a shade in him so that he could fight in
the Tourney in a few days.

*That's about all of it.*

She said it with blue eyes gleaming and a perfectly sweet smile.

Nerissa has spent thirty years listening to people lie in that room. She read
her all the way through and did not find a single untruth anywhere in her, which
was in some ways more alarming.

She did not move for a while. Her feet stayed in the water.

"You smiled," she said at last, "when you said *pigs*."

"Aye."

"Mm." She took her feet out of the tank and dried them on the hem of her robe
like a farmer's wife, and got up. "Good. I'd not trust a person who could say
that flatly."

Then she told them hers, and they were even.

---

They put it on the low table by the lamp and took it apart for her the way you
show somebody a bad joint of meat. The cloak. The tailor's tower. The ring. The
letter. The eleven coins.

And then the oiled silk. Five of them. Four still full.

Nerissa picked up the first twist. She did not open it. She held it, and her
thumb moved once across the silk.

"So he came into this city carrying five women in his coat," she said. "And he
spent one of them on a girl at Constantine's, and he had four left."

She opened it then, and let the hair out into the lamplight, and looked at it
for a long moment.

Then she asked the question that nobody else in four days had thought to ask,
and she asked it in a voice that had gone completely level.

"Beneath the wire. Is there a knot in it, or is it cut clean at both ends?"

The old woman turned it. The wire was at one end. The other end of the hank was
blunt and square, all the strands the same length.

"Cut clean."

"Then it was taken with shears, off a head, by somebody standing behind her."

She laid it down very carefully.

"It was not gathered off a comb or a pillow. Somebody got close enough to my
sister's daughter to put shears in her hair, and she did not scream, and she has
not told me."

She looked up.

"Her name is Sana. She's nineteen. She has been at the temple school for six
weeks and I have not seen her in three."

---

There is one more thing about that night that Nerissa has not told anybody and
does not intend to.

Her sister has had two letters from Sana in six weeks. The first came at the end
of the fourth week and it was ordinary. The second came eight days ago and it
was three lines, and it was *fine*, and her sister brought it to her and said
"she's settling," and Nerissa said "good."

Three lines.

In a hand she would know anywhere. From a girl who once wrote her eleven pages
about a heron.

She had read it and she had handed it back and she had said *good*, and then
she had gone and done something else, and the day after that the water went
thin and she rang a bell and a boy brought her a letter telling her to stop.

She stood up and started unpinning her sleeves.

"Bring the wolf," she said.

And she went down the colonnade toward the water-stair at a pace that a woman of
sixty ought not to have been able to manage, and nobody who was there said
anything about it, because everybody there had worked out what was driving her
and none of them were fools.
EOF

# Chapter 14 — The Drowned Street

GARDWEN HAD BEEN RUN AS A PAIR OF HANDS FOR TWO DAYS AND SHE WAS
starting to notice it. She had closed a wound with her palms and healed a leg
and hauled on a line and held a girl's shoulders in a boat, and at no point had
anybody — including, if she is honest, herself — remembered that she is a
priest with nine spells and a goddess who answers.

It came back to her at Corbie's, standing on a water-stair at one in the
morning looking at four hundred yards of black channel with a dull red light
moving on the far side of it.

The mistress of the school had been crying. She had opened the door and seen
Nerissa and her face had done something terrible.

"We sent to you at *dusk*," she said. "We sent a boat at dusk, Mother — didn't
it come?"

Nerissa went very still on the step. "No. Nothing came."

"Sana's gone. Since yesterday morning. We've had every girl out looking and
we've dragged the channel and I sent Bettan to the temple *myself*—"

And out across the water, on an island where there is nothing at all, a light
that was too low and the wrong colour was moving in a straight line, and
stopping, and after a while moving again.

"Magda," Gardwen said. "I can find out what's on that island from here, if the
Lady's willing to lend me the eyes for it. But it'll cost me, and whatever's
over there might feel it done."

"We need to know where the girl is. Do it."

---

She went down on one knee at the water's edge and put both hands flat in the
channel and said something under her breath that had the shape of a name in it.

And she felt the room open — the way the air goes when a door opens somewhere
else in a house.

Then it closed. Nothing came.

She sat back on her heels, breathing like she had run there.

"Too far. It's not the distance, it's — the water's all *hers* here, and I'm not
hers, and I was asking a favour in someone else's house. I got about halfway
across and it went out like a candle in a draught."

One magic point gone and nothing to show for it.

Nerissa had been watching her the whole time with an expression Gardwen could
not read at all.

"You reached," she said. It was not a question. "From the bank. Across running
water that isn't yours, at a rank you shouldn't manage."

"I didn't reach far enough."

"No." Nerissa was already unpinning her other sleeve. "You reached *at all*.
Girl — you were asking a favour in someone else's house because you were
standing on the doorstep shouting."

She stepped down into the channel until she was shin-deep and held out her hand.

"So come inside and ask properly. Take my hand and do it again, and this time
the Lady will hear where it came from."

Across the water, the dull red light stopped moving.

Then it went out.

---

There was one more thing, and it was the old woman who said it, and Gardwen has
thought about it since.

*Could she use a passion to augment it?*

A woman who has spent ten years looking for a taken child, being asked to find
a taken girl. It is not a trick. It is simply that the thing you love hardest
is a lever and nobody had thought to put it under this.

She took Nerissa's hand and went into the channel up to her knees, and the
second time was not like the first.

Her fingers locked on Nerissa's hard enough to hurt and her breath went out of
her all at once, and the priestess stood in the water and took it without
moving, the way you hold a rope.

Then Gardwen started talking, fast and flat, describing as she went.

"There's — the whole island's *humming*. Underneath. Not evil, just old, there's
a great deal of something old down under the weed and it doesn't care about us
at all. Above that. On the stone. There's a *working*."

"Say what you see," Nerissa said quietly.

"Same flavour as the chalk on her floor. Same hand. It's not finished — it's
*laid out*, like a table before dinner. It's cold. It's been cold a while.
Whoever set it hasn't come back to it in a day or more."

"Living things."

"Two moving." Her head turned, slowly, tracking. "Both of them wrong. Not
demons — *men*, but wrong, the way milk's wrong. They're low down and they're
together and they've stopped, they've gone still since the light went out—"

She stopped. Her whole face changed.

"There's a third. Not moving. Not wrong." Her voice cracked. "She's *small* in
it, Magda, she's gone right down small the way you do when you're hiding — and
she's above the other two, up high, in the stone."

Nerissa's grip tightened. "Is she alive?"

"She's *frightened*," Gardwen said. "You can't be frightened if you're not
alive."

Then she opened her eyes and looked straight across four hundred yards of black
water at an island where nothing showed at all.

"She's been there since yesterday morning and they haven't found her yet."

---

They gave Gardwen the plan and she took it, because it was the one thing that
night she was actually trained for. She crouched and drew it in the mud of the
bank with her finger.

Their boat first. They came out here somehow and it will be on the north side
with them, and if they are spooked they run for it, and then we have nothing and
they have a day's start. Take it or hole it before anything else happens. That
is the whole game — do that and they are on a two-hundred-yard rock with us.

Then Sana. She has been in that stone since yesterday morning with no water and
she is hiding from anything that moves, and if a Sword in armour comes round a
corner at her she will bolt into the weed in the dark and be lost for good. So
it is me and Ruhi who go up, and it is me who calls to her, because I am the
only one here who is not wearing anything.

Then the two men. Not before. Once the boat is gone and the girl is out they
have nowhere to be and nothing to bargain with, and we take them at our leisure,
from three sides, with a priestess and two Swords.

"Alive if they'll have it. Because whoever laid that working knows what the
anchor is."

She wiped the mud off her finger.

"That's my call. You said kill or capture — I'd say capture *hard*. But Magda,
they're wrong. I don't know what that means yet and neither does she. So don't
let anybody close with them alone."

---

Lost Isle up close is a street.

That is the thing that gets you. You can see the line of it — doorways and
window-holes at chest height, a gutter, the stub of a wellhead — and it is all
standing in four feet of black water with weed growing out of the windows. You
walk up somebody's road with the water at your thighs.

Nerissa went past her at the first junction and touched a doorframe as she
passed, briefly, the way you touch a coffin.

The tower-stub came up out of the weed eighty feet ahead, three storeys of it
still standing with one whole corner gone so you could see the floors inside
like shelves.

Gardwen put her hand flat on the stone and called up it, not loud, pitched to
carry that far and no further.

"**Sana.** Your aunt sent me. Nerissa sent me. She's stood in the water at the
corner and she's got her mace and she is *extremely* angry."

Nothing.

Then, from three floors up, very small and very hoarse:

"*Say what she calls my mother.*"

And neither of them knew.

It was the old woman who answered, and what she said was: *I don't know, but I
know you sent her an eleven page letter about a heron.*

A long silence. Long enough that Gardwen looked round.

"I don't— " The voice broke and came back. "I don't remember writing eleven
pages."

"You did. She's told it to me twice tonight and she's not a woman who repeats
herself."

Stone grit came down and landed in the water.

"Is she *really* here?"

"Aye. Stood in the channel at the corner with a mace in her belt and no robe
on."

A sound that might have been a laugh and was mostly not.

---

It took her a long time to come down, because she had been folded into a gap
between two floor-joists for a day and a half and her legs had stopped being
reliable. Twice she stopped and just breathed.

She came out into the weed-light barefoot in a school shift with her hair
chopped ragged on the left side of her head, nineteen years old and looking
about twelve.

Dark red hair. What was left of it.

She got hold of Gardwen's forearm and would not let go and talked in a rush,
too fast, hoarse.

"There were three of them yesterday. Three. There's only been two since this
morning — the other one went off in the boat before dawn and hasn't come back—"

"Slow down, lass."

"You don't understand." She was shaking. "They didn't come for me. They came for
the *place*. I only ran because I *saw* — I came out to look at the ruin like
everyone does and they were *already here*, and they had a girl from the school
with them, and she was walking with them like she knew them.

"Bettan. Her name's Bettan. She's fourteen. She's the one they sent to the
temple last night with the message."

---

The old woman asked the next question, and it was a better one than anybody
else in that drowned street would have thought of, and it cracked the whole
thing open.

*How well do you know this girl? Did she change recently?*

Sana made herself stop shaking to answer it properly, because she is clever.

"About a month ago. She was — Bettan's a *baby*. Fourteen and homesick and
cries at everything, and she'd got herself half-drowned in the misery of it, and
none of us were kind enough about it. Then she went quiet for about a week.
Properly quiet, wouldn't come down to meals, and Mistress Corliss had her in and
we all thought she'd be sent home.

"And then she came back *cheerful*.

"That's the bit. Not better — *cheerful*. And she started being lovely to
everyone. Girls she'd never spoken to. She sat with Ana Vell for a whole week
and Ana Vell is *horrible*. We all said it was nice. Mistress Corliss said it
was nice. Everyone was so pleased."

Then her voice dropped.

"She stopped wearing her shawl. In *February*. She'd sit in the window bay with
the shutter open at night doing her letters and the rest of us are three to a
bed with chilblains, and she'd say she was warm.

"And she started asking about people's families. All the time. Who's your
mother, where's your house, have you got sisters. And we all told her, because
she was being *nice*."

She looked at the ragged side of her own head.

"She did my hair. Three weeks ago. She said she could do the plait my aunt does
and she stood behind me with the scissors and she did it *beautifully*, and I
said thank you."
EOF

# Chapter 15 — A Reason to Stop

THE TWO MEN WERE SITTING SIDE BY SIDE ON THE EDGE OF A SLAB IN THE DARK
and they had been sitting there without speaking for twenty minutes, and it was
Nerissa who put a name to what that meant.

"Two men who have sat in the dark without speaking for twenty minutes are
waiting for something."

Magda went up the drowned street alone with the staff across her body and the
water pushing at her thighs. Past the punt in its doorway with a young Sword
folded down beside it who did not look up as she passed. Sixty yards.

Then the big room. Half a roof, no wall on the water side, so she could see
straight in from thirty feet: a stone floor above the waterline, a raised slab,
and a heap of dragged-up weed and muck stacked against the standing wall. Where
they had cleared it there was cut stone showing, deep-carved, and the carving
went on down under the water at the edge, and it was a great deal older than
anything else on that island.

The red-slide lantern sat on the slab, shut.

And the two of them were sitting on the edge of it, facing the water, facing
her, in the dark.

She was twenty feet away before either moved.

Then both of them turned their heads at once. Not together, like men who heard
the same thing. *At once* — the same speed, the same distance, like two doors
on one hinge.

Neither stood.

One of them — sandy, thirties, a boatman's forearms — said in an entirely
ordinary voice:

"You're not her."

And the other one, without any pause at all, in the same voice, finished it:

"—she was meant to bring the girl."

---

"No girl," Magda said. "Just little old me. All alone surrounded by big scary
warriors."

And the stone went out on the last word.

It took the sandy one high on the right arm, on the outside, and she *heard* the
bone go from twenty feet.

The arm dropped. It did not swing. It simply stopped being part of him and hung
there.

He did not make a sound. He did not look at it. He did not look at her.

Both of them stood up at the same moment, at the same speed, as if the slab had
tipped them.

And the sandy one said, conversationally, with his arm hanging off him:

"That's going to make the poling difficult."

And the other one finished: "—we'll manage."

---

What followed took about a minute and a half and Magda has been in enough
fights to know that it was not really a fight, it was a discovery.

She parried the billhook and rolled her wrists and took it out of his hands and
put it in the water, and he watched it go with mild interest. She pivoted and
put everything she had into the sandy one's ruined arm and took it apart again
below the elbow, so that what was hanging off his shoulder had bone through the
sleeve, six inches of it.

He went back one step from the force of it. Then he straightened up.

He looked at the ruin of his own arm — and this time he *did* look at it,
curiously, turning slightly to see it better, the way you would inspect a torn
coat.

And the other one, standing empty-handed in the water beside him, said: "That's
the arm gone, then."

"Mm," said the sandy one.

Neither of them had bled a drop.

Then Gardwen came out of the dark forty yards up the drowned street at a dead
run with the wolf ahead of her, and Ruhi took the billhook-man off his feet
into the black, and the two of them went under together in a boil of white — and
he did not thrash and he did not come up for air, because he did not need any.
He simply got a hand in the wolf's ruff and began, methodically, to work it
deeper.

Magda brought six feet of seasoned ash down into the boil with her whole weight
behind it and the water took nearly all of it, which is what water does, and it
landed on the back of his skull like dropping a log. It should not have been
enough for anything. But it *did* something, because for the first time all
night one of them made a movement that was not smooth, and the hand loosened,
and Ruhi got her hindquarters under her and came backwards out of his grip with
a great sheet of water and half his sleeve.

He sat up with the back of his head split and no expression at all and said:

"Oh — that was the wolf, was it."

And Gardwen put her hand out flat toward the sandy one and said three words in
the old tongue, and the water between them went still in a ring, and he stopped
mid-step with his weight forward and the ruined arm still swinging gently from
the momentum he had a second before.

His eyes went on moving. Something in him was furious about it and none of it
reached his face.

"Ohhh," he said. Just that. Perfectly pleasant.

Gardwen had gone white.

"It shouldn't hold," she said. "Magda — that's *Hold Person*. There shouldn't be
enough person in him to grip."

---

The other one got hold of Magda in the end and would not let go, and Ruhi took
his leg out from under him, and because he would not let go she went down into
the black with him. He lay on the bottom of a drowned street holding her
forearm, not struggling, not pushing her down, simply waiting, because he did
not need to breathe and he had all night.

Her face was about eight inches under.

Gardwen put everything she had into one word and the hand opened — all four
fingers at once, like a catch releasing — and Magda came up off the bottom into
air and lamplight coughing canal.

He sat up beside her with his hands open in his lap, palms turned upward, and
looked at them.

"That wasn't me," he said, with what might almost have been interest.

---

And here is the part that is not a fight story.

He got up. He did not come at her again. He waded, unhurried, toward the slab
and the uncovered stone behind it, with his hands still open at his sides — and
Nerissa was between him and it, and she did not move, and neither did he.

They looked at each other across four feet of black water.

Then he said: "You're the Lady's, aren't you."

"I am."

"Good," he said. "She'll want to see this."

And he stepped sideways, out of her path, and gestured with an open hand at the
cut stone they had spent a day digging out of the weed.

Magda came out of the water and planted her back foot in the mud and swung the
way you swing at a fence post that has offended you.

Six feet of ash across the temple. Nothing between it and the bone.

His head went sideways past where a head goes. He dropped straight down where he
stood, with no stagger, and the water took him and closed over.

The body did not float.

Nerissa did not move. She was standing exactly where she had been, mace up,
four feet away, with her mouth slightly open.

She lowered the mace slowly.

"He had stopped," she said. Not accusing. Just stating it, the way a woman reads
a figure back to check she has it right. "He had stopped, and he was showing me
the stone."

---

Magda went for the other one next. The held one. The one who could not move.

She broke his good arm with the staff while he was frozen and could not flinch,
and he watched the staff come down and go back up and there was nothing behind
his eyes at all, and he said, "You've done that twice now."

Nerissa came through the water and stopped beside her. She was careful not to
take hold of her arm.

"Magda." Very level. "The other one had put his hands down. I don't say you were
wrong — I don't know what these things are and neither do you. But I will not
stand here and watch you take a helpless man apart piece by piece, so tell me
plainly what you want him for, and then we'll do that thing and stop."

And Magda, from somewhere a long way down inside the noise, said the only true
thing available to her:

*I'm a berserker. That means I fight until someone convinces me to stop.*

---

Nerissa has spent thirty years in a room where people lie to her, and she has
been watching this woman since midnight, and she read her completely.

Whatever she had been going to say next, she did not say it.

She changed her footing. She stopped standing like a woman about to remonstrate
and started standing like a woman at the side of a horse that is still running.

"Ah," she said. Very quietly. "*Ah.* You're not deciding anything, are you."

She lowered the mace all the way and let it hang.

"I've seen this twice. Once in a man at the Shoals after a fire, and once in my
own father." Her voice stayed completely even — not soothing, not raised, the
pace of somebody reading a list. "You're not cruel. You've simply not been given
a reason to stop yet, and nobody in this water has thought to give you one.
They've only told you to."

She moved round until she was in front of her rather than beside her, slowly, so
that Magda could see her do it.

"So. Here's the reason.

"Sana is in a boat forty yards behind us, nineteen years old, with her hair cut
off, watching. That girl has spent a day and a half in a hole in the dark being
brave, and what she can see from there is an old woman breaking a man who can't
move.

"That's it. That's the whole reason. Not the man — he's nothing to me and I'd
hang him tomorrow. **Her.**"

She held out one open hand. Not to take the staff. Just open.

Magda did not answer, and she did not lower the staff either.

She just stopped.

Water running off her, breathing like a bellows, everything in her face still
exactly where it had been — and standing entirely still in the middle of it,
which is not the same thing as being calm, and everybody there knew the
difference.

Nobody asked her for the staff. Nerissa did not move her hand away and did not
reach any closer.

Corvin and Ash roped the prisoner in silence, working around the ruined arm
rather than through it, which was more care than Magda would have taken.

And when the ring of stillness let go and the man came back to life mid-step and
found himself trussed and sitting, he looked up, and found her, and smiled for
the first time all night.

"You're the one who did the boy in the canal," he said. "The face like a spade.
He described you before he went."
EOF

# Chapter 16 — The Man Who Said Yes to a Coat

IT WAS NOT A SLAB. NERISSA GOT THE LAMP FULL OPEN AND HELD IT OUT OVER THE
cleared patch and what they had spent a day digging out of the weed turned out
to be the top of a stair.

Four steps showing, cut into the same worked stone, going down at an angle and
disappearing into black water that did not reflect the lamp the way the rest of
the channel did. Weed hanging off the edges where it had been hacked away.

And the steps were *swept*. There was no silt on them, and there should have
been a foot of it.

Something had been using them.

Nerissa went down on her knees in the water beside it with the lamp held low and
put both palms on the carving and closed her eyes, and she could tell them
exactly what it *did* and not one thing about what it *meant*, and you could
watch that bother her more than the corpse in the water.

"It's a door. Not for people. For the drowned."

She traced the carving with two fingers, following it down, and her hand went
under the surface and kept going.

"There are old stories about the Northern Isles going under. Not one flood — a
slow one, over generations, and everything in them that died went down with the
streets. And whoever cut this cut it so that what stayed in the water had
somewhere to *go*. A way out. You lay them to rest through a thing like this."

She looked up, and there was something urgent in it.

"It isn't a Lady-stone. It's older than her presence in this channel and it
isn't in any doctrine I've read in forty years, and I could not tell you who cut
it or to what."

Behind them, roped and sitting in the shallows, the prisoner said pleasantly:

"That's what he went to fetch the boat for. You'd best hurry — he's been gone
since before dawn, and he'll not be coming back alone."

---

His name was Ellick Sarn, and he had to think about it, which was the
unsettling part.

"Ellick," he said at last. "Ellick Sarn. That's — yes. That's right, I'm fairly
sure. I poled the Forge Quarter run. Timber mostly, sometimes charcoal, and a
woman called Tam who I think was—"

He stopped. Frowned very slightly at the sky.

"There was something about Tam. It's gone."

The boat creaked. Ash rowed. Nobody had told him to start again and nobody told
him to stop.

"They came to me in the winter. Not the young lord — the *quiet* one, him that's
gone for the boat. He asked did I know the Northern Isles and I said better than
any man breathing, which was true, and he paid me eleven marks to take him out
to the drowned streets four times and say nothing. I did say nothing. I want
that noted. I kept my end."

"And then?"

"And then on the fourth time he said, would I like to not be cold any more."

He said it perfectly evenly.

"I've been cold on that water for thirty-one years, missus. Every winter. Hands
gone the colour of the sky. And he said it like he was offering me a coat."

His head tipped a little.

"And I said yes. That's the part everyone wants to skip past. Nobody did
anything to me that I didn't stand still for."

Sana had both hands over her mouth.

"What went in you?"

"Something out of the stairs." A shrug that moved the whole trussed body oddly.
"It's not unkind. It doesn't want anything much. It likes the digging." He
considered it. "It's got a lot more of me than it had at Candlemas. That's the
trade — it warms you and it *wears* you, and you don't notice the wearing
because the part that would notice is the part it's wearing."

Then, conversationally:

"You'll be wanting to know about the one on the ship. That's a different thing
entirely. That one's *furnished*."

---

He told them the rest because he was asked and because he had no particular
reason not to, with the flat helpfulness of a man giving directions.

The quiet one wants the door open. That is the whole of the digging. Four days,
and it wants to be open before the Tourney and not after — he was very hard
about that. There is a tide thing in it. He said something about the water
being *thin* on the day and it having to be while it is thin.

Nerissa's head came round at that. "He said *thin*?"

"His word."

And the door is for taking something *out*.

"That's the bit I did understand, because I asked him — I said is this for
putting things in, like you did with me, and he laughed. Only time I saw him
laugh. He said no, Ellick, that's the easy way and any fool with a knife can do
that. He said the hard thing is getting one *out* whole and putting it somewhere
better.

"Because you can't keep a thing in a boy for ever. He said that too. They wear
through. He said the one they've got has nearly used up what it was put in."

He turned his head and looked at Gardwen for the first time.

"That's why they came here. It's not a rescue they're worried about, love. It's
a *removal*. He's outgrown the boy and they've somewhere better to put him."

And Sana, very quietly, from the far thwart:

"...The girls with the red hair aren't for the demon. They're spares."

---

And then, at last, the name.

"Mine's *content*, see. It got a boatman who was cold and it's warm now and it
likes lifting stone. There's no fight in it. That's why I'm still able to sit
here and talk to you about Tam and nearly remember her."

He nodded north-west, toward where the black hull sat steaming at its pier.

"That one *fights*."

Ash stopped rowing. Nobody told him to start.

"I was aboard twice, carrying. You can hear it through the deck. Not screaming —
worse than that, it's *arguing*. Goes on for hours. Two voices out of one throat
having a row, and one of them's a boy and one of them isn't, and the one that
isn't sounds like a man who's been told to do something he thinks is
dishonourable."

He shook his head slowly.

"That's what the morning cut's for. It's not just the wear. It's to keep it
*tired*. You bleed a man to keep him from arguing.

"They've a name for it. Old-sounding. The quiet one says it like a title, not a
name." He worked his jaw, hunting for it. "Thoo— *Thuban*. Thuban something.
Eta, maybe. He's a knight out of the dragon wars and he's been in one thing or
another for a very long while, and he doesn't want to be, and he never has."

He looked around the boat at all of them.

"You keep saying *rescue the boy*. I'd think about that. There's two in there,
and only one of them's been asking to get out."

---

Nobody rowed. The boat drifted.

Nerissa said it first, slowly, the way you read something off a wall.

"Eleven nights. A knight in dragon-scale who is already dead and does not know
it." She turned to look at Magda. "And *lay the dragon warrior to rest*. Not the
boy. She never once showed you the boy.

"She showed you the **passenger**."

Her hand had gone to her breast.

"Magda — your goddess has been telling you the answer since before you left home
and none of us could hear it because we were all looking at the child."

Gardwen had gone absolutely still in the bow.

"Say the rest of it," she said. "Say it out loud so I've heard it."

Nerissa did.

"If Thuban Eta is laid to rest, he leaves. And whatever is left in that body is
your brother, and only your brother." A pause. "It is not a rescue. It's a
*funeral*. And the boy walks out of it because the funeral wasn't for him."

Ellick, helpfully, into the silence:

"That's what the door's for, mind. Same door. Only the quiet one wants him
lifted *out and moved*, and you want him lifted out and let *go*. You'll be
wanting the same night and the same stair as him, then. And the same thin
water."

And Magda, who had understood perhaps a third of it, said so, and Nerissa
stopped using her temple voice and explained it on three fingers like a woman
laying out a cart's load; and at the end of it Gardwen said, without turning
round:

"And either way my brother comes out of it empty. Alive, and empty, and his
own."

"Told you it was a funeral," said Ellick.

The sky over the Forge Quarter had gone properly grey.

One day. The Tourney was tomorrow.
