# Chapter 17 — Nobody Ever Came Back

THORNE HAS SAT IN THE SAME CORNER OF THE MOIST OYSTER FOR ELEVEN YEARS
and buys nobody a drink, and there is a widely held view in that house that he
is a harmless old man who tells stories, which he has worked extremely hard to
encourage.

He was Order of the Lake for thirty-one years before he was not, and they do not
throw you out of that for nothing.

He watched her cross the room and he had her before she reached the table.

The mail under the borrowed cloak. The mud on the hem. The particular grey-green
weed dried on her boot that grows in exactly one place in this city.

He moved his cup six inches to the left, which is an invitation, and said:

"Sit down, mother. You've had a night."

She had not said a word yet.

"Two nights, at a guess. One of them wet. One of them worse.

"I'll tell you what *I've* had, since you're wondering. I've had a girl in here
at seven this morning saying Constantine's house has a physician in it and won't
say why. I've had a lad off Renko's cart telling anyone who'll listen that some
old woman knows about horses. And about an hour ago I had two of the Baron's
people asking whether anybody's seen a big northern woman with a face like a
spade."

He looked up.

"I said no. I'd like it noted that I said no *before* I knew what I was saying
no about, which is the sort of thing I'll want paying for eventually."

---

She offered to pay him to tell them yes, and then to tell them a few other
things besides, and Thorne put his hand flat on the table and stopped her.

Because people never understand what they are buying, and he has got tired of
finding out afterwards.

"You've just offered to pay me to tell a man a lie.

"I don't sell lies, mother. I sell *stories*, and the difference is that a story
has to hold up when it's repeated by an idiot in a different tavern three days
later. You can't just hand me a falsehood and a coin. You have to give me
something that has the *shape* of true.

"A lie collapses. A story goes and gets *itself* believed."

Two conditions, and they are not negotiable. He will not put a name on anybody
who would hang for it — if the story wants a body it uses a dead one or a made-up
one, never a living neighbour. And he is told what it is *for*; not everything,
but enough that if it goes wrong he knows whether he ought to be sorry.

"Meet those and my price is small and strange: I want the *true* version.
Afterwards. All of it, in order, told to me once and never written down.

"So. What do you want Blau to hear?"

---

And then she did the thing that nobody ever does.

She gave him the true one first.

A randy young nobleman carves up a courtesan to put a lust-demon in her, gets
the charm right and botches the escape, falls in the canal and catches a
slingshot to the temple.

Thorne went very still while she talked. When she had finished he did not say
anything for a while. He turned the chalk over three times.

"You've just done the thing nobody ever does," he said at last. "You've handed
me the *true* one first."

He was, if he is honest, faintly offended by how well it worked.

"And it's better than anything I'd have built, because every part of it is
checkable. There *is* a physician at Constantine's. There *are* four houses on
the Pearl that won't take di Teufel coin by tonight once the Pearl hears why.
There *was* a young lord in that house on the night, and there are eleven people
who saw him come in and none who saw him leave.

"That's not a story I have to sell. That's a story that sells itself house to
house and comes back to me by Thursday with improvements."

Then he held up a finger.

"But you've a problem in it and you've walked straight past it. The truest
version has an old northern woman with a sling in it. And there is a man on a
ship asking after an old northern woman with a face like a spade.

"So here's the craft of it. Everything you told me stays *exactly as it is*. And
the stone comes out of nowhere.

"He fell in the canal and *the water took him*, and the Lady's channel does not
care for demon-work, and a man who profanes a Pearl house with a lust-demon and
then goes into the sacred water — well." He spread his hands. "That's not even a
lie, is it. That's a *sermon*. Half this city will believe it before I've
finished saying it, and the other half will believe it harder because the temple
hasn't denied it."

He finally drank.

"As for how I feel about the good Baron." Something moved behind his face. "I
was Order of the Lake for thirty-one years, mother. I know what a stair under
Lost Isle is for. You didn't mention one. You didn't have to — you've got weed
on your boot that only grows in the drowned streets, and you came in here asking
about the dead.

"Tell me I'm wrong."

---

She laughed and said he was not wrong, and gave him the rest of it, and nudged
the girl into telling hers.

Gardwen told it the way she told Marisette, with no shape to it. Nine of them.
The counting in the morning. The brother who was not there.

And then the name.

Thorne put the chalk down.

"Say that again."

"Thuban Eta. The knight in the boy."

---

Here is a thing about being Order of the Lake for thirty-one years. There is a
great deal of it you can put down afterwards, and a small amount that is simply
in you, and one of the things that is simply in Thorne is the second-year lesson
about the Eta company.

"Thuban Eta was real. That's not a story name. That's a *muster roll* name.

"The Dragon Kings had knight-companies, and the Eta were one of them — the
letter's a company mark, not a family. And Thuban is the one they teach you
about in your second year, because of how he died.

"He wouldn't burn a town. That's the whole of it. The company was ordered to
fire a valley and he refused, and argued it in front of the others, and about a
third of them came round to him. So the ones who hadn't took him out on the
water at night to talk it over, and they put him over the side in his mail with
his hands tied.

"Drowned. By his own company. For refusing an order that even *they* thought was
filthy — that's the part that damns them. They knew he was right and they killed
him for making them know it."

He looked up.

"And that is *exactly* the kind of dead man you can bind. You don't hold a shade
with iron, mother. You hold it with the thing it can't put down." He tapped his
own chest. "You keep him in the moment of it. Tied hands and cold water and his
own men's faces looking down at him — you keep him *there*, and he'll pull
against it for a hundred years and never once get out, and every time he pulls
you can use the pulling."

Gardwen said, very low: "That's what's in my brother."

"That's what's in your brother. And it has been for ten years, and it has hated
every hour of it, because a man who wouldn't fire a valley is not going to enjoy
being made into a champion."

He pushed the chalk away.

"Your goddess said *lay him to rest*, and everyone at this table has been
thinking that means a door and a ritual. It might not. You don't lay that man
down with a stair.

"You lay him down by *undoing the betrayal*. By someone standing in front of him
and taking it back on behalf of the ones who did it.

"The door gets him out of the boy. Something else has to make him *willing to
go*."

---

The old woman told him he was mad.

Which is fair, and is the correct response, and he was pleased with her for it.

*That was a thousand years ago. Who the fuck could do that now? The kings
themselves and all their armies were laid to rest. Every child knows that.*

"You're right," Thorne agreed. "There's no company left to answer for it and no
descendants worth the name. If it wants the *actual men*, it's impossible and we
may as well go home."

He held up a finger.

"But that's not how a debt like that works. It never wanted the men. It's been a
thousand years — Thuban knows they're dust. What holds him isn't a grudge
against nine specific bastards.

"It's that **nobody ever came back for him.**

"He went over the side and the water closed and that was the end, and no
company, no order, no god, no sister — *nobody* has stood over that water since
and said 'this was wrong, and he was ours, and we're taking him home.'"

And then the druid girl said the thing that finished it, slowly, in a voice she
had not used all night.

"There's a thing we do in the wood, for a beast that's died badly. In a snare, or
under a fall, where it couldn't get free. You don't pray it away. You go and you
*sit* with it, and you say out loud that it wasn't right, and then you carry it.
That's the whole rite. Somebody has to actually pick the thing up.

"It doesn't need the ones who did it. It needs somebody willing to *stand where
they stood* and answer for it. Not because it's theirs — because they're the one
who turned up."

Thorne let that sit exactly as long as it deserved.

Then he laid his card down.

"And who exactly do we know that serves the god of the ones nobody sings about?

"Not the battle-dead, you said. The other kind. In the bed, in the byre, in the
bad winter. A knight drowned in the dark by his own friends for refusing to burn
a village, and left out of every song since, in every land, for a thousand
years.

"Mother — whose *is* he, if he isn't hers?"

---

Nobody said anything for a moment.

Then the old woman said "Fuck me," and then "Hel," and then, with the particular
exhausted affection of a woman who has been outmanoeuvred by her own deity:

"The old lady has her ways. OK. I'll do it."

Thorne picked up his cup and finally drank from it properly, like a man closing
a ledger.

"Well," he said. "There it is."

---

And then, before she left, she took her kettle helm off and set it on the table
and leaned in across the cup and put her forehead against his.

Gently. For her.

There was still an audible knock.

Thorne sat back with his eyes watering slightly and a hand going to his brow,
and he was not displeased at all.

"*Ohh*," he said. "That's a northern thing."

"That's a northern thing."

"I've read about that." He worked his jaw. "It reads considerably better than it
feels."

The girl mopping had stopped mopping. The dog under the table had reconsidered
its position entirely. Gardwen had put her face in her hand.

Thorne straightened his collar with enormous dignity.

"Thirty-one years in the Order, two of them at the Governor's table, and no one
has ever done that to me. I've been given a chain of office and a commendation
from a Prince and neither of them landed like that."

He picked the chalk back up.

"Go on then. Get out of my corner."

And as she was standing, without looking up:

"Mother. When they ask me this morning — and they will — I'm going to say I've
never seen you.

"That's on the house."

# Chapter 18 — Terms

CROWBILL IS WIRY AND FORGETTABLE AND WOULD BE INVISIBLE IN ANY CROWD IN
the world except for a small crow inked on the back of his right hand, and he
was eating bread and cheese off a paper at his desk when they brought the pig
woman in, and he did not stop.

"The pig woman," he said. "Sit down. You've had a busy two days and I've heard
four versions and none of them agree about the wolf."

He took another bite.

"Go on, then."

She asked him whether he had ever wondered what was on the Baron's ship.

"Every day since it tied up," he said. "That's not a boast, that's my *trade*. A
foreign lord brings a deep-water hull into a canal city and moors it at a
private pier and lets nobody aboard — of course I've thought about what's on it.
So has every fence between here and the Shoals."

He wiped his fingers on the paper.

"And here's why it's still sat there with everything on it.

"**One**: ten men in scale and one way up. **Two**: it's a *ship*, so if it goes
badly they don't have to win, they just have to cast off, and then I've lost
people for nothing. **Three** —" he held up the third finger and looked at her
over it "— a Baron. Not a merchant, not a guild. A man with a border tower and
three hundred men and a long memory, who would spend two years and a lot of
money finding out who did it, because that's what men like him are *for*."

He sat back.

"Which is three good reasons, and you didn't come here without knowing them. So
you've got something that answers all three, or you wouldn't have got past my
door.

"So let's not do the part where you sell it to me. Just tell me the two things I
actually need. When is she sailing? And what do you want off her that isn't
cargo?"

---

She told him. Tonight, and everything on that ship is out of this city for ever
after that. And what she wanted off it was the champion.

Crowbill put the bread down.

He has been reading people across that desk for twenty years and he could not
read her, and he said so, because it was true and because it was the sort of
thing that tells the other party something useful about your position.

"See, now, that's a strange thing to want, and I can usually tell when someone's
shading me and I can't tell with you, which I don't enjoy." He tapped the desk
twice with one knuckle. The crow moved. "The cargo I understand. Cargo is cargo.
But the fighting man is the one item on that ship the Baron will actually
*chase*. Gold he replaces. A champion the day before the Lady's Tourney? That's
him publicly beaten in front of every Guild in this city.

"So you're not asking me to rob a lord. You're asking me to *humiliate* one, and
put my name on it, in exchange for goods I'd have to fence quietly for a year."

He leaned back.

"So here's my question, and I want the true answer, because I'm not putting
forty men on a pier for a story.

"**What's wrong with him?**

"Nobody hides a swordsman. You hide a thing that would *lose you everything* if
it were seen. And whatever it is, it's coming into my city on my boats and I'll
be the one holding it."

---

"It's not a humiliation," she said. "It's a rescue."

And then she told him, flatly, with no arrangement to it: a general dead a
thousand years, put into the body of that young woman's brother, bled every
morning to keep him quiet.

"Seventeen," Gardwen said quietly, from the side.

Crowbill looked at her, and then back at the old woman, and did not say anything
for a while.

Then: "A boy with a dead general in him."

"Aye."

"Being kept on a ship for it."

"Bled every morning to keep him quiet. There's a laundress on that pier who's
been boiling the sheets for five days and can tell you the shape of the cut."

He stood. He went to the window, which looks at a wall, and stood there with his
hands behind his back.

"I've a rule," he said to the wall. "I've a few. Most of them are about money and
one of them isn't, and the one that isn't is why I've still got a city to work
in.

"Children aren't stock. You don't sell them, you don't use them, and you don't
let anyone do it on my water and call it business."

He turned round.

"Your Marisette knows that rule. It's why we get on."

He came back to the desk and did not sit.

"So. I'd have done it for the cargo anyway. Now I'll do it *properly*, which is
different, and here are my terms — and they're not money.

"**One.** Everything on that ship that isn't the boy is mine, and nobody counts
it but me.

"**Two.** My name is nowhere. Not in the temple's version, not in your
storyteller's, not in a Governor's warrant if you ever get one. Tonight was
*thieves*, and this city has plenty.

"**Three** — and this is the one I care about."

He put one finger on the desk.

"When it's done and the boy's out and whatever you're doing with the ghost is
done, the High Priestess of the Lake Lady stands up and says publicly that the
canal folk kept her water clean. Not me. Not names. *The canal folk.*

"Because I have four hundred people who get moved on and blamed and dredged out
of the channel, and one sentence from that woman is worth more to them than a
Baron's whole hold."

He raised an eyebrow.

"Can you get me that?"

---

Then he asked the practical question, which is how forty poled men are supposed
to get past ten men in scale up one ramp, having already explained that this is
how people die.

And the old woman said: "You're the river men, I'm just a pig farmer."

And then she said the thing that made his face become interested for the first
time in the conversation.

"She has to leave to sail. Once she's off that pier she's not got four men at
the bollards and four at a ramp — she's just a hull in the dark with a channel
round her, and the channel's yours."

"It is." He was already pulling a scrap of paper over. "And she cannot get out
to sea without going through the **Mouth**, and the Mouth on the ebb is a mile
of slow water with the harbour lights behind it, and I have men who have been
going up the sides of anchored hulls in that stretch since they were nine years
old."

He drew.

"You don't need forty. You need *twelve*, in six punts with no lights, and you
take her from three sides at once while she's making way and everyone aboard is
looking forward.

"And the best of it — a ship under way has half her people at the ropes and the
rest looking where she's *going*. Nobody watches a wake."

Then he stopped drawing.

"One problem, and it's yours to solve, not mine."

He tapped the waterline on his own sketch.

"That hull *steams*. Whatever your Baron's got in her, it cooks the water where
it touches, and there's a dead slick round her the whole way out. I've had a man
put his hand in that water off the stern two days ago on a dare and he's still
got no feeling in three fingers.

"My people go up the outside of hulls. They cannot climb *that* one — not at the
waterline, and that's where you have to start.

"So. Between the lot of you, can anybody make forty feet of that hull cold
enough to touch for the four minutes it takes to get twelve men over the rail?"

---

Gardwen ruled herself out immediately, which she was right to do — she does bark
and bones and bleeding and could not cool a kettle — and then named the two who
could, and what each would cost.

Nerissa could try. It is her channel and that hull is wounding it, and she felt
it go thin from a mile off. But she had already gone past what she was sure of
once that day. She would be doing it from a boat, in the dark, in a moving
channel, against something that had been fouling her water for five days.

"Meaning she'd probably do it and it'd probably cost her more than she'd tell
us."

And then the other lot, that nobody had said out loud yet.

"The Mermaid's Court. Their chambers are *under Lost Isle*. We've been standing
on the roof of them all night and the only reason nothing came up those stairs
at us is that nothing chose to."

Crowbill set his pen down.

"**Ravella.** Siren's Call. Half of one and half of us, and she brokers for them
when they can be bothered to want anything. I've done business with her twice
and both times I came off worse and knew it at the time."

He looked up.

"She'd be able to. Water that's been made wrong is exactly their complaint, and
that hull's been bleeding into their front hall for five days."

A shrug.

"But you'd be asking the Court for a favour, mother. They don't take coin and
they don't take gratitude. They take *arrangements*."

---

Ravella came into the little room off the landing stage at the Siren's Call ten
minutes after Crowbill's name got them into it. Handsome, forty-ish, unhurried,
faint scales at the hairline that could be a trick of the light, and fingers
very slightly webbed which she made no attempt to hide, which is itself a
statement about who she thinks you are.

"You're the pig woman. You've had a remarkable two days and I've heard *nine*
versions." She pushed a cup across. "Crowbill sent you, which means you want
something from under the water. So let's save an hour: what do you want, and
what have you got that the Court might conceivably care about?"

The old woman said: "The demonologist Hanzo di Teufel and his festering shitpile
of a barge."

Ravella's cup stopped halfway to her mouth. She set it down without drinking.

"Say the rest."

And when she had heard it, the broker's smile went off her face entirely and
what was underneath it was much older and much less friendly.

"Let me tell you what 'thin' means from underneath, since nobody up here ever
asks.

"There are people living in the deep channels of this city who were here before
the causeway. Not many. They keep out of the way and they mind their own
business and their whole lives are *water that behaves*. And for five days there
has been a hot wound in the eastern channel that pushes ahead of the tide, and
every one of them has had to move — old, young, sick — and two haven't managed
it."

She said the last part very flatly. Outside the window the canal had gone glassy
in a strip about four feet wide.

"So yes. We mind."

Then she picked the cup up again and the broker came back, which was somehow
worse.

"But you'd have got that from a fishwife. Here's the part you'd have paid for.

"**They came down our stairs.**

"Under Lost Isle. Four days ago, three men with a lantern, digging out a door
that has been left shut and unmarked since before this city had a name. And they
*took* things off it — the small confused ones that sit near the threshold and
don't go through, which are ours to look after and nobody else's.

"The Court could not stop them. Won't say why and I've stopped asking. So we
have had our water burned and our threshold robbed in the same week, and we
have been able to do precisely nothing about either.

"And now an old woman walks into my house smelling of Lost Isle weed with a
dead captain's axe.

"How many of the taken have you seen?"

"Two."

"Where."

"One's dead. I put an axe through his head on Lost Isle last night and he went
face-down in the drowned street and didn't float. The other's roped in a cellar
under the Lake Lady's temple with two Swords on the door, and he talks.
Boatman. Ellick Sarn."

Something passed over her face at the name and she did not explain it.

"Ellick. He poled the Forge Quarter run. He carried for us twice."

She was quiet for a moment.

"Then you already have both of them and you didn't know what you had."

She sat back.

"Here is the arrangement, and I'll speak for the Court because they'll agree and
because there isn't time to go down and ask.

"**Give them back.**

"That's the whole price. Not the ship, not the Baron, not your boy — those are
your business and the Court doesn't care about a dead general or a barony. The
two you've got are *ours*, and they need to go back through that threshold and
be let go properly, and until they are they're neither ours nor dead nor alive,
and that is an obscenity."

She looked at her very directly.

"You should understand what you're agreeing to. The thing in Ellick Sarn came
off our threshold and it goes back to it. What's left of Ellick is — " a pause,
and she chose the word carefully " — *thin*. There isn't a version of this where
a boatman walks home to his supper. He said yes to a warm coat in a cold winter
and he has been paying for it ever since, and the kindest end available to him
is the right one.

"You'd be taking him to that stair and standing there while it's done."

She turned her cup again.

"And I understand that's your trade."

Then, briskly, the broker again:

"Do that, and I will come out to the Mouth myself tonight and put my hands on
that hull and make it cold enough to climb. For as long as you need, not four
minutes. And I will bring people who can be in the water beside it while it
happens, which your Crowbill's boys cannot.

"Two dead men, laid down properly, for one cold ship. Do we have an
arrangement?"

"Don't know where the second one is," said the old woman. "But sure. I'll do
what I can."

Ravella took her hand anyway. Her grip was cool and slightly damp and a great
deal stronger than it looked.

"You don't need to know where he is. He went into a drowned street off Lost Isle
with an axe wound in his head and did not float. He's in our water. We'll have
him on that threshold by dark and you won't have to look for him — you'll have
to *stand* there, which is the part that matters."

She stood and smoothed her dress.

"I'll be at the Mouth from the eighth bell with four of mine. And Magda — when
you're standing over those two tonight, say it out loud. Whatever your goddess's
words are.

"The Court will be listening from underneath and they will want to hear that
somebody up here said it."

---

Nerissa's answer came back across the water in her own square hand, on a scrap
of paper the size of a palm, carried by a gondolier who would have done it for
nothing.

> *Tell the crow he shall have his sentence — from the temple steps, at the
> Tourney, in front of the Governor and every Guild in this city. **The canal
> folk kept the Lady's water clean.** Those words, that place, and I will not
> soften them.*
>
> *I would have said it years ago if anyone had thought to ask me. That he had
> to buy it is a shame on my order, not on him.*
>
> *— V.*

# Chapter 19 — The Reversal

HESPER HAD NOT LEFT THAT GREEN ROOM IN THIRTY HOURS AND WHEN HE FINALLY
came out of it he had the expression of a man who has just told a demon that he
will be back shortly and been told *of course you will, dear.*

He had bought it a syllable at a time and he laid it out in a passage on the
Pearl with the door shut behind him.

"You cannot simply pull a shade out and let it go. It has to have somewhere to
be, even for a moment, or it goes into the nearest living thing standing over it
— which will be one of you.

"So a removal needs three parts. The door. The *thing it comes out of*. And the
**anchor** — something that already holds a piece of him, that he'll consent to
sit in while he's between."

He looked at her.

"The Baron carries a locket. It's the small anchor, the working one, and he's
had it on his person since before they left the border. That's what keeps the
daily ritual holding.

"But that's not the primary. And the thing in that room told me what is, this
morning, while complaining about how much *nicer* it would be to have a proper
one."

He took a breath.

"They've got his bones. Thuban's. In the Baron's border tower, where they've
been for a hundred years, because you cannot hold a man like that with anything
less."

Magda laughed. It was not a good laugh.

"Well. How the fuck are we going to do that?"

---

Hesper did not laugh back. He looked at her for a moment and then something
happened behind his eyes.

"Wait. Say the bit about the quiet one again. The timing."

"Gone since before dawn yesterday. Ellick reckoned four hours out to the border
tower and four back with a fair wind."

"And it's been thirty-six."

His hands came up.

"So he is not *at* the tower. He has been there, and he is on his way *back*,
and he is late because he is carrying something heavy and he will not risk it in
bad water."

Gardwen got there half a beat before Magda did.

"He's bringing the bones *here*."

"He has to." Hesper was talking fast now. "They cannot do a removal without the
primary anchor, and the primary anchor has sat in a border tower for a century
because nobody dared move it. But they've run out of boy. So for the first time
in a hundred years, Thuban Eta's bones are out of that tower and on the water,
and they are coming to Purewater, and they are going to the one place the work
can be done.

"Which is a stair under Lost Isle that you are already sitting on with a dozen
Swords of the Lake."

Nobody said anything for a second.

Then Hesper added it, quietly, and it landed like a stone:

"And Magda — you were never going to be able to lay that man to rest without
them. You know that. You've buried enough people."

"You don't put a man down without his bones."

"No. You don't."

He almost smiled, and it was an awful smile, because he is a man who has just
watched a problem turn inside out.

"They have spent a hundred years keeping the one thing you need locked in a
tower you could never reach.

"And tonight they are rowing it to you."
EOF

# Chapter 20 — The Mouth

THE MOUTH IS A MILE OF SLOW BLACK WATER WHERE THE HARBOUR LETS OUT TO SEA
with the city's lights behind you and nothing at all ahead, and the ebb had
started, and you could feel the pull of it under the punt, patient and enormous.

Six punts, no lights. Crowbill's twelve were exactly what he had promised: canal
men in dark wool, no armour worth the name, barefoot, each with a short blade
and a coil of line and a grapnel wrapped in sacking so it could not ring. They
talked in a low register that does not carry over water. None of them had asked
what was on the ship.

Crowbill himself was not there. Of course he was not.

Ravella was. She was in the bow of Magda's punt in something that was not a
dress, with four of hers in the water alongside — you could not see them, but
occasionally the surface did something a surface should not.

Gardwen was amidships with her staff across her knees. Ruhi would not get in the
boat and was somewhere on the north bank keeping pace, which nobody had been
able to prevent.

Magda was in mail, with a dead captain's axe across her back and fourteen stones
in the pouch, and she had said something about not being a very good swimmer and
possibly needing help, and had meant it as a joke, and it was in fact the plain
truth. Swim 27 and a hauberk. If she went into that channel she was going
straight to the bottom of it. The nearest canal man grinned at her in the dark
and tapped the grapnel line. *You go up from the boat, mother. Feet dry.*

---

Then the lights changed at the pier end of the harbour, a mile back. A lantern
up and down. Another.

She had cast off.

A long time later — twenty minutes, half an hour, an age of sitting in the dark
— she came down the channel under a scrap of canvas and the sweeps, unlit but
for a single shaded lamp at the stern, and she was enormous close to, and even
at two hundred yards you could see the white where her hull met the water and
hear the *hiss* of it carrying flat across the surface.

Ravella turned round in the bow.

"When I go in, that water will kill anyone who isn't mine for about a minute
while it turns. After that it's cold and it's climbable and I can hold it as
long as I'm conscious." She waited. "So say when, and be sure. Because I only
get to do this once tonight."

Two hundred yards. One-fifty. A hundred. Eighty. Men on her deck, forward,
looking where she was going.

"**Now.**"

Ravella did not answer. She went over the side without a splash and the water
took her like it was expecting her.

---

The water went first.

You do not see her do it. What you see is the white line along that hull *stop*
— forty feet of hissing steam just ceasing, mid-length, like a candle pinched
out, and the dead-water slick behind it going dark and ordinary and cold.

Six punts moved at once. Grapnels went up in sacking and landed with a sound
like a fist in a pillow, and canal men were on the lines before the hooks had
set, going up the side of a moving ship barefoot with knives in their teeth, and
it was the most casually competent thing Magda has ever watched anybody do.

But a ship that has hissed for five days and suddenly does not is a ship that
has changed its noise, and there was a man aft who had lived beside that sound
long enough to notice its absence.

A voice on the quarterdeck. Not a shout. A question.

Then a shout.

Then a bell.

---

She did not go up the hull. She is seventy and in mail and she knew exactly what
she was, which was a woman with a sling and a clear line at forty feet of rail
with the sky behind it.

The first man leaned out over the side with a knife, going for the grapnel lines
— which would drop three men into cold water and the ebb. Her first stone went
past his head close enough that he flinched back, which bought the line about
three seconds and no more.

She was already loading the next one. That is the thing about a sling. You are
never really out. You are only ever between.

And the second stone was the best shot she has ever made in her life, and she
would like it noted that she has no idea how.

He had turned inboard, half-lit by somebody's dropped lantern, side-on at forty
feet — and the stone took him under the raised arm where the scale gapes.

He did not fall over the side. He folded sideways onto the rail with his arms
over it, and the knife dropped past her into the water, and he stayed there
hanging half over the edge with his legs still on the deck, which is worse for
everyone aboard than if he had gone in, because now the men behind him had to
get past him and the whole rail was blocked at exactly the spot they were
massing.

Two more canal men went up the far line while that was happening.

---

Then the bell stopped. The shouting stopped. It went very quiet up there, very
suddenly, which was the most frightening thing that had happened all night.

A single lantern shutter opened on the quarterdeck and swung out over the side,
throwing a cone of light down onto the black water, and it began to sweep along
the hull, punt by punt.

Looking for the boats. Looking for her.

The lantern made him a target and he knew it and he did it anyway, which tells
you something about him.

She put a stone through the middle of him before it got there.

She *heard* it hit. Forty yards and dark and she heard it — the flat thud of a
stone going into a body that has nothing on it but wool, because the man does
not wear armour, because he has apparently never in his life expected to need
any.

The lantern dropped. Not thrown. *Dropped*, out of a hand that had stopped
working, and it went over the side and hissed out and the quarterdeck went black
again.

Somewhere up there a man said something short with no breath behind it.

---

The rage came up out of her on the rope.

She had not let it since the woods and it does not arrive like anger. It arrives
like warmth, like getting into a hot bath, everything narrowing to the next
handhold and the noise above. And it is the only reason a seventy-year-old woman
in a mail hauberk with an axe on her back got up forty feet of wet line at all.

She came over the rail into it.

A lantern on its side by the mainmast throwing everything sideways. Two Dragon
Knights down that she could see and one canal man, face-up, not moving. The mass
of it forward where the boarders had got in first — knives against scale, and the
knives winning, because there are nine of them and because a man in scale on a
wet deck at night is a slow, loud, obvious thing.

Aft, on the quarterdeck steps, Blau on one knee with a hand pressed flat into
his own middle and the other holding the rail, and he was not out of the fight.
He was *directing* it, in that voice that does not rise, and three knights were
peeling back from the bow to form on him.

And behind him, under the quarterdeck, the barred shutter — from this side a
door, with a beam across it and a knight standing in front of it who had not
moved from that spot since the fighting started and was not going to.

Vell's axe came off her back.

---

She went up that deck making a noise that stopped the fighting at the bow for a
full second.

It is not a war cry. It is older and uglier than that — the sound you make over
a byre full of dead stock in a bad winter — and there were words somewhere in
the middle of it about violators, and stealers of souls, and rapists of the
dead, and every canal man on that deck decided at once that whatever that was,
it was on their side.

The man in the way had a sword and a shield and it did not matter in the
slightest. The axe came over the top of the shield — a size larger than it had
any right to be, in hands that were not feeling the weight — and went through
the scale over his belly with a sound like somebody standing on a crate. He sat
down against the mast. His legs simply stopped being interested.

Eight feet to Blau.

He had watched all of that happen and his face had not changed.

"*That's* her," he said. "The northern woman."

A pause, and something that might have been a laugh with no air behind it.

"Nobody told me she was **seventy**."

---

It went badly for a while after that, and she will tell you so.

She evaded two spears and both evasions put her flat on her back on a wet deck
in a hauberk, which is what evading costs and what parrying does not, and Blau —
still not raising his voice, still on one knee with a hole in him — said: "Don't
crowd her. She's on her back. Spears."

Which is exactly the right thing to do to a downed woman with an axe.

She swung up from the deck at a knee and there was no power in it and no reach,
and the axe stuck for half a second in wet oak, and a spear went into her right
thigh through the mail skirt. The rage halved it. She felt the pressure of it
and nothing else, the way you feel a hand on your shoulder, which is the most
frightening thing about being like that.

Then Blau got off the steps.

He did it slowly, with one hand still pressed into his own middle, and the two
guards moved aside for him without being told, and at three feet he looked down
at her and drew a knife left-handed. A working knife. Not a duelling piece.

"You're the pig woman.

"He was a foul little animal and he'd have been the ruin of the house inside
five years." Perfectly level. "You've done the Baron a service and he will hang
you for it, and I'll be there."

He is an extremely good man with a knife and he could not make it work, because
there was a hole in his abdomen that she had put there from a boat forty yards
away in the dark, and every time he bent at the waist something inside him
refused.

He went down onto one knee to reach her and stopped halfway with his teeth
locked, and the knife came in short and slow and wide, and he had to put his
other hand on the deck to keep from going over.

Neither of them touched the other.

For a second the two of them were simply face to face on a wet deck, a foot
apart, both bleeding, seventy years apart in age and neither able to finish the
other.

Then he said, quite quietly, with what breath he had:

"Ah."

And he looked over her shoulder, past her, at the barred door under the
quarterdeck.

"*Cut the boy's throat.*"

---

She came up off the deck at him — not standing; lunging, all of it from the hips
and the one good leg, with the axe going out low and flat.

And she did not take the leg.

She took the *hole*. The one she had put in him from a boat in the dark forty
yards out, that he had been holding shut with one hand for five minutes because
he is a man who does not believe in armour.

The axe went in where his hand was and took the hand with it.

He went flat. There was a moment where he was looking at the mast, and then
there was not anybody looking at anything.

The two guards saw it happen from four feet away.

That was the second thing that night that stopped a fight. The first was the
noise she made coming over the rail. Blau was the reason those men were still
standing in formation on a deck they had already lost, and now Blau was a shape
on the boards with an old woman lying next to him.

One of them stepped back.

---

"**MAGDA — DOWN!**"

She was already down. She got flatter.

Whatever Gardwen had been saving came down the length of that deck. You do not
see it; you feel the deck go cold and wet in a rush from bow to stern — and the
entangle took the whole waist of the ship. Cordage, weed off the rigging, wet
rope coming alive off the pins and going round ankles and wrists and throats.

It caught both guards. It caught three knights forward. It caught two canal men
who would be very rude about it later.

And it caught the knight at the door, with the beam half out of the brackets,
two feet from a boy behind it.

# Chapter 21 — Two Voices, One Throat

THE BOY DOES NOT HAVE A NAME AND HAS NOT HAD ONE FOR TEN YEARS, WHICH IS
not the same as having forgotten it, and is worse.

They call him nothing. That is the honest description of it. The dressing-man
says *hold still* and the razor-man says *other side* and the one who brings the
bowl does not speak at all, and the knights outside the door refer to him, on
the rare occasions when they refer to him, as *it*.

He is seventeen. He is thin the way people are thin when somebody else decides
what they eat. The whole upper left of his chest is a long-healed, re-opened,
re-healed, re-opened mess, a wound that has been made and remade in the same
place four hundred times, and it is the only clock he has.

And there is a man in him.

---

They are not friends and it would be obscene to say so, but they have been in
one room for a decade and there is a kind of arrangement.

The man is a soldier. That is the shape of him. He is unfailingly, exhaustingly
courteous, and he apologises, and he means it, and it does not help. When they
open the boy in the mornings the man goes very quiet and stays quiet for hours
afterwards, and the boy has worked out that this is not weakness but a sort of
withdrawal, the man taking himself as far away inside as he can go so that the
boy can have the room to himself while it hurts.

When they make him fight, the man does it, and the boy is not there for that at
all, which is the nearest thing to a mercy in his life.

And in between they argue.

That is what the crews hear through the deck and cannot stand: not screaming.
*Arguing.* Two voices out of one throat having a row for hours, and one of them
is a boy and one of them is not, and the one that is not sounds like a man being
told to do something he thinks is dishonourable.

The morning cut is not only for the wear. It is to keep them tired. You bleed a
man to keep him from arguing.

---

That night the ship changed its noise.

The boy noticed before anyone. He has nothing to do but notice. The hiss along
the hull that has been there for five days stopped, all at once, and the cabin
got colder by a degree, and the man in him came awake so fast that it hurt.

*Something is happening.*

Then the bell. Then the bell stopping, which was worse. Then a great deal of
running about that was not the ordinary running about.

Then a noise from somewhere forward that neither of them had heard before, and
the man — who has been in this boy for ten years and has, in that time, been
enthusiastic about precisely nothing — said, in the boy's own head, with
something the boy could only describe as *appetite*:

**"Oh. Oh, that's the death-goddess. Listen to that."**

---

There were two of them in the cabin with him and neither was a soldier.

The one with the bowl was already backing into the corner with his hands up. The
one with the razor was standing over the cot, and he had heard the order come
down from the deck — *cut the boy's throat* — and he had not moved yet.

The boy watched him not move. He would like to be able to say he was brave about
it. He was not. He was seventeen and tied into a routine and he lay there and
watched a man decide whether he was the kind of person who does that, and he
could not think of one single thing to say that would help.

Then the beam came out of its second bracket and the door went inward.

---

What came through it was an old woman.

She was in bloodied mail and she filled the doorway and she was screaming, and
she had an axe, and there was something behind her on the deck that had recently
been an extremely dangerous man.

The razor-man dropped the razor. It hit the boards and skittered under the cot.
Then he sat straight down on the deck with his hands on his head — which was the
single most sensible thing anybody did on that ship all night — and started
saying *I only do the dressings, I only do the dressings* over and over.

And the boy said "*Don't*—"

And the man in him finished it, in a voice a thousand years older:

"— **she's not here for you.**"

---

The old woman pointed the axe at the razor-man and did not move.

The boy understood, later, that she was trying with everything she had not to
close those eight feet, and that it was costing her more than the fighting had.
At the time it simply looked like an old woman shaking in a doorway making a
noise through her teeth that was not words in any language.

And the man in him got an elbow under them and sat up, and the ruined chest
moved, and he winced on the boy's behalf.

"**Woman of the death-goddess.**

"I have been listening to you come up this ship for a quarter of an hour. I know
what you are and I know who sent you, and I have been waiting for somebody to
come with that particular smell on them for a *very long time*."

Then the boy's face contorted, because they were both trying to use one throat
at once.

"— hurts, it hurts when he talks, *please* —"

"— **I know. I am sorry. It will not be much longer now.**"

And then, to her:

"Get us off this ship before the other one comes back with my bones."

She got two words out. Ground through her teeth. Not a greeting and not a
promise — the acknowledgement one soldier gives another across a yard.

"**General Thuban.**"

And the man in him said, with something like relief:

"*Ah. Good.*"

Then she turned round and went back out onto the deck, because that was where
the rest of them were, and the boy did not see the next minute and the man did,
and the man did not describe it to him, then or ever.

---

Some time after that a woman came and stood in the doorway and did not come in.

She had a staff in her hand and she had one hand on the frame and she stood
there for about a minute and a half.

The boy did not know who she was. He wants that understood. He looked at a
stranger of about twenty-one in woodland leathers and felt absolutely nothing at
all, and was ashamed of it, and could not help it.

*Do you know her?* the man asked. Not out loud. He can do that.

*No.*

*Look again.*

And it was the man who worked it out, because the man has a thousand years of
faces and the boy has ten years of a cabin, and what the man said next he said
gently and out loud so that she would hear it too, and it was short, and
afterwards the boy's whole face changed.

Then the man did the last generous thing available to him.

He stepped back.

He took himself as far away inside as he could go and gave the boy the room, the
way he does in the mornings, except that this time it was not so that a child
could be hurt privately.

And the boy's mouth moved.

What he said was one word, and it was not her name, because he was seven when
they took him and there are things a seven-year-old calls a big sister that are
not a name.

Her legs went. She caught herself on the edge of the cot and then she just put
her forehead down on his shoulder — carefully, on the right, away from the wound
— and stayed there, and he got one arm up around her head, and neither of them
made any sound that carried as far as the door.

A wolf came over the rail from somewhere, soaked, and poured herself into that
cabin and lay down under the cot without being asked.

And the man in him, from a long way off, said one thing more, and then nothing
at all for the rest of the night:

**"Good. Now hold on to that, because I am going to need you to be very brave
tomorrow, and you have already been braver than anyone will ever tell you."**

# Chapter 22 — You Said Take Them

RAVELLA ASKED FOR ONE THING BEFORE ANY OF IT AND MAGDA HAD SAID YES
without much thinking about it, in a room at the Siren's Call, the way you agree
to a price when your mind is on the goods.

Two dead men laid down properly, for one cold ship.

The Court had kept its half before she had done anything at all. When the temple
boat came in on the south side of Lost Isle an hour before midnight, there were
two shapes lying side by side on the stone under a sheet at the top of the
cleared stair: Ellick Sarn, and the one she had put an axe through, brought up
out of the drowned street by people who live down there.

She walked over to them on a bad leg with the axe still in her hand because she
had forgotten she was holding it, and she knelt down on the wet stone, which
hurt, and she pulled the sheet back off their faces, because she has never in
her life said words over a covered face.

Behind her everybody stopped moving. Nerissa took her lamp two steps back. Under
the stair the water went very still and it was not the wind that did it.

She said it.

*"Mother of the darkness. Take these drowned back to their rest. It's time they
went home."*

And nothing happened.

The water stayed still. The lamps went on burning. The two men on the stone went
on being two men on the stone and Ellick Sarn's face did not change in any way
at all.

She waited. She gave it a good while, because she has stood at enough gravesides
to know that the words sometimes take a minute.

They did not.

Somewhere down that stair, under the black water, something was *listening* and
had not been given what it needed.

---

Ravella came and crouched on the other side of the bodies and looked at her
across them, and she was not angry, which was worse.

"It's not the words," she said quietly. "The words were right."

"Then what?"

"You said *take them*." She laid two fingers on Ellick's forehead. "You're
asking her to come and fetch. She won't. She never does — that's the entire
nature of your goddess, isn't it? She takes the ones nobody sings about, and she
takes them *when somebody finally brings them*."

She looked up.

"Your storyteller told you this and you were listening to the other half of it.
Nobody ever came back for Thuban. Nobody has come back for *these two* either.
Ellick's wife thinks he ran off, and that one's people don't know he's dead."

She stood.

"You have to do the part that costs you. Not ask her to take them. **Give them
to her.** Say whose they are and say what was done to them and say that somebody
came back — and you have to mean the last one, because you're the somebody."

Nerissa, from behind, very quietly: "That is exactly how it works, Magda. In
every faith I know."

And Hesper, who had been listening while he unpacked his bag, and who had gone
rather pale:

"And if that's the shape of it for two drowned boatmen who died last week..."

He did not finish it. He did not need to.

---

She muttered *I'm not a fucking priest* at the stone.

And then she did it anyway, kneeling on wet stone with a bad leg, in the voice
you would use across a yard.

*"Oi. Listen up then.*

*"Brothers, workers, toilers, men. You lived your lives as we all do — with
imperfect plans, a little hope, a little selfishness, likely with much love and
sadness when you died. In this place. In the water. The water that takes all
things.*

*"But then these bastards brought you back. To haul, and work, and toil. Because
it helped them.*

*"So fuck 'em.*

*"Come with me, brothers. Rage with me at the loss and the death — and then go
back to the dark deep sea. Go to your rest. Go now, my brothers. Go."*

She was, at this point, shouting at a hole in the ground.

---

The water at the foot of the stair did not part, and it did not glow, and it did
not do any of the things a story would have it do.

It went *warm*.

That was all. It came up the steps past her knees like a draught from an open
door in a cold house, and every lamp on that island bent toward it at once, and
Nerissa made a small sound behind her.

And the two men on the stone let go.

There was no light. There was a *slackening* — she has seen it four hundred
times in byres and beds and she would know it anywhere. Whatever was still
holding the shape of Ellick Sarn's face stopped holding it, and what was left
was just a boatman who died, and looked it, and looked *finished*.

The warmth went down the stair and took something with it.

Then the water was only water.

---

Nobody said anything for a while.

Ravella had both hands flat on the stone and her head down, and she stayed like
that a long time. When she got up her face was wet and it was not canal water.

"They're through. The Court has them."

She looked at Magda and for once there was no broker anywhere in it.

"You said whose they were. Nobody has said whose anybody was down here in four
hundred years."

And Hesper, staring:

"Magda. That was two men who died *last week*, and it took everything you had."

Out on the black water, north-east, one of Ravella's people whistled once. Low,
two notes.

A small boat. One man. Something heavy amidships.

"Shut up, old man," said Magda. "Give me a drink so I can get ready for the
next."

# Chapter 23 — Might Come In Handy

HE CAME ROUND THE EASTERN POINT WITH ONE SET OF OARS, UNHURRIED, NO
lantern, and along the drowned street with the confidence of a man who has done
it four times before, and he landed exactly where Ellick had landed his, and
shipped the oars, and stepped out into the water without a sound.

He was a long time getting the thing out of the boat. It took him three tries
and a great deal of care.

Oiled cloth, roped, about five feet long. He carried it up the drowned street on
his shoulder with his back bent under it and set it down on the stone at the
foot of the stair — *gently*, the way you set down somebody sleeping — and stood
there breathing.

Then he said, to nobody, in a voice that carried beautifully across still water:

"**Ellick. Get up here and help me with him.**"

Nerissa did not even signal. She said, quietly, "*Take him*," and the wall came
alive, and four Swords came over it at once and two more out of the water behind
him, and he was face-down on the stone with a knee in his back before the echo
of *Ellick* had finished coming off the far wall.

He did not struggle. He did not shout.

He turned his head sideways against the stone, and what he did was *look*. At
the shuttered lamps coming open one by one. At twelve Swords of the Lake. At
Nerissa. At Hesper.

And then at the oiled bundle lying eighteen inches from his face, which he had
set down so carefully, and which he was now not going to be allowed to touch
again.

He was younger than anyone expected. Late thirties. Unremarkable in the way
Crowbill is unremarkable, except that Crowbill chose it and this man was simply
born with it. Ink on two fingers.

Hesper crouched over the bundle and did not touch it either. He looked at the
ropework for a long moment — the way it was tied, what it was tied with — and
his mouth thinned.

"That's a *reliquary* knot," he said. "That's not how you tie cargo. That's how
you tie something you're afraid of."

---

They asked him.

He answered exactly three questions and they were all the wrong ones.

*Is that Thuban Eta in the cloth?* — "Yes." *Will the removal work at this
stair?* — "Yes." *Will you tell us how?* — "No."

And then he settled his shoulders against the wall and stopped.

Hesper tried for a long while, and he is good at it, and he went at it from
underneath, professional to professional — *you've done this and I haven't and
I'd very much like to know how the seat is kept clean* — and you could see the
man enjoying it, and enjoying not answering more.

At the end he said one thing unprompted, almost kindly:

"You'll open him at the wrong point and put a thousand-year-old knight into a
priestess. I'd rather like to see that."

Nerissa stepped back from him and looked like she wanted to wash.

And then Hesper stopped mid-word with his hands coming away from his face and
looked over Magda's shoulder at a tower-stub where a druid was sitting with her
arm round a seventeen-year-old boy.

"Magda. We have been extraordinarily stupid.

"There is a man not thirty feet from us who has been *inside* one of these for a
thousand years. Who was put in by experts and has had every day since to feel
exactly how the seat is fastened.

"Why are we asking the gaoler? **Ask the prisoner.**"

---

Magda's answer to that was to start undoing buckles.

Nobody said anything for the first few, because everyone assumed it was the leg,
or the fatigue, or the fact that she had been in mail since dawn.

The kettle helm went on the stone. Then the coif, and her hair came out flat and
grey and wet. Then she went at the hauberk, which is a two-person job at the
best of times, and Nerissa — who had been watching with a deepening frown — came
and took the weight of it without being asked, and the two of them got it off
over her head, and it went down on the stone with the noise a hauberk makes,
which is like a great deal of money being dropped.

She was in a soaked wool shirt, in the cold, seventy years old, with a
spear-hole in her thigh, standing on a drowned island in the dark.

Hesper had gone very quiet. Nerissa said, "Magda." And then, when she did not
answer, she looked at the black water at the foot of the swept stair — water
they had put a man into, in his mail, with his hands tied — and you could watch
her arrive somewhere she did not like.

"*Magda.*"

She was going to beat him out of the boy. Unarmed and unarmoured and in the
rage, the only way she knows how to do anything, and she went to the tower-stub
and said so to his face.

---

And Thuban Eta said no.

The boy's face was wet and frightened and seventeen. Then it changed — you could
watch it happen by then, the way you watch someone step forward in a doorway —
and the other one was looking out. He took his time. He looked at her bare arms,
and the spear-hole, and the axe she had left thirty feet away on the stone.

"**No.**"

A pause.

"But I understand why you thought of it, and I want you to know I would have
taken that offer from you gladly, if it worked.

"Understand what you are proposing. You would beat me out of a child. **I do not
feel your hands, woman. *He* does.** You would break his ribs and I would watch,
and at the end of it I would still be here, because I am not held in his body by
his body.

"They have been cutting him open every morning for ten years to do exactly what
you just described. If pain could shift me I would have been shifted four
hundred times."

He let that sit.

"Now hear the rest, because you were closer than your priest is.

"There *is* a fight. You were right about that. But it is not yours, and it is
not with the boy.

"They did not fasten me in with iron. Your storyteller told you and he was
correct — **they fastened me in with the night I died.** Every hour I have spent
in here I have spent back on that boat with my hands tied, going over the side,
looking up at Corran and Vey and the rest of them not doing anything.

"That is the room I have been kept in. Not this child. *That.*"

The old voice went thin.

"And I cannot leave it, because to leave it I have to accept that it happened
and that nobody came, and I have not been *able* to accept that, because it is
unbearable, and I have had a thousand years of finding it unbearable.

"So. You do not need to fight me out. **You need to come and get me out of that
water. Say it was wrong. Say whose I am. Say somebody came.**

"And you must mean it, and I will know if you don't, because I have had a very
long time to learn what people mean.

"Open my bones and open your door. And then stand where they stood, and do not
look away when I go under, because they did.

"That is all it ever needed. It has only ever needed one person to turn up."

---

So she went and got her grandmother's country back out of wherever it had been
sitting for fifty years, and it did not come as instructions. It came as smells.
Woodsmoke and wet wool and somebody's aunt weeping professionally.

You put his weapons back in his hands. A man goes out armed, and whatever was
taken off him when he died is given back, and if you have not got it you give
him yours, and that is better anyway.

You say the name. Out loud. First. Before anything, so that everyone standing
there has to hear it.

Then you tell the tale. Not a prayer — a *telling*. Who he was and what he did
and how he died, said in front of witnesses, in the open, at full volume.

You settle the debt. If a man was murdered somebody stands up and says so, and
names it, and the wrong goes into the air where it can be heard. Nobody goes
into the ground with an unpaid killing on him.

Then fire. Or water, for a drowned man. You give him back to whatever took him,
on purpose this time, with people watching.

And then you feast, and you brawl, and you get disgracefully drunk, because a
death that nobody celebrates is a death that did not count.

And then she hit the thing at the bottom of it, and it stopped her where she
stood.

**Valhalla is not his.**

That is for the battle-dead. For the ones who fell with a sword in the hand and
the enemy in front. Thuban Eta went over a gunwale in the dark with his hands
tied by his own people. He was *cheated* of the death that buys that hall, and
he has been paying for their crime with his afterlife for a thousand years.

Which is exactly, precisely, why he is Hel's.

And the wound is not the water and it is not the rope.

It is that in a thousand years, nobody has ever told his tale.

---

Hesper cut the reliquary knots, naming each one as it came off.

The oiled cloth came back.

Bones. Long ones, brown with age, laid the way you lay a man. And around the
wrists, corroded almost to nothing but still there, still *on him* after a
thousand years, two turns of iron wire.

They had put him in the water tied and nobody had ever cut it off.

Gardwen made a sound.

Nerissa said, "*Give me the shears*," and cut them, and dropped the wire in the
water, and that alone changed the temperature of the air on that stair.

---

And then Magda did everything right and it was not enough.

She said the name. She put Vell's axe in the bones' hands. She stood at the head
of the stair where his company had stood over him and said the wrong out loud —
*these men murdered you, and it was cowardice, and it was never answered for* —
and she told his tale in a market-day voice to twelve Swords of the Lake and a
priestess and a mage and a druid and a wolf and a whole Court listening from
underneath.

It was the first telling he had ever had.

And she felt it not land. It is like putting your shoulder to a door that turns
out to be a wall. Everything she had went into it and the world did not move an
inch.

The water at the foot of the stair stayed cold. The lamps did not lean.

The boy on the stone started to shake, and the old voice came out of him ragged
for the first time all night:

"— *I can't* — woman, I can't *reach* it, there's something across—"

Hesper was already up and moving. "The seat's still fastened. Something's still
holding him and it is not the bones and it is not this stair—"

And the roped man against the wall, who had said nothing for twenty minutes,
started to laugh.

It was a quiet, delighted, entirely genuine laugh.

"Oh, that's *good*. That's very good. You've done all of it properly and you've
done it beautifully and you have forgotten one thing.

"He isn't only held by the bones."

He tipped his head back against the stone, thoroughly enjoying himself.

"**The Baron wears the rest of him around his neck.** And the Baron is at the
Governor's table three miles from here, being toasted."

---

She picked the axe up off the stone on the way past without breaking stride.

*Say that again. Damn you. Explain. It. To. Me. Slowly. And fucking clearly.*

He watched her come and he was *still* smiling, and then at about six feet he
stopped smiling.

And then he did not flinch and he did not talk. What he did was look up at her
with an axe six feet from his face and say, quite gently, like a man explaining
something to a child at a funeral:

"You're not going to. If you were, you'd have done it before you asked."

And he closed his eyes and leaned his head back against the stone and was simply
*done* with the conversation, and there was nothing behind that face she could
reach with a weapon.

Hesper gave her the explanation anyway, because he did not need the prisoner for
that part. The bones are the primary anchor. The locket is the working one, the
piece they carry, the one the daily ritual runs through. It is not a spare. It
is the *latch*. They cut a piece off him a century ago and every morning they use
it to hold the seat shut.

"So the door is open. The bones are open. He is *willing* — you did that, and it
worked, and I want you to hear that it worked.

"But there is a lock on this and it is around Hanzo di Teufel's neck."

Nerissa, into the silence: "The Tourney is at noon."

And Gardwen, with her brother shaking against her: "Then that's where we go.
Because that's where *he'll* be. In the Governor's box, in front of the whole
city, wearing my brother round his neck."

---

Magda did not join the strategising.

She stood at the edge of it with the axe hanging from one hand and watched the
roped man, and he knew she was watching, and after a while he opened his eyes
and looked back, and the two of them held that for a long time while everybody
else worked out how to get into a Governor's box at noon.

Nerissa was saying "—then Emeric has to hear it from Sana herself, and not in an
anteroom—"

And she walked over and did it.

It took one.

The sound afterwards was the sound of everyone on that island stopping at once.

She found a grain sack by the stair, tipped out what was in it, put the head in,
knotted the top, and said it to nobody in particular:

"Might come in handy."

---

Corvin — twenty-two, who had taken a rope out to that island for her the night
before — turned round and walked twenty feet away and was sick against a wall.

Hesper closed his eyes. Just for a moment. Then he opened them and went back to
the bones, because he is a practical man and there was work, and he did not look
at her again for some time.

Ravella did not react at all. She looked at the body, and then at the water, and
said quietly to one of hers: "Not that one. He doesn't go down there."

Gardwen looked at her for a long moment. She did not say *why did you do that.*

She said: "Was he still worth anything?"

And Nerissa came and stood in front of her. Her face was perfectly still and her
voice did not rise, and every Sword on that island could hear her.

"He was bound. On my island, under my cordon, taken by my people who had orders
to hold him."

She let that sit.

"And he was the only living soul who knew where **Bettan** is. Fourteen years
old. Cheerful. Cutting girls' hair at a school on the Northern Isles for people
who fill them up."

Her hands were shaking slightly and she was doing nothing to hide it.

"I gave you a reason to stop, once, and you took it. So I will not pretend I did
not know what you were.

"But you have just taken that child away from me and I do not know how to get
her back."

She turned and walked away toward the boats.

Twelve Swords of the Lake watched her go, and then looked at Magda, and none of
them said anything at all.

---

It was Gardwen who found the way round it, and she did it by putting the sack
out of her mind, because there was a job.

She could not track a girl through a city with no ground. But she had found two
men on Lost Isle from four hundred yards across open water without ever seeing
them, because she had not been looking for men. She had been feeling for what
was *in* them.

"Bettan's been filled. If she's carrying one of those things then she doesn't
read like a girl any more, and I don't have to find *her*. I have to stand
somewhere near that school and ask what's *wrong* in it."

She met Magda's eye and did not soften it.

"I'd need Nerissa. Who has just walked off to the boats and will not want to
look at you.

"Go and tell her anyway. Not sorry — she'd smell that. Tell her you've got a way
to find the girl, and let her decide what she does with you afterwards."

---

So Magda shouted "Oi. Priestess!" across a drowned street at the High Priestess
of the Lake Lady, and walked over, and said it, and did not apologise, because
she was not.

*Don't look for the girl. Look for the demon. Gardwen can do it for you if you
put her in the right place. Spare me your delicacies and so-called purities. The
rot's in your city and it's not going to leave because you ask it nicely.*

Nerissa listened to the whole thing without interrupting.

Then:

"You've mistaken me."

Very level.

"I did not object because it was *unclean*. I have buried men off the tide-flats
with their throats opened by people I then had to bless at Solstice. I'm
sixty-one and I run a temple in a port."

She took a step closer.

"I objected because you cut up the only map to a fourteen-year-old girl and then
said *might come in handy*.

"That isn't purity, Magda. **That's arithmetic.**"

She held her eye until she was sure it had landed, and only then did the rest of
her arrive, because she had already been thinking about the thing Magda had
actually come to say.

"—and yes. Yes, that would work. I can put my hands in the water at Corbie's and
hold the channel for her the way I did last night, and if that child has
something in her then it will show like a lamp through a shutter." Her jaw
tightened. "It's better than anything I had, which was *ask the school again and
hope*.

"We go at first light. Not before — the girls will be at breakfast and I want
them in one room and counted while it's done."

Then, as Magda turned to walk away:

"Magda." Not raised.

"I will work with you until this is finished, and I will do it wholeheartedly,
and I will not pretend at you afterwards. When the boy is out and the Baron is
down, you and I are done, and you will not be welcome on Temple Isle."

A beat.

"Sword-Captain Vell's axe stays with you. She'd have wanted that and I'm not
petty."

She got in the boat.

Magda shrugged at her back.

"No. I killed him because he deserved it. Fucker wasn't going to tell you
anything anyway. I don't even know what arithmetic is."

"No," Nerissa agreed. "You don't."

---

At first light, at Corbie's, with forty girls in a refectory being counted and
treating it as an outrage, Nerissa went into the channel to her knees and
Gardwen took her hand and put the other flat on the wall of the school.

It took about four seconds.

"There," she said.

Then, immediately: "*No.* Wait—"

And her grip tightened hard enough to make the priestess wince.

"There's **three**."

Bettan, fourteen, cheerful, in the refectory with the others. And two more in
that room. Girls who went quiet for a week sometime in the last month, and came
back lovely, and started asking everyone about their families.

Nobody had noticed. Why would they? A homesick child getting happier is the
thing you *want* to see.

"Magda — Santo had five twists of hair. He'd used one. Four left, and Sana's was
one of them." Gardwen was grey. "They weren't collecting *vessels*. They've been
**filling** them. Here. For a month. In a school full of forty girls, four
hundred yards from that stair."

Nerissa came up out of the water very slowly.

"The four twists were the ones they hadn't done yet," she said.

She looked at the lit windows of the refectory, where forty girls were being
counted and complaining about it.

"Then how many *have* they done?"
