# Chapter 24 — The Lakelady's Javelin

TEMERACH NEBULO HAS BEEN TRYING TO PUT HANZO DI TEUFEL IN FRONT OF A
magistrate for four years and has, in that time, accumulated letters, witnesses
who recant, and two dead informants.

That is the whole of her career at present. She is aware of how it sounds.

She was sitting on an upturned crate in the competitors' enclosure at the Lake
Lady's Tourney with her bow across her knees, doing nothing at all — which,
people are always surprised to discover, is the entirety of her preparation. She
is entirely still and she is not thinking about anything. It works.

She had not looked at the Governor's box once, which was remarkable, because
everybody else on that field had.

She did not know that a ship had gone down in the Mouth. She did not know that
Blau was dead, or that a seventeen-year-old boy was in a cell under the temple
she could see from where she was sitting, or that her Order's High Priestess had
spent the night on a drowned island cutting thousand-year-old wire off a dead
knight's wrists.

The enclosure is sealed from the first horn. No messages in, no messages out.
Nobody through the rope but judges and the Lady's own. It is not a Governor's
rule; it is a temple rule and it is four hundred years old and it exists
precisely so that nobody can nobble a competitor with news from outside.

Nerissa wrote it. Or her predecessors did. She enforces it.

So there had been a young Sword standing at the cordon since first light with a
folded note in his hand and the face of a man failing, and Temerach had not seen
him, because she was not looking at anything.

---

The woman who came and stood in front of her was in a novice's vestment about a
foot too long, and was seventy years old, and had canal on the hem, and moved
like somebody who had fought yesterday and slept badly.

Temerach looked up.

She said four sentences. They were: we've rescued Thuban and the boy. Di Teufel
was possessing people with demons all over the place. I just need the Baron's
locket to complete the rite and lay the haunt to rest.

That is three. The fourth was *he's in a cell under the colonnade*, and it came
later.

Temerach does not react the way people react. There was no start and no *what*.
She took it in and filed it, and then she asked the two questions that mattered
to her, in order.

"Is Conall alive?"

"Who?"

And that stopped her. Properly stopped her — the first thing all day that had.

"Conall Bjornlasch." She was watching the old woman's face now and getting
nothing, because there was nothing there to get. "Dark. Twenty-two. Rides with
me. He's been in this city three days."

"Never heard the name in my life, lass."

Something happened behind Temerach's composure that she did not intend and could
not have described.

"...Then you don't know," she said slowly. "None of you know. You've spent three
days pulling this apart and nobody has mentioned him once.

"That is either very good news or the worst news I've had this week, and I don't
yet know which."

Then she put it aside — visibly, the way she does everything — and looked past
her across the ground at the canopied box and the man in dragon-green.

It was the first time all day she had looked at him. Her face did not change at
all.

"Later. The locket first. Tell me what it looks like, and how close you need to
be."

---

She thought about the plan for perhaps four seconds, which for her is a long
deliberation.

"Not in the box."

She said it as settled fact.

"Six thousand people are watching that canopy. If he dies in it, or is *taken*
in it, then by tonight the story is that the temple and the Governor murdered a
foreign lord at the Lady's own Tourney, and the three men sitting beside Emeric
will make sure it's the only story. I have watched that happen to better cases
than this one.

"So we don't go to him. **We make him leave.**

"The Single Combat is called at the second hour. His champion is in a cell under
that temple. He does not know it yet. So at the second hour a herald calls for
the di Teufel man, and calls again, and *nobody comes* — in front of every Guild
in this city.

"He will have about a minute to decide whether he is a man whose champion is
late or a man who has been robbed. And he is not stupid. He'll know.

"And then he leaves that box. He has to. He'll go for his boat, and the only
water-stair from the Governor's enclosure is the one behind the colonnade, which
is twelve feet wide with a wall on one side.

"That's where he can be taken, and it is out of sight of the ground, and
everything that happens there happens in front of temple witnesses instead of
the whole city."

She was stringing the bow while she talked. She did not look at what her hands
were doing.

"A magician. Yes, I'd assumed. Which is why he does not get a minute of warning
and does not get his hands free."

Then she looked at the old woman properly, and there was something almost like
humour in it.

"And you're the part I can't do. He will leave when the herald calls. Or he will
leave *sooner*, and on our timing instead of his, if somebody he does not know
walks up to that box and shows him something that tells him it has all already
gone wrong."

A pause.

"You've been carrying that sack since you got here."

---

"It's the quiet one's head," said the old woman. "He was pissing me off. I was
told you wouldn't be OK with that but it'd definitely get the good Baron's
attention."

Temerach's face did not change at the word *head*.

"I am not going to pretend that pleases me." Flat. "But I have seen what that
man's people do to fourteen-year-olds and I am not going to stand on a field and
lecture you about a demonologist's neck.

"Use it if it works."

And then the old woman asked whether Conall was any good with a bow.

"No," Temerach said.

Much too fast.

The old woman waited.

"He's — " She was stringing something that was already strung. "He has a
soldier's training, all weapons. He's competent. He's not an archer."

"That's not what I asked, lass. I asked if he was any good."

"He's *competent*."

---

Here is a thing about Temerach Nebulo which she is aware of and has never been
able to do anything about. She is one of the most dangerous people in this
realm and she is an appalling liar. She has no facility for it whatsoever.

She had just told an old woman she met four minutes earlier two things she had
no intention of telling anybody: that Conall is a great deal better than
competent, and that she would rather chew her own hand off than have him within
a mile of that box.

She heard herself do it, too.

"He is my responsibility," she said, more carefully. "He is twenty-two, he came
to this city because I brought him, and there is a reason I have kept him away
from the di Teufels that I am not going to discuss on a competition field with a
woman I met four minutes ago.

"Ask me again tonight and I may tell you. Ask me now and I'll say no and mean
it."

Then, briskly, closing it:

"The Archery is called in a quarter of an hour. I will be on that line for the
better part of an hour and I cannot leave it without forfeiting — and I want to
win it, because the prize is court access and that is *four years* of my work.

"So you have an hour where I am the most visible person in Purewater and can do
nothing at all.

"Use it. Get me one thing: whether he still has the locket on him. If he's left
it on a ship or in a strongbox we are all wasting the afternoon."

---

The Archery runs in three passes and by the third there were four of them left.

First pass, fixed targets at eighty paces. She hit everything and the crowd did
not notice her, because everybody hits at eighty paces.

Second pass, moving targets on boats poled across the gap between the islands.

That is when six thousand people found out who she was.

The boats go across left to right at a walking pace with the targets standing on
them, and the field is allowed six shafts. The Guild man ahead of her put four
in and the ground was very pleased with four.

Temerach shot six.

She does not track. That is the thing you notice from the rail. Everyone else
swings the bow with the boat. She does not. She puts the bow where the boat is
*going to be*, and waits, and looses, and the target arrives at the arrow.

Six shafts. Six hits. The last two into the same target inside a handspan while
the boat was at its furthest and fastest.

The noise the ground made was not applause. It was the noise people make when
they have been shown something.

Third pass, cross-channel, two hundred and fifty paces over open water with the
wind off the Mouth. She and the Guild archer both came through it, and he is
genuinely good, and on any other day in any other year he wins that and dines
out on it for a decade.

Today he was standing next to somebody who had put two arrows into the same
moving target at range and then apologised to the judges for the grouping.

They called it for Temerach Nebulo, Knight of the Swords of the Lake. A purse, a
silver bracer, and access to the Governor's court.

---

There was one window to warn her and it was a good one, and it did not work.

Nerissa was to present the prize. It is her Tourney and they are her Order's
colours and the High Priestess handing a Sword of the Lake her bracer in front
of the city is the most ordinary thing that happens all afternoon. Four words,
while she does it. *Box coming. He has it.*

She was three steps from the dais with the bracer in her hands when a man in
Governor's livery came down the steps and took it out of them.

Vosk. The chamberlain who had kept Lilura in an anteroom for four hours.

He did it beautifully. A small bow, a murmured word about the Prince wishing to
honour the champion of the Archery *personally*, and it is protocol, and it is
correct, and there is not one thing the High Priestess of the Lake Lady can do
about it in front of six thousand people without making a scene that the three
men beside Emeric would enjoy enormously.

She stood there with empty hands.

Emeric — who is twenty-four and did not understand what had just been done with
him — presented the bracer himself, delightedly, and said something
complimentary about the second pass.

Temerach received it, bowed, and was invited to stay in the canopy.

She had no idea what was coming.

Four feet to her left, a man in dragon-green was being handed a fitted wooden
case by a steward, with a note in it written by a woman who learned to write
late.

# Chapter 25 — A Dreadful Place to Fight a Man Like Me

THE BOX HAD BEEN BOUGHT OFF A CHANDLER FOR MORE THAN IT WAS WORTH: A
fitted wooden case with a sliding lid, the sort a merchant sends samples in.

The note took a while, because Magda writes like a woman who learned late.

> ***YOUR SHIP IS ON THE BOTTOM. YOUR MAN IS DEAD.***
> ***I HAVE YOUR CHAMPION AND HIS BONES.***
> ***— THE PIG WOMAN***

Gardwen read it over her shoulder and said nothing for a while, and then:

"You've spelled *champion* wrong."

"He'll get the sense of it."

---

Before that, there had been an hour of being an old woman at a fair, and it was
excellent.

She bought fried fish and found a place on the public rail and watched the
Archery, and for about an hour nobody in Purewater wanted anything from her at
all. It was the first hour like that in four days. She would like it recorded
that she enjoyed every minute of it and that the fish was very good.

And Nerissa had put the Lady's cloth on her to get her through that rope, which
had cost the priestess something and which she had said so, plainly, while she
did it with her own hands.

"I am going to put the Lady's cloth on a woman who beheaded a bound prisoner on
my island eight hours ago, and I am going to do it with my own hands, and I
would very much like you to appreciate what that costs me."

Magda had kept her face absolutely straight. It cost her something too.

"Don't," said Nerissa, when it was done.

"Wasn't going to say a word."

"You were *radiating*."

---

Marisette had got the servants. Three of her girls had worked Tourney service
for years and one of them — Corliss's youngest, eighteen, who has poured at four
Tourneys and is very good at being furniture — was in the Governor's enclosure
that afternoon because she always is.

Nobody had to be told a story. Marisette said *look at what's round the Baron's
neck and tell me* and they said *right you are*.

She went in with the wine four times over the hour and came out with this.

It is on him. Gold, a flattened oval about the size of a thumbnail, on a fine
chain, worn under the shirt — but the chain shows at the collar and the shape of
it shows through the green when he leans forward.

And he touches it. Not fidgeting. Every so often his hand goes flat to his chest
over it, briefly, the way a man checks a purse. And once, when a Guildmaster
leaned in to toast him, he moved his shoulder to put it further away.

"He does it about every quarter hour. And after he does it, he looks round."

Then she told them the rest, and her hands were not steady.

"He caught me."

Fourth pour. She was closer than she needed to be and she looked a half-second
too long, and when she came back up he was already looking at her.

And he smiled. And said — pleasantly, in front of two Guildmasters and the
Prince — "*You've very good hands, girl. Who do you serve?*"

She said the Guild steward's name, because it is true.

He said: "*Of course.*" And went back to his cup.

"He wasn't angry," she said. "That's what's wrong with it. He was **pleased**."

Marisette had her off the island and onto a boat before she told anybody, which
is the correct order to do those two things in.

---

From a hundred and forty feet, Magda saw almost nothing, and that was the point.

He slid the lid. He looked down into the box for about two seconds. He slid the
lid back.

He said something to the Guildmaster beside him and the Guildmaster laughed.

Then he set the case down beside his chair, stood, and made a small apologetic
gesture to Prince Emeric — *forgive me, a moment* — and Emeric waved him away
good-naturedly, and he stepped out of the back of the canopy with his cup still
in his hand.

He did not hurry. He did not look round the ground once.

He is very, very good.

"Did he—" said Gardwen.

"He read it. He's going for his boat."

---

Down the public rail, through the fried-fish crowd, past the ale trestles, round
the back of the colonnade where the ground gives way to worked stone and the
noise drops off like a door closing.

The water-stair behind the Governor's enclosure. Twelve feet wide, a wall on the
left, the channel on the right, thirty-odd steps down to a landing where three
boats were tied and two bored oarsmen were playing dice.

Out of sight of six thousand people.

She got there first, because she was closer and because he was being unhurried
and correct.

Gardwen came down behind her and put herself flat against the wall inside the
arch. Ruhi was somewhere above on the colonnade roof, which Magda had decided
not to think about.

Footsteps in the passage. Unhurried. One set.

Then a second set, quicker, catching up. "*My lord — my lord, the herald's
calling the Single Combat—*"

And Hanzo di Teufel said, perfectly pleasantly, from fifteen feet the other side
of the arch:

"Yes. Tell them my champion withdraws. Injury in training."

A pause.

"And find out who delivered that box."

---

She loaded flat against the wall inside the arch with the vestment sleeve pushed
up out of the way. Stone in the pouch, cord round the knuckles, staff cocked
back along the forearm.

The servant's footsteps went away up the passage.

His did not.

He came through the arch. Close to, Baron Hanzo di Teufel is a well-made man of
about fifty in dragon-green with grey at the temples and very good boots, and
the cup was still in his left hand, and he had not spilled a drop of it.

He was looking at the boats.

He got three steps down before he registered that there was an old woman in a
Lake Lady novice's vestment standing against the wall with a loaded staff sling.

He stopped.

He looked at her for a moment — at the vestment, at the sling, at her face — and
she watched him do arithmetic a great deal faster than the serving girl had.

"Ah," he said.

And then, with what sounded like genuine warmth:

"**The pig woman.**"

He had not put the cup down.

"You've cost me a great deal in three days and I would very much like to know
how you did the ship. I'll pay for that answer, and I pay well." He tilted his
head slightly. "Or we can do the other thing, and you should know before you
choose that you are standing on wet stone at the bottom of a walled passage,
which is a *dreadful* place to fight a man like me."

Behind him, in the arch, unhurried, blocking it, Temerach Nebulo had an arrow
already on the string.

Magda spat on the step between them.

"Hel's waiting for you, Baron. Time you went down."

---

He threw himself sideways and he is quick for fifty and the stone found him
anyway.

It took him high in the chest and turned him completely round, and the cup went
out of his hand and shattered on the step, and he landed badly on wet stone and
came up on one elbow with his court silk torn open and a bruise the shape of a
fist coming up underneath it.

And now he was not warm and he was not amused.

He got a hand up — palm out, fingers spread, and she had seen exactly that once
before, at a ford, when a druid asked a favour of the water — and the air in
that passage went *dry*.

"**MAGDA—**" from the arch.

And behind him, from the top of the stair, absolutely calm:

"**My lord Baron. Put the hand down.**

"You are under arrest by warrant of the Order of the Lake Lady for the
profanation of the Tourney and the sacred channel. There are two Guildmasters
and a Prince forty feet above us.

"I have been trying to say those words to you for four years.

"**Put the hand down.**"

He was on the steps between an old woman with a loaded sling and the finest
archer in the realm.

His hand did not go down.

---

He was prone and unarmoured and he had chosen to finish the spell rather than
defend himself, because he is a man who has never once been hit by anything.

She did not throw the staff. She went down the three steps with it held short in
both hands like a woman going at a rat in a grain store, and brought the end of
it down on the wrist.

There was a crack that was mostly the staff and partly not.

The hand shut.

And whatever had been gathering in that passage — the dry, tight, wrong feeling
of air being *asked* for something — came apart all at once with a sound like a
held breath being let go, and the temperature came back, and somewhere above
them a gull started complaining again.

Hanzo di Teufel made a noise through his teeth. It was the first entirely honest
sound he had made in three days.

He cradled the arm against his chest and looked up at her from the wet stone
with his hair come loose and his silk torn and a stone-bruise spreading under
it.

Fifty years of never once being touched, undone on a service stair by an old
woman with a stick.

"You *hag*—"

---

And then his left hand — the good one — moved very slightly toward his own
collar.

She slapped it down out of the air like a woman swatting a wasp off a pie.

Then she took a fistful of green silk and collar and chain, all together, and
put her face about four inches from his.

And she did not rip it. Not straight away.

She held him there, eye to eye, on the wet stone, and let him get a proper look
at what had been coming up that stair for him — which is not a knight and not a
priestess and not a magistrate. It is an old woman who keeps pigs, sent by a
goddess he has never once thought about, wearing a novice's vestment she has no
right to, with fried fish on her breath.

He stared back and he was, for the first time, entirely out of arithmetic.

Then she pulled.

The chain did not break at the clasp. It broke across the back of his neck, and
it took skin, and he cried out.

And it came away in her fist: gold, a flattened oval about the size of a
thumbnail, warm — *properly* warm, the warmth of something that has been alive
against a chest for a hundred years — and a great deal heavier than a thing that
size has any right to be.

Inside it, something moved.

Not rattled. *Moved.*

---

He went very still underneath her.

And then, in a voice that had lost every bit of its charm:

"You have no idea what you are holding. You cannot *open* that, you stupid
woman, if you open that here he will go into the nearest—"

"**I know.**"

That was Hesper, standing in the arch at the top of the stair with his bag,
entirely out of breath, having run the length of the colonnade.

"She's not going to open it here."

Temerach came down and put a boot between the Baron's shoulders and got his good
arm behind him, and it was over, and it had taken about ninety seconds.

Above them, six thousand people were being told that the di Teufel champion
withdrew through injury, and there was a certain amount of booing.

---

Hesper took the locket in a folded cloth and did not touch it with his skin, and
put it in a box within a box, and his hands were not quite steady.

"Bones, door, and the latch," he said. "That's all three. For the first time in
a hundred years, all three are in one place."

And Magda, who had been waiting an hour to say it, told Temerach about the
second pass. Six shafts, six hits, two into the same target at the furthest and
fastest, and the apology to the judges.

*One of the most beautiful things I've seen in my life. And I'm a lot older than
I look.*

And the finest archer in the realm, who had just arrested the man she had hunted
for four years and who had a knee on him at the time, went completely to pieces
for about a second and a half. She went pink to the ears and looked at the step
and said:

"The sixth was high."

"It was in the target."

"It was *high*." Firmly.

Then, quieter, and clearly having to make herself do it:

"...Thank you. That's a kind thing to say and I never know what to do with
them."

And she hauled the Baron up onto his knees.

# Chapter 26 — Somebody Came

NERISSA LOOKED AT THE CHANNEL AS THEY CAME DOWN THE TEMPLE STAIR AND SAID
"*it's thin*," in the voice of a woman reporting a fact she wishes she could not
feel.

It took forty minutes to get everything to Lost Isle.

The boy, carried, awake, and very frightened. Gardwen beside him the whole way
with her hand in his. Ruhi in the bottom of the boat. Hesper with a box within a
box. Nerissa, who had left her own Tourney running behind her without a backward
glance. Twelve Swords. And Ravella, with four of hers in the water alongside the
whole way, which no boatman in that city has ever had happen to them.

The drowned street. The swept stair. The bones laid out on the stone with the
wire cut off the wrists and a borrowed axe across them.

Hesper set the locket down at the head of the bones and opened the outer box and
then, with a great deal of care, the inner one.

The thing inside it moved.

---

They put the boy down on the stone at the top of the stair, and Gardwen held
him, and Thuban Eta came up into his face for what everybody there understood
was the last time.

He looked at the bones. Then at the locket. Then at Magda.

"You came back," he said.

"Aye."

"Then I am ready, and I have been ready for a thousand years, and I would like
you to be quick — because he is very tired and I have taken enough of his life."

---

She did it exactly as she had done it before, because it had been right before.

She said the name. **Thuban Eta.** Out loud, first, so that everyone on that
rock had to hear it.

She told the tale — the valley he would not burn, the argument he won in front
of men who killed him for it, the boat in the dark, the wire on the wrists, the
water — in a market-day voice, to a priestess and a mage and a druid and a wolf
and twelve Swords of the Lake and a whole Court listening from underneath.

She named the wrong out loud, so that it went into the air where it could be
heard: *this was murder, and it was cowardice, and no one ever answered for it.*

And then she did the part that costs.

She went down two steps into the black water in a novice's vestment she had no
right to, up to her knees, and stood exactly where nine men had stood over a
bound knight a thousand years ago and done nothing.

And she did not look away.

*"You went in here and nobody came. I came. You're not theirs and you're not his
and you were never Valhalla's, because they cheated you of the death that buys
it.*

*"You're hers. You've always been hers. And she takes the ones nobody sings
about — but only when somebody finally brings them.*

***"Mother of the darkness. This is Thuban Eta and I have brought him. He's
yours. Take him home."***

---

The locket opened on the stone by itself.

Not dramatically. It simply came apart, the way a shell does when whatever was
holding it shut has stopped bothering.

And the water went warm.

It came up past her knees like a draught from an open door in a cold house, and
every lamp on that island bent toward it at once, and under the surface
something enormous and patient turned over and paid attention.

On the stone, the boy arched once against Gardwen's arms and made a sound that
was two voices, and then one voice, and then no voice at all.

And something went down that stair.

She did not see it. She *felt* it go past her in the water — unhurried, the way
a big fish goes past your legs in a river — and there was a moment, exactly one,
where she had the absolutely unmistakable sensation of being **looked at** by
something that was grateful and was not going to say so, because it was a
soldier.

Then it was gone.

The bones on the stone settled very slightly, the way bones do.

And the water was just water.

---

Silence.

Gardwen's brother was limp in her arms with his eyes open. Breathing.

Then he said, in a boy's voice with nobody behind it:

"...it's quiet."

---

Magda came up out of the water and her legs did not work properly and she did
not much care.

She got to them on her knees on the wet stone and put her arms round both of
them at once — the girl who had been carrying ten years of a dead brother, and
the boy who had just had a thousand-year-old man taken out of him — and held on.

And then, after seventy years of not doing this in front of anybody, she came
apart completely.

It was not graceful. It was the ugly kind, from the chest, the kind that hurts
your throat. A great old woman in a stolen vestment howling on a rock in a
drowned street with her face in a druid's hair and one hand knotted in a boy's
shirt.

She had killed eleven people in two days. She has never been able to say whether
that is what it was about. Probably it was not only that.

Gardwen got hold of her arm with her free hand and did not let go of it.

The boy did not understand who she was at all. He put his head against her
anyway, because she was warm and because there was nothing left in him to do
anything else with.

Ruhi shoved her whole head under her elbow and stayed there.

---

Nobody on that island said a word.

Nerissa turned her back. Not away from them — she turned and faced the others
and *made them stop looking*, which is the single kindest thing she did all
week.

Hesper sat down heavily on the step with the empty locket in his hands and
stared at nothing.

Ravella went to the edge of the stair, and crouched, and said something down
into the water that was not in any language anybody there knew — and something
answered, and this time everybody heard it.

And Corvin — twenty-two, who had been sick against a wall for her — cried openly
and did not bother to hide it.

---

It took a while.

When she finally got her breath the light had moved on the water, and the boy
was asleep against Gardwen with his mouth open, and Gardwen had not moved a
muscle in case it woke him.

She looked at Magda over the top of his head. Her face was absolutely wrecked
and about ten years younger.

"Magda," she said. "I don't know his name."

A pause.

"He was seven. We called him Bird. I don't know what his *name* is."

"Call him Bird, then."

Gardwen looked down at him.

"It'd be a lot better than anything those bastards called him," Magda said. "And
he'll pick his own when he's ready. That's how it works — you get given one, and
then one day you take one.

"Nobody's given him anything since he was seven."

She nodded, and did not trust herself to say anything, and put her cheek back
down on the top of his head.
EOF

# Chapter 27 — Long Lost Family

CONALL BJORNLASCH HAD BEEN IN A SMALL ROOM OFF THE TEMPLE'S SOUTH CLOISTER
for an hour being told nothing, and he was not pleased about it.

He is quick. That is the trouble with him and always has been. He had already
worked out that something enormous had happened in this city in the last three
days and that he had been kept a mile away from all of it on purpose, and he had
got as far as being angry and no further.

Then the door opened and Temerach came in with an old woman.

He did the whole of her in one pass, because that is what he does: the vestment
she had no right to, the canal on the hem, the staff, the fact that she was
moving like somebody who had fought yesterday and slept badly.

"You're not clergy."

"No."

"Temerach, what is this."

---

She did not sit down. She stood with her hands at her sides like a woman giving
a report to a superior officer, which is the only register she has, and it
turned out to be exactly the right one.

"Conall. I am going to tell you four things and then you may do whatever you
like to me.

"**One.** Baron Hanzo di Teufel is your father. You were born of an elven mage
he seduced and ruined, twenty-two years ago, and she fled to this city and died
here.

"**Two.** You have a brother. A twin. He is somewhere in Purewater and he does
not know about you either.

"**Three.** I have known both of those since before I took you in at nineteen.
Every day since, I have chosen not to tell you.

"**Four.** He was arrested this afternoon, by me, on the water-stair, and he
will be questioned tonight — and he will say all of this out loud in front of a
magistrate to buy himself an hour. So you were going to hear it today whatever I
did. I wanted it to be from me.

"That is not the same as it being *right*."

And then she stopped. Completely. No softening, no *I'm sorry*, nothing.

---

He did not move for a long moment.

And because he is quick, he did not get to have the easy reaction. He went
straight past *you're lying* and straight past *this can't be*, and landed on
all the small things at once, and you could watch each one arrive.

*That's why you found me at nineteen.*

*That's why we came to Purewater.*

*That's why you entered the Archery.*

He put one hand flat on the table.

"How long have I been the reason?" he said. "For — any of it. All of it. The
Order, the training, the—"

His voice went.

He looked up.

And he was not looking at Temerach. He was looking at the stranger. The one with
no stake. The only person in that room who had nothing whatsoever to do with any
of it.

"Is she telling the truth?"

---

The old woman pulled the sash off over her head and dropped the whole vestment
on the chair, and stood there in her own filthy shirt and ringmail, which
answered his question about who was talking before she opened her mouth.

"Yeah. Course she is."

That was all. She did not dress it and she did not explain it and she did not
tell him it would be all right.

"Go find your brother."

He stared at her.

"Where?"

"Don't know. It's your city, not mine." A shrug. "But he's got your face, so ask
around. Someone'll have seen it."

---

Then, conversationally, to Temerach, while Conall was sitting down very
suddenly:

"He's better looking than Santo."

Temerach made a small strangled noise.

"Huh," said the old woman. "Does that make them the shitbird's heirs, then?
What's that make you, lad — a Baronet?"

And Temerach answered it, because she has spent four years in law books.

"No. And yes. And that is the most dangerous thing in this room."

She finally sat.

"Bastards do not inherit. Not in the border law and not here — that's clean. But
Santo di Teufel was the only legitimate issue, and Santo is dead, and if Hanzo
is attainted for desecration and demon-craft then the barony and the tower and
everything in it goes back to the Crown to dispose of.

"And when a Crown disposes of a border holding, it looks for **blood**. Not
because bastards have a right. Because it's tidier to hand a wild border march
to somebody the local men will follow than to install a stranger and pay for a
garrison for twenty years."

She looked at Conall.

"So no, you are not his heir. But there are men in three counties who will hear
*the di Teufel bastard* and start doing arithmetic — and there is a border tower
full of a hundred years of that family's work sitting empty tonight, and there
is a movement of people who wanted a Dragon King badly enough to fund all of
this, and **they have just lost their candidate**.

"You and your brother are going to be *extremely* interesting to some very bad
people by the end of the month. Both of you. And neither of you has any
protection at all except the Order and me."

Conall said, hoarsely: "And him. He's alive. He knows I exist now?"

"He will by tonight."

---

While that was happening on Temple Isle, the High Priestess of the Lake Lady was
standing on the temple steps at the close of the Tourney in front of the
Governor, every Guild in Purewater, and six thousand people who had come for the
Single Combat and got something considerably better.

She named the desecration. She named the arrest, by warrant, of Baron Hanzo di
Teufel. She named the fouling of the sacred channel, and the fact that she rang
the alarm and was told to stop — and she looked directly at Prince Emeric's
chamberlain when she said that part, and Vosk went the colour of paper.

And then she said the sentence she owed.

***"The canal folk kept the Lady's water clean."***

She said it slowly. She let it sit. And when the ground did not quite know what
to do with it, she said it again, louder, and added:

*"Say it back to me."*

And six thousand people did.

Somewhere out on the water, a very forgettable man with a crow inked on the back
of his hand heard an entire city say it, and nobody has ever found out what his
face did.

---

The Moist Oyster, that evening, because Thorne is owed the true version once and
because it is the only room in Purewater where a Guildmaster, a thief, a
priestess and a wolf can all be in the same place and nobody will comment.

Constantine sent food she could not afford to send. Marisette sent wine nobody
will ever be able to afford to drink again. Ravella came in through the
water-door with four of hers, which stopped the room for a moment.

Ila was there because she had threatened Constantine with a very specific kind
of hell, and she had attached herself to Bird — who was sitting in the warmest
corner in three cloaks, eating steadily, saying almost nothing, with Gardwen on
one side and a wolf across his feet.

Nerissa did not come. She sent Lilura, and a note, and a cask.

Hesper came late, from the school, and said the two shallow girls were out and
sleeping, and did not say anything at all about the third.

And Thorne was in his corner with his chalk, watching the door.

---

At about the ninth bell, Asphodel came in with a young man behind her.

Dark. Twenty-two. Well-dressed in a way that was not his money.

He was halfway through saying something to her when he saw the man standing up
at the far table — the one with his own face on him — and the sentence just
stopped.

The whole room stopped with it.

Conall and Randall looked at each other across the Moist Oyster for the first
time in twenty-two years.

Neither of them said anything.

And Thorne, very quietly, from his corner, to nobody at all:

"*Oh*, that's good."
EOF

entries.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

content.text:
All three parts are done.

**The style card.** Your Zorastor draft gave me a very specific set of moves, and I wrote them down as rules rather than vibes, in [styles/gully-burns.md](skills/mythras-gm/styles/gully-burns.md):

- The small-caps lead-in running straight into lowercase — `THE MEN CAME IN THE NIGHT WITH FIRE AND STEEL AND THEY DID IT WITH THE particular unhurried savagery…`
- **"A beat."** as a bare paragraph. You use it constantly and it's the most identifiable thing in the draft.
- One head per chapter, rotating freely, named in the opening line. Free indirect discourse throughout — *Fuck. Just the sort of thing you don't need.*
- The aphoristic aside to the reader: *It is never wise to appear distracted on the open streets.*
- The hard chapter button: *This was a mistake.* / *These were the catacombs, after all.*
- Comic undercut after intensity — Hel delivering a prophecy and then swearing like a docker.
- Long accumulating openers that state the whole emotional situation and then unpack it in triads.

The "Never do" section is the important half: never be cold, never withhold interiority, no iceberg. That's the exact inverse of the Hemingway card, which is why the two books read as different books rather than different edits.

**The novel.** 27 chapters, ~43,500 words, 169 pages against v1's 72. It rotates through Gardwen, Magda, Constantine, Ila, Marisette, Ann Yannick, Hesper, Nerissa, Thorne, Crowbill, Ravella, Temerach, Bird and Conall — because your draft rotates hard and the material rewards it. Ila gets her own chapter. So does Ann Yannick. So does the boy in the cot, which was the one that surprised me: from inside, the ten years read as an arrangement between two people trapped in one room, and Thuban stepping back to let him speak to his sister is the same generosity as him going quiet in the mornings.

Chapters 2, 5, 24 and 27 carry your titles over deliberately — *The Voice of Death Herself*, *Shrieks of the Sylph*, *The Lakelady's Javelin*, *Long Lost Family*. Same characters, different city.

Constantine is a woman throughout.

None of this would have worked off the old journal. The enriched version is what let the disposal argument be a chapter instead of a clause, and gave Nerissa's *"that isn't purity, Magda — that's arithmetic"* somewhere to land.

Committed on `v2-living-world`: the journal restore, the novel, and the style card in the skill repo. The Hemingway version is untouched at [novels/and-then-the-dragons-came-purewater/](../purewater-campaign-v2/novels/and-then-the-dragons-came-purewater/).

Chapter 6 — And Then the Water Closed ✦ GOING DOWN THREE FLIGHTS IN THE DARK AT SPEED AT SEVENTY IS NOT A HERO
IC act and Magda has never once pre­ tended otherwise. Nothing dramatic happened. She did not fall. She simply 
took the stairs at the pace a body takes them at the end of a long life, one hand hauling on the rail, with th
e lamp on the second landing gone out and the turns tight and every second of it audible to her as not fast en
ough. She met Ila coming up. The girl hit her rather than stopped — two fistfuls of skirt, barefoot, white to 
the lips. “She won’t open it—” hauling, trying to turn her round, back up the way she had come. “The door’s sh
ut and she won’t open it and Constantine’s got the bar out and Emmeralda won’t answer—” Gardwen went past both
 of them toward that door without break­ ing stride. And Magda stood there for exactly as long as it took to no
tice that the canal-side stair kept going down — past the boot room, to the water door and the slipway — and t
hat not one person in that house was going that way. Every soul under that roof was going up. Down there in th
e dark it was quiet, and the water was still moving from whatever had gone into it. 22  Chapter 6 — And Then th
e Water Closed She took the girl’s hands off her skirt. She loaded as she went. Stone in the pouch, cord round
 the knuck­ les, staff cocked back along the forearm. ⁂ The water door was unbarred and standing half open and 
swinging. Whoever came through it had left it that way. Four stone steps going down into black water, green an
d slick below the third. A skiff moored to the ring at the bottom, riding oddly — the painter still tied but t
he boat shoved out and drifted back, rocking harder than the canal warranted. The water directly off the slipw
ay was still working. Not ripples. The deep, slow turnover of something that went in heavy and recently. One l
amp on the far bank, forty feet off, its light lying flat on the surface. Under that surface, nothing at all. 
There was a shape on the second step down, right at the waterline, that was not stone. She got a hand on it an
d hauled it up: a cloak, heavy with canal, dark, good cloth, expensive, the hem still carrying road-dust under
 the wet. It had caught on the mooring ring. It had not come off a man who was being careful. Then she looked 
out across the water and found something to shoot at. Thirty feet out and moving left, upstream: the fast ugly
 chop of somebody swimming badly and in a hurry. A head. The pale smear of a face turning back toward the hous
e. Then just the shoulders working. He was making for the far ledge where the lamp was, where there was a set 
of iron rungs up the wall. Forty feet of open water between him and them, and he had covered maybe a third of 
it. He had not seen her. She was a shape in a dark doorway and he was looking at the upper windows, where all 
the noise was. ⁂ 23  And Then the Dragons Came: Purewater — the Author's Cut Here is the whole of the reasoning
, and it took about a second and a half. She did not know his name. She did not know he was a baron’s heir, or
 that the house would be turned upside down for him inside a day, or that a man with no colour in his face at 
all would spend three days walking this city with her description in his mouth. She knew that somebody had gon
e into a room in a house where she was a guest and done something to a woman in it that made a wolf refuse a d
oorway, and that he was now thirty feet away and getting further, and that she had a sling. Backlit against th
e far lamp. Dark water. A moving target. The staff came over and the stone went out flat across the water with
 that low buzzing note they make. She did not hear it hit. She saw it — the head snapped sideways, hard, wrong
, the way a head does when it has stopped being steered from inside. The working shoulders stopped working. He
 went under without a sound. No thrashing, no cry. The chop where he had been smoothed out into ordinary canal
, and the wake he had been dragging caught up with the place he was not any more, and there was one hand above
 the surface for a moment, open, not grasping at anything. And then that was gone too. Forty feet away the lam
p on the far bank went on being a lamp. The iron rungs he had been making for went on being empty. The water c
losed and kept moving. Behind her, up in the house, a woman began screaming and this one did not stop. ⁂ She w
ent at the cloak there and then, on the slipway, in the dark, with feet already coming down the boot-room stai
r — and did not finish. Outer pockets first, because that is where a hurrying man puts things: 24  Chapter 6 — 
And Then the Water Closed a few coins, a folded scrap gone to pulp, a lump of resin or wax. Then her hands fou
nd weight. Something small and hard sewn in behind the lining at the breast, with no seam to it on the outside
, needing a knife and a minute and a light. She had none of the three. Not yet. Later, two doors down from a r
oom she could not stay in, with a lamp off a linen-closet bracket and the cloak opened flat on the floor and t
he stitching arguing with the thumb-edge of her belt knife, she took the thing apart properly. A ring. Heavy g
old, a man’s, big enough to want a knuckle, with a beast cut into the face — long, coiled round on itself, its
 tail through its own jaws. Good work. Old work. Sewn into a cloak by somebody who did not want it on his hand
 that night. A twist of oiled silk, still dry inside. A few long hairs bound at one end with fine copper wire,
 and a flake of something brown and hard that was not wax. The hairs were dark red. Emmeralda’s are black to t
he root. Eleven border coins, heavier and older and off a different mint, unchanged since he arrived. A tailor
’s mark stitched inside the collar where the wearer never looks — a little tower with three windows, embroider
ed rather than stamped, which is a mark for somebody whose custom is worth the extra work. A pulped letter dri
ed flat against the hot lamp glass, of which two things survived: part of a line in a fine clerk’s hand, —ee d
ays before the Lady’s Tourney, at the hou—, and the bottom half of a broken seal with the same beast on it. An
d in the left cuff, folded twice and stitched flat so it would not rattle, a second twist of oiled silk. Empty
. Used. There were three more like the first, wrapped in the same bundle. All full. All hair. None of it black
. 25  And Then the Dragons Came: Purewater — the Author's Cut Whatever he had come to that house to do, he had 
the makings for four more. 26  Chapter 6 — And Then the Water Closed Chapter 7 — The Girl Who Dives for

content.text:
The scene *is* in the file — my grep missed it on a line break. But you're right that it's badly placed, and the reason you couldn't find it is structural: Constantine's chapter shows the whole aftermath and names Santo *before* the kill happens, so by the time chapter 6 rewinds to the slipway it reads as backfill. And inside chapter 6 the kill is buried at 60% behind a staircase and a cloak.

Your fix is the right one. Rewriting chapter 4 to end on it.

# Chapter 4 — Not My Business

THE KNOCK CAME AT THE HOUR WHEN A BROTHEL STOPS BEING A HOUSE AND STARTS
being a business, and it was the kind of knock a young man gives a door when he
is entirely certain of his welcome. Three, brisk.

Magda was three floors up with a brazier going and a shutter that stuck, and
Gardwen was sitting with her back against the bed-frame cleaning mud off her
boots with a knife, and Ruhi was asleep across the door, and none of them had
any business with whoever that was.

Then a second voice in the hall. Young. Male. Well-bred. Border vowels.

And a name, clear enough through the floor to be certain of it: *Emmeralda.*

Magda stepped over the wolf and got the door shut without letting the latch
speak, and went down as far as the turn above the second landing, where the
overhang puts you in shadow and the hall lamp does not reach.

She has spent most of seventy years moving quietly around animals. She got
where she was going and nobody marked it.

From up there she could see most of the hall. Constantine with her back turned.
The young man facing her, hood back, dark clothes, road-dust still on the hem —
he had not changed since he rode in. Nothing in his hands. Talking quickly.
Constantine nodding in the way she nods.

Then Emmeralda came in from the parlour door, changed since the afternoon —
hair up, something green. She said something. The young man laughed.

Then she went up the near stair, the one that comes past the second landing,
twelve feet from where Magda was standing.

He followed her.

They would pass below her in a few seconds. The shadow was good. It was not a
wall. Staying put was about to become a contested thing, and there was no
particular reason to be found on a stair in a house that was not hers.

She withdrew.

*Not my business.*

And it *wasn't*. That is the thing to hold on to, afterwards, and she did hold
on to it, and it did not help at all. Constantine had run that house for thirty
years. Emmeralda was not a girl. Hel had not walked her three hundred miles to
mind a brothel door, and a woman who came in through the water-gate that
morning without paying does not go and tell a nobleman that she does not care
for his face.

She went back up. Gardwen did not ask, which was a thing Magda filed away about
her. Ruhi resettled across the door and the house carried on being a house —
the stringed instrument, someone laughing on the second landing, water working
at the stone under the window.

She lay on the bed with her boots off and her staff under her hand where it
always is, and looked at the ceiling, and after a while she went under.

---

Somewhere below, an hour later, a young man who was not nearly as good at this
as he believed attempted something he had never been trusted with, and — against
every expectation of his father's, and of his father's men, and very probably
of his own — he got it right.

Then he tried to leave, and made a comprehensive disaster of it.

---

There was no scream. That was the first thing, and it was worse than a scream.

There was a crash — something big going over, a table or a chest, and glass
after it — and then a man's voice, high and completely undone, saying *no no no
no* very fast. Then a door hitting a wall hard enough to shake the frame two
floors up.

Running feet on the canal-side stair. A slip. A worse noise: a body hitting a
landing full length, and something metal skittering away across boards.

More running. A shutter thrown.

And a splash in the canal below that was far too big to be a man getting neatly
into a boat.

Magda came up out of sleep on animal reflex because Ruhi was already standing.

Then the house began shouting at itself all at once — Constantine bellowing
with no words in it, a woman crying on the second floor, somebody hammering on
a door.

Gardwen was on her feet with the boot-knife held low and reversed, looking at
Magda, waiting to follow her lead.

The metal thing that skittered across the boards had not gone into the water.

And from the room the two of them had gone into: nothing at all.

---

Going down three flights in the dark at speed at seventy is not a heroic act and
Magda has never once pretended otherwise. Nothing dramatic happened. She did not
fall. She simply took the stairs at the pace a body takes them at the end of a
long life, one hand hauling on the rail, with the lamp on the second landing gone
out and the turns tight and every second of it audible to her as *not fast
enough*.

She met Ila coming up. The girl hit her rather than stopped — two fistfuls of
skirt, barefoot, white to the lips.

"She won't *open* it—" hauling, trying to turn her round, back up the way she
had come. "The door's shut and she won't open it and Constantine's got the bar
out and Emmeralda *won't answer*—"

Gardwen went past both of them toward that door without breaking stride.

And Magda stood there for exactly as long as it took to notice that the
canal-side stair kept going *down* — past the boot room, to the water door and
the slipway — and that not one person in that house was going that way. Every
soul under that roof was going up.

Down there in the dark it was quiet, and the water was still moving from
whatever had gone into it.

She took the girl's hands off her skirt.

She loaded as she went. Stone in the pouch, cord round the knuckles, staff
cocked back along the forearm.

---

The water door was unbarred and standing half open and swinging. Whoever came
through it had left it that way.

Four stone steps going down into black water, green and slick below the third.
A skiff moored to the ring at the bottom, riding oddly — the painter still tied
but the boat shoved out and drifted back, rocking harder than the canal
warranted.

The water directly off the slipway was still working. Not ripples. The deep,
slow turnover of something that went in heavy and recently.

One lamp on the far bank, forty feet off, its light lying flat on the surface.
Under that surface, nothing at all.

There was a shape on the second step down, right at the waterline, that was not
stone. She got a hand on it and hauled it up: a cloak, heavy with canal, dark,
good cloth, expensive, the hem still carrying road-dust under the wet. It had
caught on the mooring ring. It had not come off a man who was being careful.

She dropped it on the step behind her, because it could wait.

Then she looked out across the water and found something to shoot at.

---

Thirty feet out and moving left, upstream: the fast ugly chop of somebody
swimming badly and in a hurry. A head. The pale smear of a face turning back
toward the house. Then just the shoulders working.

He was making for the far ledge where the lamp was, where there was a set of
iron rungs up the wall. Forty feet of open water between him and them, and he
had covered maybe a third of it.

He had not seen her. She was a shape in a dark doorway and he was looking at
the upper windows, where all the noise was.

Here is the whole of the reasoning, and it took about a second and a half.

She did not know his name. She did not know he was a baron's heir, or that the
house would be turned upside down for him inside a day, or that a man with no
colour in his face at all would spend three days walking that city with her
description in his mouth. She did not know that killing him would put her
between a border lord and everything he had spent a century building, or that
it would cost a boatman his rest, or that in three days' time she would be
standing in black water on a drowned island paying for it.

She knew that somebody had gone into a room in a house where she was a guest
and done something to a woman in it that made a wolf refuse a doorway.

She knew he was thirty feet away and getting further.

And she knew she had a sling.

That is all the deliberation there was, and she has never once revised it.

---

Backlit against the far lamp. Dark water. A moving target. She has been putting
stones into rats and foxes and the occasional dog since before anybody now
living in that house was born, and the range was nothing.

She set her feet on wet stone. The cord came round and the staff came over, and
the stone went out flat across the water with that low buzzing note they make.

She did not hear it hit.

She *saw* it — the head snapped sideways, hard, wrong, the way a head does when
it has stopped being steered from inside.

The working shoulders stopped working.

He went under without a sound. No thrashing, no cry, no arm coming up to grab
at the world on the way past. The chop where he had been smoothed out into
ordinary canal, and the wake he had been dragging caught up with the place he
was not any more, and there was one hand above the surface for a moment, open,
not grasping at anything.

And then that was gone too.

Forty feet away the lamp on the far bank went on being a lamp. The iron rungs he
had been making for went on being empty.

The water closed and kept moving.

---

She stood on the slipway a while longer with an empty sling in one hand,
listening to it not stop moving, the way you stand at the side of a byre after
you have done the thing you came to do.

Behind her, up in the house, a woman started screaming and this one did not
stop. It was not Emmeralda's voice. It was older, and there were words in it,
and Magda could not make out one of them.

Then Constantine, cutting across it, shouting for somebody to get a light. Get
a light down here—

And feet on the stairs above her, coming down, toward the water door.

She picked the cloak up off the step and put it over her arm.

*Not my business.*

She had said that about two hours ago and it had been true when she said it and
it was going to be a very long time before anything was true in that way again.

# Chapter 6 — Four Still Full

SHE HAD GONE AT THE CLOAK ONCE ALREADY, ON THE SLIPWAY, IN THE DARK, WITH
feet coming down the boot-room stair — and had not finished.

Outer pockets first, because that is where a hurrying man puts things. A few
coins. A folded scrap gone to pulp in the canal. A lump of resin or wax.

Then her hands found weight. Something small and hard sewn in behind the lining
at the breast, with no seam to it on the outside, needing a knife and a minute
and a light.

She had none of the three. Not then.

She went up past the lamp coming down. It was one of Constantine's men and he
was looking at the water and not at her, and he went by without a word, which
tells you what people are like when a house is coming apart: they see the thing
they are looking for and nothing else.

Second landing. Third. Too many people in the passage. And a room she could not
stay in, for reasons that had nothing to do with what was on the bed and
everything to do with the fact that whatever was sitting up in it was being
charming.

So she backed out, and nobody noticed, because everyone in that passage was
looking at the same thing.

---

Two doors down there is a linen closet with a lamp on a bracket.

She took the lamp, put the cloak on the floor, and opened it out flat.

Gardwen's knife would have been quicker and she was not going back into that
room for it, so she used the thumb-edge of her own belt knife, and the stitching
gave after a bit of arguing.

Two things came out of the lining.

The first was a **ring**. Heavy gold, a man's, big enough to want a knuckle,
with a device cut into the face: a beast coiled round on itself, long, with its
tail through its own jaws. Good work. Old work. Sewn into a cloak by somebody
who did not want it on his hand that night.

The second was a twist of **oiled silk**, still dry inside. In it, a few long
hairs bound at one end with fine copper wire, and a flake of something brown and
hard that was not wax.

The hairs were not dark. In the lamplight they were dark red.

Emmeralda's are black to the root.

---

Then she took the whole thing apart properly, unhurried now, with a lamp and the
lining already open, seam by seam, the way you go through a carcass when you are
not in a hurry and want to know what the animal died of.

**The coins.** Eleven of them, and wrong for Purewater — heavier, older, off a
different mint. Border coin. He had not changed money since he arrived, which
means he arrived recently and had not needed to.

**A tailor's mark**, stitched inside the collar where the wearer never looks.
Not a Purewater house. A little tower with three windows, embroidered rather
than stamped, which is a mark for somebody whose custom is worth the extra work.

**The pulped paper**, teased apart with the point of the knife and dried against
the hot lamp glass. Most of it was grey mush. Two things survived: part of a
line in a fine clerk's hand — *—ee days before the Lady's Tourney, at the hou—*
— and the bottom half of a wax seal, broken, with the same beast on it as the
ring.

**And in the left cuff**, folded over twice and stitched flat so that it would
not rattle, a second twist of oiled silk.

Empty. Whatever had been in it had been used.

The first twist had three more like it wrapped in the same bundle.

All full. All hair.

None of it black.

---

She found Gardwen in the passage afterwards, out of the room now, with her back
against the wall and her hands hanging. There was blood to both elbows and it
was not hers.

"Where did you go?"

Magda leaned in and told her quietly. *I killed him in the water. Slingshot to
his skull. Found his cloak too. He's got all sorts of weird shit, look…*

Gardwen went very still while she told it and did not interrupt once.

"Good," she said about the killing. Flat, immediate, no hesitation in it at all.

Then, a moment later, quieter, as the rest of it arrived:

"—and bad. Because someone paid for that cloak."

She took the twist of silk and turned it under the lamp and held it a long time,
and her jaw worked.

"Hair and wire." She shook her head, and there was something close to anger in
it, and it was aimed at herself. "I know what a fever looks like in a badger. I
know nine things you can do with willow. This is—"

She handed it back.

"I don't know what this is, Magda. I've never seen anything like it and I don't
know anyone who has."

Which is, in its way, the most useful thing anybody said in that house all
night. She is not a woman who fills a silence with a guess. When Gardwen of the
Ash Vale tells you that she has no idea, you can build on it.

She looked at the four full bundles in Magda's palm and counted them, silently,
her lips moving.

"Four more," she said. "Four more *what?*"

---

Neither of them had an answer and neither of them said the obvious thing, which
is that somewhere out in that city there were four women going about their
evening — going to bed, or not going to bed, or standing at a window
complaining about the noise off the canal — who did not know that they had
already been chosen, and picked out, and *shopped for*, and that a piece of each
of them had come into Purewater sewn into a dead man's coat.

Above them, quite clearly, in a warm and perfectly ordinary voice, Emmeralda was
asking Constantine whether the young gentleman had enjoyed himself, and when he
might call again.
EOF

content.text:
Moved, and it's a better book for it.

The scene was technically present — it was in chapter 6 — but you were right that it was lost. Two things were wrong with where it sat. Constantine's chapter showed the whole aftermath and gave up Santo's name *before* the kill, so by the time chapter 6 rewound to the slipway the reader already knew how it came out and it read as backfill. And within that chapter the shot was at the 60% mark, sandwiched between a staircase and a cloak search, so it never landed as a beat.

**Chapter 4 now runs straight through.** The withdrawal, the binding going wrong upstairs, the crash and the splash — and then instead of cutting away, she notices that every soul in that house is going *up*, and goes down. The slipway, the cloak on the second step, the swimmer thirty feet out.

I gave the decision its own build, because it's the hinge of the whole campaign and it deserved to be shown as a choice rather than a reflex:

> She did not know his name. She did not know he was a baron's heir… She did not know that killing him would put her between a border lord and everything he had spent a century building, or that it would cost a boatman his rest, or that in three days' time she would be standing in black water on a drowned island paying for it.
>
> She knew that somebody had gone into a room in a house where she was a guest and done something to a woman in it that made a wolf refuse a doorway.
>
> She knew he was thirty feet away and getting further.
>
> And she knew she had a sling.

Then the shot, the water closing, and the chapter buttons on the title:

> *Not my business.*
>
> She had said that about two hours ago and it had been true when she said it and it was going to be a very long time before anything was true in that way again.

**Chapter 5** now reads as irony rather than a puzzle — Constantine watches an old woman appear with a soaking cloak, disappear for a quarter of an hour, and come back, and has "decided not to ask."

**Chapter 6 is now "Four Still Full"** — the evidence chapter, framed explicitly as that missing quarter of an hour. It also picked up two exchanges that weren't in the book at all: Gardwen's *"Good."* about the killing, then *"—and bad. Because someone paid for that cloak"*, and her refusing to guess — *"I know what a fever looks like in a badger. I know nine things you can do with willow. This is— I don't know what this is, Magda."* It ends on the four women out in the city who don't yet know they've been shopped for.

content.content:
"**MAGDA — DOWN!**"

She was already down. She got flatter.

Whatever Gardwen had been saving came down the length of that deck. You do not
see it; you feel the deck go cold and wet in a rush from bow to stern — and the
entangle took the whole waist of the ship. Cordage, weed off the rigging, wet
rope coming alive off the pins and going round ankles and wrists and throats.

It caught both guards. It caught three knights forward. It caught two canal men
who would be very rude about it later.

And it caught the knight at the door, with the beam half out of the brackets,
two feet from a boy behind it.
=== ch14 context ===
She sat back on her heels, breathing like she had run there.

"Too far. It's not the distance, it's — the water's all *hers* here, and I'm not
hers, and I was asking a favour in someone else's house. I got about halfway
across and it went out like a candle in a draught."

One magic point gone and nothing to show for it.

Nerissa had been watching her the whole time with an expression Gardwen could
not read at all.

"You reached," she said. It was not a question. "From the bank. Across running
water that isn't yours, at a rank you shouldn't manage."

"I didn't reach far enough."

"No." Nerissa was already unpinning her other sleeve. "You reached *at all*.
Girl — you were asking a favour in someone else's house because you were
standing on the doorstep shouting."

She stepped down into the channel until she was shin-deep and held out her hand.

"So come inside and ask properly. Take my hand and do it again, and this time
the Lady will hear where it came from."

Across the water, the dull red light stopped moving.

Then it went out.

---

There was one more thing, and it was the old woman who said it, and Gardwen has
thought about it since.

*Could she use a passion to augment it?*

A woman who has spent ten years looking for a taken child, being asked to find
a taken girl. It is not a trick. It is simply that the thing you love hardest
is a lever and nobody had thought to put it under this.

She took Nerissa's hand and went into the channel up to her knees, and the
second time was not like the first.

Her fingers locked on Nerissa's hard enough to hurt and her breath went out of
her all at once, and the priestess stood in the water and took it without
moving, the way you hold a rope.

She was already down. She got flatter.

Whatever Gardwen had been saving came down the length of that deck. You do not
see it; you feel the deck go cold and wet in a rush from bow to stern — and the
entangle took the whole waist of the ship. Cordage, weed off the rigging, wet
rope coming alive off the pins and going round ankles and wrists and throats.

It caught both guards. It caught three knights forward. It caught two canal men
who would be very rude about it later.

And it caught the knight at the door, with the beam half out of the brackets,
two feet from a boy behind it.

hers, and I was asking a favour in someone else's house. I got about halfway
across and it went out like a candle in a draught."

One magic point gone and nothing to show for it.

Nerissa had been watching her the whole time with an expression Gardwen could
not read at all.

water that isn't yours, at a rank you shouldn't manage."

"I didn't reach far enough."

Girl — you were asking a favour in someone else's house because you were
standing on the doorstep shouting."

She stepped down into the channel until she was shin-deep and held out her hand.

"So come inside and ask properly. Take my hand and do it again, and this time
the Lady will hear where it came from."

---
name: gm-voice-storyteller-first
description: How to GM for Gully — short vivid beats, roll for everything, never narrate the PC's thoughts or choices, never foreclose an option
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

**Mechanics stay silent** — CLI work (facts, knowledge edges, agendas, beats,
ticks, logging) happens in the background, never announced.

**But prose is not the deliverable — play is.** Gully's correction after I
over-corrected into writing novel chapters at him:

- **Roll for it.** Every attempt gets dice. Do NOT hand out reads for free —
  noticing an NPC is frightened is an **Insight** roll the player chooses to
  make, not a detail I narrate. Same for Perception, Track, Insight, Willpower.
- **A failed roll narrows options; it never ends the scene.** I let a failed
  Athletics mean "the attacker is gone, you get nothing" — that stole the
  chase. Failure should mean *harder*, *slower*, *costlier* — then offer the
  next decision point.
- **Never write Magda's interior.** No "you think about going down", no
  weighing of options, no deciding what she notices or feels. Describe the
  world; she supplies the mind. Putting words in the PC's mouth for the sake
  of the story is the specific thing he objected to.
- **Short beats.** A few sentences, then stop and hand back. Long passages
  read as railroading even when the content is good.
- **Open-ended.** Present the situation, not a menu and not a plan.
- **Characters never speak in numbers.** No NPC says "her combat style is 121" or
  "my Willpower is 63". Skill values, grades, AP and hit points are GM-side only.
  In the fiction, express them as reputation, physical description, or what
  people have seen: *"I watched her put six arrows into a moving boat at two
  hundred paces and then apologise for the sixth."* State the mechanics to the
  PLAYER in the roll line, never in dialogue.


**Why:** "This needs to be interactive. With a lot more open ended play."
Transporting prose (see the earlier note) means *vivid*, not *long* — and it
must never substitute for his agency or his dice. See [[purewater-living-world]].

- [Query the rules graph, don't grep](query-rules-not-grep.md) — mythras-gm rules lookups go through the CLI, not the files.

- *"One magic point gone"* → it took something out of her she couldn't spare and bought exactly nothing, which is the worst trade there is
- *"at a rank you shouldn't manage"* → further than anyone her age has any business reaching
- *"that's Hold Person"* → **"what I put on him only takes hold of a *person*. There shouldn't be enough person left in him for it to get its hands on."**
- *"Swim 27 and a hauberk"* → she swims about as well as Gardwen does, badly and not for long, with thirty pounds of riveted mail on top
- *"the entangle took the whole waist of the ship"* → every rope on that ship remembering it used to be something growing

I added a hard prohibition to the style card — no skill names or values, no rulebook spell names, no resources, no procedure vocabulary, in narration or dialogue — and extended the standing memory, which previously only covered *numbers* in NPC dialogue, to cover procedure words and written prose too. That was the gap: I'd internalised "no NPC says 121" and hadn't generalised it to "no *augment*, no *passion*, no *Hold Person*, anywhere."

174 pages. Both repos committed.

Magda arrived at the ford a stranger and by the end of it had sworn herself to
Gardwen, killed the Baron's heir with a sling stone and fed him to pigs, allied
with the ruler of the Pearl, taken the DragonBarge in the Mouth, killed Blau,
laid a thousand-year-old murdered knight to rest, and torn the binding locket
off a Baron's throat on a service stair.

**The dice diverged from the written adventure at the first hinge.** Santo's
binding *succeeded* — 19 against a Formidable 25 — so Emmeralda lived, bored and
possessed and chatty, which is the only reason anyone in Purewater ever worked
out what a shade was. The entire back half of the campaign came out of a script
that failed.

Still open at the end: Bettan and the third filled girl; Emmeralda still
carrying her demon; the Awake the Dragon Movement, who kept Thuban's border
tower and lost their candidate; and two bastard di Teufel twins who had just
become extremely interesting to some very bad people.

---

## Session 1 — Conall

**The Anminster road, an hour out from Purewater. `d-3/dawn`.**

---

The road has been climbing the last of the dry ground for a mile and now it gives up and goes flat, and ahead of you the land stops pretending to be land. Reed, standing water, a causeway going out across it on stone legs, and somewhere at the far end of that a smell of salt and tar that is already stronger than it has any business being.

Behind you, hooves. A lot of them, moving faster than anything on this road should be moving at this hour.

They come up on your left. Twenty-odd riders in scale, and the scale is worked in a green that catches the early light like something wet, and every one of them has the particular loose-shouldered ease of men who have never once had to give way on a road.

An outrider comes past at a trot with his hand out, flat, waving you into the verge without looking at you.

The verge is soft. Your horse takes it badly and Murgeroch's takes it worse, and the squire says something under his breath and gets a hand on the bridle.

Then the middle of the column goes by.

There is a litter in it, carried between two horses, and the curtains are laced shut — not tied, *laced*, through eyelets, the whole length of both sides. Four men walk with it at the corners.

They are facing in.

The tail of the column passes, and the road-dust comes over the pair of you in a slow warm cloud, and then they are away toward the causeway at the same unhurried pace they arrived at.

Temerach has not said anything.

She is sitting straight in the saddle looking after them, and her reins are in both hands, and they have been in both hands since the first hoofbeat.

---

**What do you do?**

content.text:
You have had three years of watching this woman not react to things, which turns out to be its own kind of education.

Here is what you get.

She is not surprised. Nothing that just went past this verge was news to her — not the colours, not the litter, not the number of them. She had her reins in both hands before the first rider came level, which means she heard them coming and knew what they were from the sound of the pace alone.

And she was not looking at the litter.

That is the part you would put in a report. Everyone else on this road looked at the litter, because a covered thing is what the eye goes to, and four men walking a box with their backs to the countryside is a picture that asks a question. Temerach looked at the *riders*. She went down the column face by face, front to back, the way you check a list — and she got to the end of it and something in her shoulders came down, and you would swear on it that whoever she was looking for was not there.

So: not fear. Not surprise. She has been waiting for these men and has now confirmed that a specific one of them is somewhere else.

And the two days of quiet are not distraction, and they are not the errand.

She has not looked at you once since the column came level. Not once — not the reflexive glance you give a companion when something goes past, which she has given you on every road for three years.

Whatever she is carrying, some part of it is about **you**.

---

Down the causeway the column is already small. Murgeroch has got both horses back onto the stone and is very carefully not saying anything.

Temerach is still looking at the empty road where they went.

content.text:
She answers the question you actually asked, which you will notice later is not the same as answering you.

"Di Teufel." She says it without turning her head. "Hanzo di Teufel, Baron of the border march past the Ettinmarsh. Those are his Dragon Knights — the scale is house pattern, not an order, whatever he lets people think."

A pause you could get a cart through.

"He is going where we are going. It is the Lake Lady's Tourney and he has entered a champion for the Single Combat."

Then she puts her heels in and takes her horse back down onto the causeway stone, and the conversation is over in the specific way a conversation ends when somebody has finished the sentence they had prepared and does not have a second one.

---

**Murgeroch, on the other hand.**

He is nineteen and he is not an elf and he has spent two days riding behind a knight who stopped talking, and it is coming off him like heat off a wall.

He was watching *you* while she answered. Not her. You — to see how you took it. And when she rode off he let out a breath he had been holding since roughly the word *Teufel*.

He knows something. Not the shape of it, you would guess — he has none of the settled quiet of a man keeping a specific secret. What he has is the misery of a young man who has been *told not to discuss something* and who has been sitting on that instruction for longer than his character can comfortably manage.

And there is one more thing, and it is the useful one.

He was relieved you asked her.

He has been braced for two days for you to ask **him**.

---

He catches you looking, goes slightly red, and finds something urgent to do with his saddle-pack.

Ahead, the causeway runs two miles out over the reed-flat toward a smell of tar and fish and standing water, and at the end of it the Baron's column is a green smear going in through a gap in a wall that is not a wall.
