content.text:
Your list, in full — **Arcane Casting 73**, seventeen magic points:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Seeing** | Witchsight · Detect Magic · Read Magic · Read Thoughts · Locate Object · Find |
| **Not being seen** | Incognito · Change Appearance · Invisibility (Lesser) · Invisibility Radius · Darkness · Mimic · Ventriloquism |
| **Illusion** | Illusion (Lesser) · Illusion (Greater) · Audible Illusion · Mirror Image · Colour Cascade |
| **Getting on** | Friendship · Babble · MindSpeech |
| **Practical** | Knock · Light · Protection · Coordination · Shocking Grasp |

That is an investigator's kit and almost nothing else. One offensive spell, and it requires you to be close enough to touch a man.

**Witchsight** is your Detect Evil. **Incognito** and **Change Appearance** are how you go where you are not welcome. **Knock** is how you get into what you are not meant to open.

---

The causeway takes most of the morning, because everything on it moves at the pace of the slowest cart.

Purewater has no wall worth the name — it has water instead. The road runs into a stone throat with a chain-boom across it, a customs pontoon lashed alongside, and the whole of tourney week trying to get through at once.

Temerach pays for the three of you without discussion and is waved through on the strength of the blue-green, and the customs man does not ask her a single question, which he asks everyone else about four of.

Inside, there is no ground.

That is the thing nobody tells you. There are buildings, and there is water, and between them there are ledges a yard wide with no rail, and the traffic that matters is *underneath* you — poled and rowed and shouting. Bunting everywhere. Somebody's cousin selling favours in dragon-scale green off a tray, three for a copper, doing very well out of it.

At the first bridge Temerach stops.

"I'm billeted at the Swords' barracks on Temple Isle. You are not." She says it to the canal rather than to you. "Find yourself an inn that nobody has heard of. Not on the Pearl, not in the Merchant's Quarter."

She hands you a purse that is heavier than an errand needs.

"Do what you do. Walk it, map it, learn who owns what." A pause. "And Conall — the Tourney opens in three days. Until it does, I would take it as a kindness if you stayed away from anything green."

Then she turns her horse, and Murgeroch turns his, and the squire looks back at you once over his shoulder before the bridge takes them out of sight.

You are alone in a city built on water with a full purse, a licence to ask questions, and a spell you have been saving for a litter that went through this gate an hour ahead of you.

content.text:
**Streetwise 95 against 67 — failure. Influence 28 against 20 — failure. Insight 73 against 88 — success.**

---

The schmoozing goes badly.

Not disastrously. Just — badly. You buy a bowl of something fried at a trestle by the fish market and try to be charming at the woman selling it, and she is pleasant to you in the way that costs her nothing, and tells you the weather. You buy a drink for a rope-walk foreman and get twenty minutes on the price of hemp. You try, once, to be light with a woman coiling line on a barge, and there is a pause afterwards long enough to hear the water, and then she says "mm" and goes back to the line.

You are extremely good at working out what people are. You are, it turns out, close to useless at making them like you.

---

The other thing goes worse, and you do not find out until later that it went worse at all.

You ask after where a man might find work with a blade, and where a man might find a game, and who a stranger talks to if he wants a thing carried without a customs stamp — and every single person you ask *answers* you. Cheerfully. At length.

By late afternoon you have a map of the underside of Purewater that is confident, detailed, and wrong. Two of the streets do not exist. The tavern you have been told is the mercenary house is a chandler's that closed last winter. The name you have been given three times as the man who moves goods quietly is a joke that dockhands play on out-of-towners, and you have now repeated it back to four separate people.

You are a well-dressed stranger with a full purse, asking after criminals, in a city with forty thousand visitors in it.

---

**What you do get is the mood**, and you get it properly, because that is what you actually are.

The city is *happy*. Tourney week is money and everyone from the Guildmasters down is having a good one. Nobody is frightened of anything.

The Baron is the entertainment. He came in at midday and let the city look at him and the city liked it — he is generous, he is handsome at fifty, he is being fed by half the Governor's council, and the whole town is enjoying a nobleman who does not obviously despise them.

And his champion is the joke of the week. He has entered a man for the Single Combat and not one soul in Purewater has been allowed to look at him. The odds are moving. Two Guildmasters have money on it. Everybody thinks it is a marvellous piece of showmanship and half the bets on the board are people betting on the *mystery* rather than on any man.

Nobody thinks that is strange. That is the first thing that snags.

It is enormous and it is packed — tourney week, dockside, the best trade of the year. Old beer soaked into older wood, tar, wet rope, fried fish, and the tide going under all of it. Sixty-odd people minimum. A girl mopping a floor that is not going to get any cleaner. A dog under a table that looks at you and decides against it. Somebody near the fire is singing and being comprehensively shouted at.

Nobody marks you coming in, because in a room like this at this hour a man coming in fast off a ledge is just a man who wanted a drink.

You get your back to the corner of the stair-side wall, which gives you both doors.

He does not look for you. He goes straight to the bar with the entirely convincing weariness of a man off a shift, buys a drink, and takes a spot along the wall from which he can see the street door and about two-thirds of the room. He never once turns his head your way.

**25 against 88. His 67 against 62.** You take it off him comfortably, and he knows it before you have finished the sentence.

He looks at you for a second and a half. Then he lets his shoulders down about an inch and something goes out of his face — not fear; *effort*. The effort of being a man off a shift.

"No," he says. "We don't."

He takes the drink.

---

Here is what you get off him while he is deciding to be honest, and it is a good deal.

**He is not a robber.** He has had a dozen clean chances at that purse today on ledges with nobody about, and he has taken none of them, and a man does not walk a mark past that much opportunity unless taking the purse was never the job.

**He is not the Watch.** Wrong boots. Wrong way of holding a cup. The Watch stand like men who expect to be argued with, and he stands like a man who expects to be ignored.

**He has been on you since roughly midday** — since about the third or fourth person you asked where a stranger finds a game.

**He is not frightened of you.** Not in the slightest. Which tells you rather more about whoever he answers to than it does about him.

And when you asked *do we know each other*, his eyes went first — fast, before he could stop them — not to the street door behind you.

To the **water door**. Where the woman in the carter's smock is still not coming in.

---

He drinks about a third of it and sets it down and looks at the cup rather than at you.

"You've had a busy day, friend." Mild. No edge on it at all. "You've been up and down the working canals since noon asking who fences, who fights for coin, and who moves a thing without a stamp. You've asked about nine people. Four of them told you about a man called Sump, which — " he almost smiles " — you'll want to stop repeating."

He turns the cup a quarter-turn.

"Nobody's angry with you. Nobody's touched your purse. You've not been rolled and you're not going to be, tonight."

Now he does look up.

"But a stranger with money asking those questions in Tourney week is either a mark, or he's somebody's, or he's the law. And until a man knows which of the three you are, he walks behind you."

A beat.

"So. Which is it?"

content.text:
**98 against 55.** He gets nothing.

You watch him try. He is not bad at it — you can see the attention arrive — and it slides off you and finds no purchase anywhere, and he knows it has failed, and that is worse for you than if he had simply decided you were lying.

He sits with the cup for a moment.

"Eleven years I've done this," he says, almost conversationally. "I can usually tell inside four words. Drunk, frightened, greedy, or lying — that's most men, and you can have the lot of them off the way they hold their shoulders."

He looks at you with something that is not quite hostility and is a good deal more careful than it was ninety seconds ago.

"I can't tell what you are at all. And *a flavour of the law that isn't the city or the king* is either the most honest thing anybody's said to me this month, or it's the answer a very clever man gives when he's worked out what I'd want to hear."

He pushes the cup an inch away.

"So I'm not going to decide. That's above me and I'd rather be told off for bringing it than for missing it."

---

Then he answers the thing you actually asked, and he answers it plainly, because you asked it politely and the answer costs him nothing.

"Nobody's angry with you because the man whose water you've been walking about on all day doesn't get angry at people he hasn't met. He gets *curious*. That's worse, but it's slower."

He turns the cup a quarter-turn.

"**Crowbill.** He owns the canals nobody draws on a chart. If a thing moves through this city without a stamp on it, he knows about it, and generally he moved it. He's not a crime lord out of a story — he keeps ledgers and he keeps his word and he's the reason this town works at all in Tourney week."

A beat.

"You spent a day asking the whole waterfront who does his job. He'd have been insulted if he *hadn't* put someone on you."

---

He stands, and takes his coat off the back of the chair, and does not look at the water door.

"Here's where we are. Nobody's touching you tonight. I'll say what you told me and I'll say I couldn't read you, and he'll want to look at you himself, because he doesn't like the ones he can't place either."

"So — do you want to walk to Gallows Reach with me now and get it over with, or do you want to sleep somewhere and have him send for you in the morning?"

Behind him, at the corner table, the old man with the chalk has been watching the whole exchange and has not touched his cup once.

"Him," Kerrin says, and does not look over.

He also drops his voice, which he has not done once in this entire conversation, including the parts about Crowbill.

"That's Thorne. He's been in that corner longer than I've been working. Buys nobody a drink, drinks nothing himself as far as anyone can establish, and knows every single thing that has ever happened in this city and a fair number of things that haven't yet."

He gets his arm into the coat.

"He was Order of the Lake. Thirty-one years. Two of them at the Governor's table, which is as high as a man from nowhere gets. And then he wasn't, and nobody will tell you why, and I'd not ask him if I were you — I've watched two men ask and I've watched what he did to them afterwards, and neither of them got hit."

A pause.

"He deals in stories. That's not a figure of speech, that's his *trade*. He'll take one off you and pay you fair for it and you won't notice you've been paid until you're outside. Half of what my own people know about this town, we know because Thorne decided we should."

Then, finally, he does glance over — one flick, and back.

"And no. He doesn't miss much. He's been watching you since before you came through the door, same as I have, and he'll have had the whole of that off our shoulders without hearing a word of it."

He settles the coat.

"Gallows Reach is twenty minutes by ledge. I'd rather not be out on the water after the ninth bell."

---

The room is still doing its best trade of the year. The woman in the carter's smock has finally come inside and is standing at the end of the bar with her back to it, not drinking.

The old man in the corner has picked up his chalk again.

He has written something on the table.

He is not looking at it, and he is not looking at Kerrin.

He is looking at **you**, and he has left it lying there face-up on the wood where you would be able to read it — if you were close enough, which you are not.

"Exactly the same," he says. "And I want you to understand that I am not being loose with the word.

"People say *the very image of his father* and they mean a nose and a way of laughing. That is not what I am looking at. I am looking at the same face. The same set to the eyes, the same distance between them, the same slightly wrong left eyebrow that sits a hair higher than the right one and always has. The same chin. If you shaved you and him and stood you side by side in the same coat, I could not tell you apart, and I have made a thirty-year living out of telling people apart."

He turns the chalk over.

"There is exactly one difference and it is not in the face. It is what's been done to it. He's got a white line under the jaw from a knife that came up in a doorway when he was about sixteen, and a nose that has been broken and set by somebody who cared. You've got neither of those and you've got something else instead — you sit like a man who's been taught to hold a line, and he sits like a man watching for the exit.

"His name is Randall. No second name that anybody uses. He turns the chalk over.

"Which is why the answer to your next question is no."

---

"Put the purse away. I mean it — put it away before Crowbill's boy sees you do it, because he is standing by that door working out what to tell his master and *the stranger tried to buy Thorne* is a sentence I would rather he didn't have.

"I don't take coin for silence. Not because I'm above it. Because the day I do, I'm a man who can be paid, and then everything I've ever said is worth nothing, and I'd have to go and get an honest living at seventy."

He sets the chalk down.

"You may have it for free. I have not seen you. There are not two of that face in Purewater. If somebody asks me tomorrow — and after tonight somebody will — I will look tired and old and I will tell them about the tourney odds until they go away."

A beat.

He almost smiles.

Then he holds up a finger, and this part is not generous, it is accurate:

"Understand what my silence is worth, which is *less than you want it to be*. I can hold my version. I cannot hold what other people saw.

content.text:
Twenty minutes on the ledges in the dark, and Kerrin walks them like a man in his own hallway.

He does not talk much. Halfway across he says, without turning round: "For what it's worth — I've told him worse news than you." And after the next bridge: "Don't offer him money either."

The woman in the carter's smock is behind you the whole way and never closes to less than thirty feet.

---

**Gallows Reach** smells of tar.

It is a working stretch — bonded warehouses, a crane, boats tied three deep — and the counting-house at the end of it is a narrow brick thing with a lamp over the door and two men outside who do not look at you as you pass between them.

Inside, a third takes your sword off you without discussion and puts it on a hook on the wall six feet away, in plain sight, where you could get to it in about two steps.

That is deliberate, and it is a courtesy, and you are meant to notice.

The room beyond is small and warm and lined floor to ceiling with ledgers.

---

The man behind the desk is wiry and about fifty and so completely forgettable that you would lose him in a crowd of four. Plain coat. Ink on his fingers. He is eating bread and hard cheese off a folded paper and reading something, and he does not look up when the door opens, because people come through that door all evening.

"Kerrin," he says to the page. "You're late and I've eaten."

"Aye."

"Is this him?"

"Aye."

So he looks up.

---

And Crowbill stops eating.

It is not dramatic. He simply stops, mid-motion, with a piece of bread about four inches off the paper, and he holds there for a good two seconds looking at your face.

Then he puts the bread down, and wipes his fingers on the paper, slowly, and folds it closed.

On the back of his right hand there is a small crow inked into the skin, and it moves when his fingers do.

"Kerrin," he says. Still looking at you. "Go and stand outside."

"Boss—"

"Outside. Shut the door."

The door shuts.

---

He sits back.

"Twenty-two years I've worked this city," he says. "I have had a great many surprises in this room and most of them were about money.

"You've got Randall's face."

He lets that sit.

"So before we do anything else — before I ask you a single thing about why you spent all day asking my water who fences and who fights for coin — you are going to tell me what you are to that boy.

"And I'd think carefully about the answer, because I've known him since he was nine years old, and I am extremely fond of him, and I have not yet decided whether you are a very strange coincidence or something that has come here to happen to him."

**Crowbill's Insight: 39 against 75 — he reads you, and he reads you clean.**

---

"Crowbill's what people say. It's not a name, it's this—" he turns his right hand over so the little inked bird catches the lamp "—and a joke about my nose that stopped being funny about fifteen years ago. It'll do. Everyone else uses it."

---

"I don't know your god," he says. "Ehrindill's not a name that's ever come up the canal. So the oath does nothing for me, which you should know, because half the men who come in here swear on something and I've buried a few of them."

He is quiet for a second, looking at you.

"But I've been reading faces across this desk since before you could walk, and I don't need the god. You didn't know. You'd never heard the name. Thorne wrote it on a table in front of you and that was the first you had of it."

Something in the room comes down about a quarter of an inch.

"Right. Good. That's the thing I actually cared about and you can have the credit for answering it straight instead of clever."

---

He pulls the folded paper back toward him, thinks better of it, and pushes it away again.

"Here's my position, and I'll give it to you plain because you gave me yours.

"I have a rule. It's the only one I've got that isn't about money and it's the reason I've still got a city to work in: **the people who grew up on my water are not stock.** You don't sell them, you don't use them, and you don't come here and do something *to* one of them and call it business.

"Randall is one of mine. Not on my books — he's freelance and he's a nuisance and he's stolen from me twice that I know about. Doesn't matter. Corliss's house raised him, then Asphodel's, and I've watched him come up since he was nine years old, and if you had come in here to be something that happens to him, you would not have got as far as sitting down."

A beat.

"You didn't. So we're past it."

---

Then he leans forward on his forearms and the friendliness goes out of it, not into hostility — into *work*.

"Now the other half.

"You said you ask questions because that's what you do. And you said you'd act on behalf of your masters *when the time comes*, which is a phrase a man uses when he has been trained not to say a shorter one.

"So." The crow moves. "I've a foreign lord in my city with twenty-odd armoured men and a covered box, half the Governor's council eating off his hand, and a champion nobody's allowed to look at. And on the same day, a stranger arrives who investigates things for people he won't name.

"I'd like to know if those two facts are related, and I'd like to know before I decide what you get from me.

"**Who do you serve, and what did they send you here to look at?**"

**57 against 74. His 46 against 62.** You both hold — but you hold higher, and he is the one who moves.

---

For a moment nothing happens at all.

Then Crowbill sits back, and something at the corner of his mouth does a small dry thing that is not quite a smile.

"Mm."

He taps the desk twice with one knuckle. The crow moves.

"That's fair. That's — yes. That's entirely fair, and I'd have thought less of you if you'd handed it over, and I'd have believed about a third of it if you had."

He does not sound annoyed. He sounds like a man revising a figure.

"I'll tell you what that was. That was me leaning on you to see whether you'd fold, because Kerrin couldn't read you and I wanted to know whether that was training or nerve. It's nerve. Fine. Noted."

---

"So let's do this the other way round, since you've earned it.

"I don't need the name of your master. I withdraw it. You're right that it's a personal question and you're right that I wouldn't answer it either."

He leans forward again, and this is the real business.

"What I need is smaller and you can give it me without breaking anything.

"**Does your business touch mine?**

"That's the whole question. I don't care who pays you. I care whether what you've been sent to look at runs across my water, my boats, my people or my arrangements — because if it does, I'd rather find out now, over bread, than in three days when one of my crews walks into the middle of it.

"You can answer that with a yes or a no and never say a name."

---

He picks the folded paper back up, opens it, and returns to the cheese, which is somehow the most reassuring thing that has happened since you came through the door.

"And after you've answered it, I'll tell you the thing about Randall that Thorne doesn't know, because Thorne watched him grow up in a tavern and I watched him come up on the water, and they're different stories."

content.text:
He does not answer straight away. He chews, swallows, and folds the paper closed again, and you have the distinct impression he is putting the answer where he will be able to find it later.

"'I don't know, and I'll come and tell you to your face if it changes.'"

He says it back to you exactly, which is a habit you will come to recognise.

"Yes. That's fair. That's better than fair — that's the answer of a man who intends to still be able to say it in a week."

He points at you with two fingers, briefly.

"And I'll hold you to it, and you should know what holding you to it means. It doesn't mean I'll come after you. It means that if it turns out your business *did* run across mine and you didn't come and say so, then you were a liar in my counting house, and this city gets very small for liars. Not violent. **Small.** No boat will take you, no house will let you a room, and every question you ask will get answered wrong by everyone, all day, for as long as you stay."

He picks the bread back up.

"That's it. That's the whole threat. It works better than the other one."

---

"Right. Your side's paid. Here's mine."

---

"Thorne'll have told you the tavern version. Pearl-born, raised in the houses, thieves like a gentleman, Marisette's known him since he was four. All true.

"Here's what nobody says out loud, and it's the bit that's going to matter to you.

"**Nobody knows where he came from.**

"He wasn't born in a house on the Pearl. He *arrived* there. Corliss took him in and Corliss is still alive and still on that island, and the story on the water — and this is thirty years of dockside talk, so take it at the weight it deserves — is that his mother came in off a *ship*. Not a Purewater woman. Came in sick, or came in and got sick, and did not last long, and the houses did what the houses do and the boy stayed."

He turns the cheese over.

"When he was younger, people used to call her *a sad story*. That's the phrase. Not a name — nobody I've ever met has used a name. And Randall heard it early and worked out it was a door people didn't want opened, and he has never once, in thirteen years that I've known him, asked a single question about her.

"Not one. That boy will pick a Guildmaster's pocket for the entertainment and he will not ask a woman on his own island who his mother was."

---

He looks up.

"Now. You were left with a watch captain four days' ride away, and told a birthday somebody guessed at.

"He was left on the Pearl with a dead foreign woman and no name at all.

"Same face. Same year, near enough."

A beat.

"I've no idea what that means. I'm a smuggler, not a priest. But I've been sitting here for the last two minutes doing the arithmetic and I don't like where it lands, because it means somebody *split* you — and people don't split babies for a good reason."

---

He sets the last of the bread down uneaten.

"So here's my one condition, and it isn't business.

"That boy has spent twenty-two years not asking. You are about to walk up to him and be the answer.

"Do it properly. Don't do it in a tavern for Thorne's entertainment, whatever the old goat offered you. And **don't do it tonight**, because it's the ninth bell and he'll be three drinks in and working, and you'll get a version of him that isn't him."

He nods at the door.

"Sleep at Meaney's. I'll know where you are by breakfast anyway — Kerrin's earned that much. Come back tomorrow and I'll put you in a room with him with nobody watching, and I'll stand outside the door myself."

The thin man arrives and stops about four feet away and looks at you for a long moment.

Close up he is unremarkable in every possible respect. Plain dark coat, grey at the temples, ink on two fingers, a face you would fail to describe an hour after meeting it. The bag hangs at the end of his arm.

"Good morning," he says. His voice is the least interesting thing about him. "Don't struggle against it, you'll only pull something. It goes off on its own in a few minutes."

Then he takes your chin between finger and thumb — the way a physician does, entirely without malice — and turns your face to the light.

You watch him find it.

His eyes go to the underside of your jaw, and stop, and stay there about a second longer than they should.

"Hm," he says.

He turns your face the other way and looks at your nose, and there is a second small pause, and then something in him settles that you would very much have preferred to stay unsettled.

"That's clever work," he says quietly. "That's *very* clever work, actually. I'd have said it was impossible on a face at this range."

He lets go of your chin.

Then, to the cord man, in exactly the same unremarkable voice:

She stands very still for a moment, and then something in her shoulders comes down.

"Cut him loose."

"Marisette—" from the dark.

"He named Thorne, Crowbill and Meaney's in one breath and he named *you two* back at you before he did it, which means he was listening on a ledge with his hands tied, which is not what a frightened liar does." She does not turn round. "And I can wake all three of those men before the second bell. Nobody invents an alibi that can be checked by breakfast.

"Cut him loose."

Somebody behind you does. It takes a while, and the cord man is as unhurried about undoing it as he was about doing it.

---

"You asked what this is about."

She pulls a stool over with her foot and sits on it, which puts her below your eye-line, and you understand after a second that she has done it deliberately.

"Last night, some time after the ninth bell, a young man came to a house on the Pearl called the Sylph's Embrace. He came in through the front door like a customer. He paid, he was pleasant, and he asked for a particular woman by name.

"Her name is Emmeralda. She has worked that house for nineteen years and I have known her for most of them."

Her hands are folded and completely still.

"He took her upstairs. And then he cut her open from the hollow of her throat to her hip — one cut, drawn slowly, with something barbed — and he chalked a figure on the floor around the bed while he did it, and he said words over her that the girl in the next room heard through the wall and cannot repeat.

"And then he left. Down the back stair and out the water door, unhurried, and nobody laid a hand on him."

A pause.

"She is alive. She should not be. Constantine has had her since three in the morning and there is no healer in this city who will tell me she'll keep."

---

"Two people saw his face properly. Constantine, in her own hall, with a lamp on him. And Emmeralda, from about a foot away, for rather longer than that."

"From parents," Marisette agrees. "Yes."

Eleven days, and she was lucid for about six of them, and every single time anyone asked she smiled and changed the subject — and she was *good* at changing the subject, which I thought at the time was manners and have never once thought about since."

She looks at the floor.

"She was running from something. I knew that on the first day. I decided it was none of my business because she was dying and it seemed a cruelty to press, and I have been comfortable with that decision for twenty-two years."

---

Hesper says, quietly, "Marisette. The man last night."

"I know."

"Say it anyway."

She looks up.

"The man who did that to Emmeralda has that face. Which makes him theirs. A brother, a cousin, an uncle — I don't know the word yet, but it is a *family* word, and it means the thing that came off that ship did not stop with her."

---

And Randall speaks for the first time since the elven blood, and his voice has gone somewhere flat.

"You said one baby."

Marisette does not answer straight away.

"I carried one baby down those stairs," she says. "I know what I carried. I have thought about it every year on the day and I could tell you what he was wrapped in."

"Then where was he?" He does not look at you. He is looking at her. "If there's two of us and she came off a boat with one — where was I, or where was *he*, and who had him?"

"I don't know."

"You've known me since I was four."

"I have. And I have never had one useful thing to tell you about the first year of your life, and I have let you not ask me about it for eighteen years because it was easier for both of us." Her hands are flat on her knees. "That is mine. I'll carry it."

---

Then she stands, and she is entirely the woman who runs the Pearl again, and it happens in about a second and a half.

"Right. **Corliss.** She took the boy in and she is seventy-one and she is still on that island and she was in the room when that woman died, and I have never in my life asked her a single question about it.

She turns to you.

"And you. You offered to work for nothing, which either means you are very rich or you have just found out you have a brother and would like an excuse not to leave the city." A beat. "I don't care which.

"Emmeralda is at Constantine's on the Pearl. She is awake, she is in a great deal of pain, and she looked at that man from a foot away for longer than anybody else alive.

content.text:
**61 against 73. 49 against 72.** Both hold.

---

The room stinks. Not of blood — under the blood. Scorched hair, and something sweetish beneath it like fat gone over in a pan, and a third thing further down that you have no name for and that closes the back of your throat on its own.

The bed is soaked black from the middle down and the black has run off the edge and dried in a fan on the boards.

---

**What is not here** is the first thing you notice, and it is the most useful.

There is no weapon. He took it with him — and a man who is running does not stop to look for a knife on a dark floor, which means he was not running. He finished, he collected his instrument, and he walked out through a house full of people and down a back stair.

There is nothing of his in the room at all. No glove, no button, no cloth. He came in with what he needed and he left with all of it.

That is not luck. That is a man who has done this before, or been very carefully taught by somebody who has.

---

**What is here** takes you about a quarter of an hour on your knees.

The chalk is not chalk. It is soft white stone, dressed and cut into a stick, and there is a place at the foot of the figure where the line stutters and doubles — he redrew that section, twice. Whatever goes there had to be *exact*.

And in the scuff at the head of the bed, worked into the join between two boards where a hurried man's fingers would never reach, there is a small twist of **oiled silk**.

It is scorched through on one side and it is empty, and when you get it up on the point of your knife there are three or four long hairs still caught in the fold, bound at one end with a turn of fine copper wire.

They are dark red.

You have now spent a quarter of an hour four feet from a bed belonging to a woman with black hair.

---

**And the figure.**

Seeing it changes it. It is a seat — you had that from the description and you were right — but it is not a well-made one.

It is *copied*. You can see it in the hand: the long strokes are confident and the joins are hesitant, the way a man writes in a language he can read but does not speak. He knew what shape to make. He did not know why the shape was that shape.

There is a break at the foot where the line is scuffed clean through, and the scuff has the shape of a boot heel, and it is on the inside of the figure.

He was standing in it. And at some point he stepped backwards out of it in a hurry.

---

Hesper has come in quietly behind you and is looking at the same break in the line.

"He didn't finish," he says. "He *stopped.* Or something stopped him."

Then he looks at the twist of silk on your knife-point, and the red hair in it, and goes the colour of the plaster.

"That is not hers."

"No," Hesper agrees. "Not hers."

He takes the twist off your knife-point with a pair of tweezers out of the bag, which tells you something about how he expects the rest of his day to go, and folds it into a paper.

"That colour is not common in this city. Not on the Pearl at all, that I know of — I would have noticed, and I notice for a living." He seals the fold with his thumbnail. "Marisette will know. She knows who is on that island the way a farmer knows his own stock, and she will be able to tell you inside a minute whether there is a red-haired woman on the Pearl and probably what she had for supper."

He puts the paper in an inside pocket rather than the bag.

"And if there is not one on the Pearl, then he brought it *in* — which means he came to this city with it already in his coat, and it was cut off a head somewhere else, and the woman it came off has no idea that any of this has happened."

He looks at the bed.

"Which would mean last night was not the beginning of anything. It was the *second* thing at least."

---

On the other question he takes so long that you think he is not going to answer.

"My story," he says eventually. "Mm."

He puts the tweezers away and closes the bag and sits down on the edge of a chest, which is the first time you have seen him do anything that was not necessary.

"Good. Then we want Marisette, and she went to Corliss."

Corliss's house is four doors along and across a footbridge, and it is the oldest thing on that row — a wide, low, extremely clean building with a door that has been painted so many times the carving on it has gone soft.

The old woman who runs it is seventy-one and she is sitting in her own front room with her hands in her lap and she has been crying, and she stops when strangers come in, in the way of a woman who was raised to.

Marisette is standing at the window with her back to the room.

She turns round when Hesper says her name, and whatever passed between those two women before you came in is still on her face and she does not trouble to put it away.

---

Hesper puts the folded paper on the table and opens it with one finger.

Marisette looks at it for about two seconds.

"Where."

"Worked into the boards at the head of the bed. He'd have needed a knife-point to get it out and he didn't have time to look."

"It's scorched."

"It's *spent*," Hesper says. "Whatever it was for, he used it."

---

Marisette picks it up. She separates the strands with one fingernail, precisely, laying them out flat on the paper the way you would lay out evidence.

"Emmeralda is black to the root," she says. "Everyone in that house is. Constantine won't take a girl she can't put in green."

She does not look up.

"There are two women on this island with hair that colour. I know them both, and neither of them works, which is why your man" — a small nod at Hesper — "has never laid eyes on either of them."

She lays the last strand down.

"One is a Watercrafter's daughter. Sixteen. Her father sits on the Guild board and she is not allowed out after dark and never has been."

A pause.

"The other is nineteen, and she is the High Priestess of the Lake Lady's own **niece**."

---

The room goes very quiet.

Old Corliss says, from her chair, to nobody: "Oh, that poor child."

And Marisette folds the paper closed and puts it inside her wrap, and when she speaks again her voice has gone somewhere completely level and businesslike, which after five minutes in her company you have learned is the most alarming thing she does.

"Right. I need to know which of them it came off, and I need it before dark, and I cannot walk up to either of those houses and ask — because if I am wrong I have told a Guildmaster or a temple that somebody has been cutting his daughter's hair off in her sleep, and if I am *right* I have told the man who did it that we know."

She looks at you.

"You are a stranger with a face nobody on Temple Isle has ever seen, an investigator's licence to ask questions, and a patron in the Swords of the Lake that you very carefully have not mentioned to me and that Hesper has very carefully not mentioned either."

**45 against 53** — Courtesy 41, plus twelve for the passion. Without it you would have missed by four.

---

You give them the address the Order uses rather than the one the street uses, and you give it to the older of the two rather than the nearer one, and you keep your hands where they can be seen without making a performance of it.

"Good morning. My name is Conall Bjornlasch. I've no letter and no appointment and I know exactly how that sounds.

"I would like to ask you to carry a message to the High Priestess, on a matter of some urgency, concerning **her niece**."

---

The younger one's head comes round so fast you hear his collar.

The older one does not move at all. He looks at you for a second and a half, and something in his face closes down very hard, and when he speaks his voice has gone extremely careful.

"Say the last part again."

"Her niece."

"What about her?"

"That's for the High Priestess."

---

He does not send the younger one. He goes himself, at a pace that is not running and is not walking either, and he leaves you standing at the gate with a nineteen-year-old Sword who has his hand back on his hilt and is now not looking at you in a way that requires effort.

You wait about four minutes.

The water goes through the temple behind them the whole time, and it is the only sound on that whole colonnade.

---

Then a woman comes down it at a pace that is not quite running.

She is perhaps thirty, in blue-green over a shift, wet to the knee, and she is not a guard — and she arrives in front of you and looks at your face with an intensity that has nothing polite in it at all.

"Who told you to say that?"

"Nobody told me to say anything."

"Then how do you—" She stops herself. Starts again, harder. "Where did you get it? Who *are* you?"

Behind her, the older Sword has come back and taken up a position about eight feet away, and he has not put his hand back on his hilt but he has not gone back to the gate either.

The young woman is breathing like she came a long way.

"I'm sorry," she says, and does not sound it. "I'm Lilura Deepcurrent. I serve the High Priestess.

"And she has been awake for a day and a half, and I have spent the whole of it telling people she is not to be disturbed — and you have just said the one word that means I have to go and disturb her.

"So you will understand why I need to know, before I do that, whether you are about to break her."

content.text:
**8 against 85 — critical.** She reads you all the way down, and what she finds is a man who does not know what he has walked into.

---

But she catches the thing you said before she catches anything else, and she catches it *hard*.

"Stop. Go back." Her hand is up. "You said *paraphernalia*. You said it suggested he had already done it to someone with red hair."

"That's how it looked to me."

"But what did you *find*?"

"A twist of oiled silk, scorched through, worked into the floorboards at the head of the bed. Empty. Three or four long hairs still caught in the fold, bound at one end with fine copper wire."

Lilura closes her eyes.

"Hair," she says. "Not — " and her voice goes somewhere very thin " — you found *hair*. Cut hair. In a wrapping."

"Yes."

"That is not the same thing at all." She opens her eyes and there are tears standing in them and she is completely ignoring them. "That is not a girl who has had something done to her. That is a girl somebody has *taken a piece of*, to do something with somewhere else."

She puts a hand flat on the gate post.

"Which means she may be perfectly well this morning and not know one thing about any of it."

---

And then she says the rest, because you gave her yours and she is not the sort to hold on to hers after that.

"Three weeks."

"I'm sorry?"

"The Mother has not seen Sana in three weeks. She is at the school on the Northern Isles — she went in the spring, she is nineteen, she is clever and her mother wanted her out of the Merchant's Quarter. Two letters in six weeks. The second one came eight days ago and it was three lines and it said she was *settling*."

She wipes her face with the back of her wrist, once, briskly, and is done with it.

"Her aunt read it and said 'good' and put it down. And she has been sitting with that for a day and a half on top of everything else, and she has not said the word *Sana* out loud to me once, which is how I know she is frightened of it."

---

She straightens up and becomes, quite suddenly, entirely professional.

"Right. You are coming in. Not because I am satisfied — because you are the first person in a day and a half to bring her something she can *do something about*, and she has been standing in that water going out of her mind for want of exactly that."

She turns to the older Sword.

"Corvin. Nobody follows him in and nobody talks about this on the gate."

"Mother's asleep."

"Mother is not asleep. Mother has not been asleep since yesterday noon and you know it as well as I do."

---

The colonnade takes you past the great tank where the channel runs through the temple itself, and the sound in that room is enormous — water on stone, everywhere, no other noise at all.

The far end is dark. There is one lamp on a low table and a woman sitting on the step of the tank with her feet in the water and her sleeves pushed up, doing nothing whatsoever.

She does not get up.

"Lilura," she says, without turning round. "I said nobody."

"I know what you said, Mother."

A pause. The water goes on.

Then the High Priestess of the Lake Lady turns her head and looks at you — grey through dark hair, sixty-odd, and awake in a way that has gone well past tiredness into something harder.

"Well?"

I ran two beats past your decision — that was mine, not yours. Pulling back to the colonnade, where the line lands.

---

Lilura stops at the mouth of the tank room.

You can see her lose her nerve. Not about you — about the door. She has spent a day and a half turning people away from it and there is a habit in that which is now working against her.

"She hasn't slept," she says. "Not since yesterday noon. She stood in that water eleven hours yesterday and I could not make her come out of it, and if I take you in there and this turns out to be nothing—"

"I think you should wake her. Don't you?"

She looks at you.

Then she pushes the hair off her face with both hands, and something in her decides.

"Yes. I do."

---

The colonnade takes you past the great tank where the channel runs through the temple itself, and the sound in that room is enormous — water on stone, everywhere, and no other noise at all.

The far end is dark. There is one lamp on a low table and a woman sitting on the step of the tank with her feet in the water and her sleeves pushed up, doing nothing whatsoever.

She does not turn round.

"Lilura. I said nobody."

"I know what you said, Mother."

"Then why is there a man on my colonnade at eleven in the morning."

"Because he came to the gate and said *your niece*."

---

The water goes on running through the room.

Nerissa takes her feet out of the tank and dries them on the hem of her robe like a farmer's wife, and stands up, and turns round — grey through dark hair, sixty-odd, and awake in a way that has gone a long way past tiredness into something considerably harder.

She looks at you for a moment.

"Sit down," she says. "There's a stool. You'll want it."

And then, with no ceremony left in her whatsoever:

"Marisette doesn't send people to me and neither does anybody else. So say the worst of it first, and we'll work backwards."

content.text:
**10 against 80.** One point off a critical, and it may as well have been one — she has you inside the first three sentences and spends the rest of it watching your hands.

---

"Mother," she repeats, when you have finished. "You gave me the right address at the gate as well. Where did a capital investigator learn how to speak to a lake-priest?"

"Somebody taught me to be careful."

"Mm."

She has not sat down. She has stood through the entire thing with the water running behind her, and she has not interrupted once, and the only movement she made in ten minutes was at the word *shears*.

---

"Right. I'll tell you mine and then we'll be even, because you have not asked me for a thing and that is going to stop being true in about a minute.

"Yesterday. Four minutes after noon. This channel went **wrong**."

She turns her hand over toward the tank.

"Not fouled. I have had fouled — fouled is a dead ox in the intake and a week of prayers and a great deal of tedious correspondence. This went *thin*. The Lady's presence in her own water went thin, the way a voice goes thin at a distance, in about ten heartbeats. I have served here since I was nineteen and it has never once done that.

"So I rang the tower.

"And by the third peal there was a boy from the Governor's household at my gate with a written instruction to *cease* — on the grounds that the city was welcoming a distinguished guest and the bells were causing alarm during a formal entry."

Her hands have closed.

"Written and sealed by Prince Emeric. Who is twenty-four and well-meaning and has been told by three separate men on his council this fortnight that his uncle would like the Tourney to go smoothly.

"And I stopped. Because I am the High Priestess of a temple that is paid for by this city's Guilds, and because I had *nothing* — a thin feeling in the water and no cause I could name in front of a magistrate."

She looks at you.

"I have been standing in that tank for a day and a half with no cause I can name. And you have walked in off a public ferry and handed me one."

---

Then she puts her hand out, palm up.

"Show me the hair."

---

And you do not have it.

Hesper lifted it off your knife-point with tweezers and folded it into a paper, and Marisette put the paper inside her wrap on Corliss's front step, and neither of them asked you and neither of them was wrong to take it, and you did not think about it once until this moment.

Nerissa's hand stays out for about two seconds longer than is comfortable.

Then it comes down.

"Of course you don't," she says — not unkindly, and that is somehow worse. "The madame has it. She'd be a fool to let it out of her hands and she is not a fool.

"So what you have brought me is a *description* of a thing, out of your mouth, and what I need to know cannot be established from a description. There are three questions I would ask that twist and every one of them requires me to hold it."

She looks at the lamp.

"Whether the ends are cut clean or knotted. Whether it was taken with shears or a knife. And whether it came off the head of a living girl or was gathered off a comb after."

A pause.

"Because those are three completely different mornings for my sister's daughter, and I have spent a day and a half not being able to ask anybody anything."

content.text:
"Emmeralda," Nerissa says.

Not sharply. She says it the way you would hand somebody back something they had dropped.

"Her name is Emmeralda and she has worked that house nineteen years and she is going to be a very long time dying or a very long time mending, and either way she will do it with a name. You may use whatever word you like on the Pearl and Marisette will not correct you, because Marisette is running a business.

"I serve a goddess of water and poor people. In here she gets her name."

A beat.

"Now say the rest of it again, because the rest of it was right."

---

She listens to it a second time — *assume the worst, act accordingly, find her, make her safe, look around her* — and something happens in her face while you say it that is not gratitude and is a good deal more useful.

"A day and a half," she says. "A day and a half I have had a thin feeling in my own water and a letter from a prince telling me to be quiet, and I have been sitting in that tank waiting for a *cause*, because I am a woman who was raised to have a cause before she moves.

"And you have just told me that I have had it the whole time and it is a nineteen-year-old girl."

She is already unpinning her sleeves.

"Lilura."

"Mother."

"The school. Corbie's, the Northern Isles. I want the fast boat and I want it at the water-stair when I get there, and I am going myself."

"Mother, the Tourney—"

"The Tourney opens the day after tomorrow and I have opened nine of them and they will manage." She is pulling the outer robe off over her head. "Corvin rows. Ash rows. Fetch my sister — no. Don't fetch my sister. Not until I know."

---

Then she stops, halfway through it, and stands there with the robe in her hands.

"And you should understand what I am about to do, because you asked me to assume the worst and I am going to, and it has a price on it.

"The High Priestess of the Lake Lady does not go to a school. Ever. If I cross that channel in daylight with two Swords and no announcement, then by supper there are forty girls who saw me come, and a mistress who will talk, and boatmen on both landings who will each have a version.

"And if the man who cut that girl's hair is anywhere near this island, I will have told him — loudly, in the middle of the day — that we have found the thread and are pulling it."

She looks up.

"I would rather be loud and early than quiet and late. But you have run more of these than I have, and you have been right about two things already this morning."

The water goes on running through the room behind her.

"So tell me if I am wrong."

content.text:
She does not answer for a moment. She stands there holding her own robe.

"You are a stranger who walked through my gate ninety minutes ago," she says. "And I am considering sending you to a house with forty girls in it to ask questions about my sister's daughter."

"Yes."

"And the reason I am considering it is that you are right, and I have known you were right since about the third word."

She drops the robe on the step.

---

"Corvin goes. Out of colours — he has a brown coat somewhere and he will hate wearing it, and he will do it. He rows you, he stands where you tell him, and he does not open his mouth once, and if you need to leave in a hurry he is the reason you can.

"Not Lilura. She is temple to look at even in a shift, and half those girls know her face."

She crosses to the low table and writes four lines on a scrap, fast, in a square hand, and folds it once.

"Mistress Corliss keeps that school — *not* the Corliss on the Pearl, her cousin, and if you get those two women confused in front of either of them you will not recover it. This gets you in the door and no further. It says you are mine and it does not say why."

---

"Now the part that matters."

She holds the note but does not hand it over yet.

"Sana is nineteen. She is clever, she is not biddable, and she has been at that school six weeks in a room with three other girls, and if you walk in wearing an investigator's manner and start asking who has been near her, you will get nothing, and worse — one of those forty girls will have it round the island by dark that the temple came asking, and that reaches the man you want faster than a boat.

"So you do not announce anything. You ask the mistress, quietly, whether Sana is in the house this morning. That is the only question that matters and it is answerable in four seconds.

"If she is — you look at her, you look at her *hair*, and you say nothing to her at all. You come back and tell me and we do the rest properly.

"If she is not—"

She stops.

"If she is not, then you may do whatever you think best, and I will answer for it afterwards."

---

Then she gives you the note, and one more thing with it.

"And if you find yourself needing that girl to trust you and there is nobody there she knows — tell her this.

"Two years ago she wrote me a letter about a heron. **Eleven pages.** One bird, standing in the reeds off the school landing, for eleven pages, in a hand I would know anywhere. I have it still.

"Nobody living knows about that letter except her mother and me."

She sits back down on the step of the tank and puts her feet in the water, and it is the first time she has looked her age.

"Bring me back something I can act on. I have not been able to move since yesterday noon and it is making me ill."

**To your question — yes.** Lilura is a genuine cleric of the Lake Lady, not an administrator with a title. **Piety 78**, and an Insight of **85** that is the best in that building including the woman who runs it. She is also the only person there with real Lore of the water spirits.

Nerissa answers it herself when you ask.

---

"Lilura? She's ordained. She took the water at nineteen and she has more of the Lady in her than she is comfortable being told about." A small dry look. "She reads people better than I do and she has never once believed me when I say so."

Then she works out why you are asking, and she does not like it.

"You want a caster with you."

"It had occurred to me."

"Yes. It would." She rubs her eyes with the heels of both hands. "And I said no and I am going to go on saying no, and here is why, and it is not stubbornness.

"Lilura Deepcurrent has been going out to that school four times a year since before those girls could read. She has taught in it. She examined half of them on their catechism in the spring. There is no coat in this city that makes her not the temple — if she walks up that landing stage, forty girls know inside a minute that the Order has come, and the mistress will have a boat away to somebody before you have got your second question out.

"You would be trading the whole of your quiet for one pair of hands."

A pause.

"Corvin cannot cast and he can row, and nobody has ever looked twice at him in his life, and that is worth more to you today than a spell would be."

She looks up.

"If it turns out you need a caster out there, then you have already lost, because it will mean somebody is *there* — and in that case what you actually want is to be back in this room telling me about it."

---

She holds out the folded note.

"Corvin's getting the brown coat on. He'll meet you at the west water-stair, and he will be sulking about it, and you may tell him I said he looks like a bargeman."

content.text:
Corvin is indeed sulking, and the brown coat is indeed too short in the arm, and he says exactly nothing for the entire crossing, which is the most useful thing anybody has done for you all morning.

The **Northern Isles** are forty minutes out — low, scattered, quieter than anywhere you have been since the road. Reed beds. Working boats. A cormorant on a post that does not move as you go by.

**Corbie's** is a squat old customs house with a wall round it and a landing stage that has seen better decades.

---

There is a light burning over the door.

At eleven in the morning.

---

The woman who opens it is about sixty and she has been crying, and she gets one look at the folded note in your hand — before she reads a word of it, before you have opened your mouth — and her face does something that turns your stomach over.

"Oh, thank God," she says. "*Thank God.* Where is she — is she with you? Did she get there?"

"I'm sorry. Who?"

And you watch the hope go out of her like a lamp being carried out of a room.

"Bettan," she says. "I sent Bettan. Last night, at dusk, in the boat with old Marrec — I sent her to the temple because I could not go myself and I have forty girls in this house."

Her hand has gone to the doorframe.

"Are you telling me nothing came? Nothing came *at all*?"

---

You give her the note. She reads it twice and does not appear to take in one word of it.

"Mistress Corliss?"

"Yes. Yes." She is not looking at you. "You're from the Mother."

"I am. And she sent me to ask you one thing, quietly, and I would like you to answer it before anything else."

"Ask it."

"**Is Sana in the house this morning?**"

---

The old woman puts both hands over her mouth.

"Since yesterday *morning*," she says, through them. "She has been gone since yesterday morning.

"We have had every girl out. We have walked the whole island twice and we have dragged the channel off the landing, and I have not slept, and I sent to her aunt at dusk because there was nothing else left to do —"

She takes her hands down.

"— and you are standing here telling me that the boat I sent did not arrive."

---

Behind her, in the hall, you can see perhaps a dozen girls of various ages who have all stopped what they were doing and are all looking at the door.

Corvin has not moved from the landing stage. He is looking past the house.

Four hundred yards across open water, low and black and weed-choked, there is a drowned island with broken roofs standing out of it.

content.text:
**58 against 88.** Comfortable.

---

**What she tells you.**

Sana was at breakfast yesterday morning. Nine girls at that table can put her there and two of them talked to her. She was ordinary — no tears, no letter, no quarrel with anybody. She ate, she took her plate through, and she went out into the yard at about the second hour and that is the last anybody in this house saw of her.

She was not carrying anything. Her box is upstairs, untouched. Her shoes — her *good* shoes, the ones she came with — are under her bed, which means she went out in the old ones, which means she was not going anywhere that mattered.

They missed her at the noon meal. They thought she was sulking. They went looking properly at dusk.

Since then: the whole island walked twice, the channel dragged off the landing, and a girl sent to the temple who has not arrived.

---

**And one thing you have to ask twice to get.**

"Is a boat missing?"

She looks at the floor.

"The small one. The flat one we keep for the reeds."

"Since when?"

"I don't know. I noticed it last night." Her hands are working in her lap. "It could have been gone a week. Marrec doesn't count them and neither do I."

Then, because you wait:

"The girls row out to the ruin. Across the channel." She says it fast, like something she has been holding. "They're forbidden. They have been forbidden for forty years and they do it anyway, every spring, one or two of them, on a dare — and I know they do it, and I have always known, and I have always thought it was better to let a girl do a silly thing on a still day than to make it exciting."

She looks up at you and her eyes are terrible.

"I have thought that for eleven years and I thought it was wisdom."

---

**And here is what she does not tell you, which you get anyway.**

She is not carrying guilt about Sana.

She is carrying guilt about **somebody else**, and it is sitting so close to the surface that it comes off her every time the conversation touches the word *girls*, and she has not once connected it to why you are here.

Twice while she was talking about the boat she started a sentence about another child and turned it into something else. Once she said "and I had *her* in, and I—" and stopped and drank some water she did not want.

Whoever that is, she had that girl in this room, in this chair, over something that worried her — and she decided it was nothing, and she is now sitting in the wreckage of yesterday morning with that decision in her hands.

She has not made the link. You can see quite clearly that she has not.

---

"The other one," she repeats.

And she does not open. You watch her close instead, and it is not evasion exactly — it is a woman putting both hands on a lid.

"There is no other one. There's forty girls in this house and every one of them is somebody's daughter and I have every one of them accounted for except Sana."

That is not what you asked and she knows it is not what you asked.

She stands up and goes to the window with her back to you, which is the first thing she has done in ten minutes that was not sitting.

"You'll want to talk to the girls who were at that table. Ana Vell was next to her. She's a horrible child and she notices everything, which today makes her the most useful person in this house."

---

**And here is what your read gives you, for free, because you had already made it.**

She did not relax when she said *there is no other one*. She got *tighter*.

That is not somebody who has run out of things to say. That is somebody who has just been walked up to a door and has put her back against it, and the effort of doing that is now sitting all over her shoulders.

Whatever it is, she is not going to hand it to you in this room this morning. She would have to say it about a child, out loud, to a stranger, and she is not able.

She will say it to somebody. Not to you, and not yet.

---

Then she says, to the window, in a completely different voice:

"Marrec came back."

"I'm sorry?"

"The boatman. I said I sent Bettan to the temple last night with old Marrec." She still has her back to you. "He came back. Of course he came back, he lives on this island, he was at his own table by the third bell.

"I did not ask him anything, because I assumed the child was at the temple and safe and would come back this morning with the Mother behind her."

She turns round.

"He's two hundred yards up the shore in the third house past the boat-shed. He has been there all night and all morning and nobody has spoken one word to him about it.

"You could ask him whether she got out of his boat."

content.text:
**34 against 88.**

---

He does not stop mending while he talks. He tells it the way old men tell things — flat, in order, with the interesting part treated as no part at all.

"Aye. Took her out at dusk. Mistress come down herself and said temple, quick as you like, and I'd not had my supper but you don't say no to Mistress about the girls."

"How far did you get?"

"Middle of the channel. Bit past."

He bites off a length of twine.

"And then she asked me to turn round."

---

You wait. He goes on mending.

"Turn round."

"Aye. Said she'd changed her mind. Said she'd been thinking about it and she'd sooner go in the morning, and to put her back on the north shore."

"And you did."

"'Course I did." He looks up for the first time, mildly surprised at the question. "She's the one going. It's her errand. I'm the boat."

---

"Where did you put her ashore?"

"Reed landing. North side, past the school wall — nobody uses it but the girls, it's all mud." He shrugs. "She said she'd walk up. It's five minutes."

"Did you watch her go?"

"I turned the boat."

---

**And here is what he does not say, because to him it is not a thing.**

He is completely untroubled. That is the finding. A girl of fourteen turned a boat round in the middle of a channel at dusk on an emergency errand about a missing friend, and asked to be put back down on a mud landing on the wrong side, alone, in the dark — and this old man has not thought about it once, and he is not thinking about it now, and when you ask him he answers as though you had asked him about the tide.

He was not charmed and he was not compelled. He was simply *told*, cheerfully, by somebody certain, and it did not occur to him to weigh it, and it has not occurred to him since.

You have watched a man be steered and not know it, and the steering was done by a fourteen-year-old girl.

---

Two other things come out sideways.

"She talk to you at all, on the way out?"

"Bit. Asked after my sister at the Shoals." He frowns very slightly, for the first time. "Which — she's not met my sister. Don't know how she knew I had one."

And:

"Was she cold? Dusk, on the water, this time of year."

He thinks about it.

"No shawl on her," he says. "Now you say it. Sat up in the bow the whole way with no shawl and never once put her arms round herself." He shakes his head, dismissing it. "Young, isn't she."

---

Four hundred yards south-west of that reed landing, across open water, Lost Isle sits low and black with the weed growing out of its windows.

content.text:
Not the same Corliss — and Nerissa warned you about exactly this at the tank.

*"Mistress Corliss keeps that school — **not** the Corliss on the Pearl, her cousin, and if you get those two women confused in front of either of them you will not recover it."*

Cousins. The Pearl Corliss took in a baby off a ship twenty-two years ago; this one has forty girls on a reed island. It is a family with a habit, and that is worth remembering later — but the woman in front of you never met your mother.

---

Mistress Corliss takes *she turned the boat round* standing up, with one hand on the back of a chair.

"She asked to go back," she repeats. "She asked him to *turn the boat round*."

"Yes."

"And he put her on the reed landing. In the dark."

She does not cry. Something in her face goes past that into a place that is much harder, and you understand that whatever she could not say to you an hour ago has just been answered by somebody else.

---

**Ana Vell** has produced one thing, and the mistress delivers it flatly.

Sana talked at breakfast about going to look at the ruin. Not as a plan — as a complaint. She said the second-years had been daring each other about it all week and she thought it was pathetic, because the whole island can see anybody who rows out there in daylight and *"there is no point going where somebody is already looking."*

Ana Vell, who is a horrible child and notices everything, says Sana then went quiet and did not finish her bread.

---

**Your kit, for a shoreline and a drowned island.**

**Witchsight** is the one you have been saving since the causeway. It shows auras — enchantment, binding, spirits sitting where they should not. At two miles it was a Hard shot you sensibly refused. From the north shore, four hundred yards, it is a much better proposition — and if there is anything worked on that island it will show.

**Find** does what its name says and it is the workhorse. It wants a description and it wants proximity: a thing, on ground you are standing on. Good for a landing, a boat, a scuffed track, something dropped in reeds.

**Locate Object** needs a specific object you can name and picture — Sana's shoes are under her bed and her box is upstairs, and something of hers in your hand makes this a real option.

**Detect Magic** is the blunt version of Witchsight and costs less.

**Invisibility (Lesser)** and **Darkness** are how you get onto something you do not want to be seen getting onto.

**Read Thoughts** if you find a person.

You have **sixteen magic points** and no way to get more before dark.

---

Corvin has the boat off the shed and is looking at the four hundred yards of open channel with an expression that suggests he has been thinking about it for a while.

"It's flat water and full daylight," he says — his first words since the temple. "Anything on that island will see us the whole way across."

No core record for it — Invisibility (Lesser) is off the Classic Fantasy arcane list, so it runs on the general rule:

> **Duration: the scene**, unless the spell is Instant, Concentration, or has a special duration. **Ranged:** up to your Magic skill in metres. Success costs **1 magic point**.

So: **the scene.** Not minutes counted on a clock — it holds while the thing you cast it for is happening, and it ends when that ends. One point, and you have sixteen.

But Corvin has just put his finger on the problem, and the spell does not solve it.

**It covers you. It does not cover him, and it does not cover the boat.**

An invisible man in a rowing boat on flat water in full daylight is a rowing boat on flat water in full daylight, with one oar apparently working itself — which is considerably *more* interesting to anyone watching than two ordinary men going out to cut reeds.

Your **Invisibility Radius** would take in Corvin as well. It still leaves the boat, and the wake, and four hundred yards of open channel.

---

Corvin, unhelpfully and correctly: "There's no cover on that water at all until you're inside the weed. After that there's plenty — it's all broken wall and reed and you could hide a barge in it. It's the crossing that's naked."

He scratches his jaw.

"Mind, it's naked *both ways*. Anything sitting on that island watching this shore has been watching it since dawn and has already seen a schoolmistress walk this beach twice and forty girls out looking yesterday. They know they're being looked for."

A pause.

"And there's the reed landing. That's this side. Whatever the girl did after she got out of that boat, she did it on *our* bank — and nobody has to cross anything to look at that."

The world does not light up. That is the amateur's idea of it. What happens is that a second set of information arrives on top of the first, the way a smell arrives, and for about two seconds you have to hold still and let your head sort out which is which.

Then it settles.

---

**Underneath everything, there is the island.**

Not the ruin — *under* the ruin. Down through the weed and the drowned street and the mud below that, there is something very old and very large and entirely uninterested, and it registers the way deep water registers under a boat: not as a thing you can see, as a *pressure*. It has been there a great deal longer than the houses that fell into it.

It does not care that you are here. You get the strong impression it has not cared about anything for a long time.

---

**North side, four hundred feet, at the edge of what you can resolve.**

There is a **working** laid out on stone.

Even at this range and through two broken walls you know the hand. It is the same hand that chalked the boards at the Sylph's Embrace — the same confident strokes and hesitant joins, a man writing in a language he can read and cannot speak.

It is not finished. It is *laid out*, the way a table is laid before dinner, and it is stone cold. Nobody has stood in it. Whoever set that out did it a day or more ago and has not come back to it.

And around it, at the edge of the water, there is a **threshold** — that is the only word that arrives — something cut into the ground that is much older than the working sitting on top of it, and the old pressure from below comes up through it like a draught under a door.

---

**And there are people.**

**Two of them are wrong.**

They are the ones moving the stone. Man-shaped, man-sized, and lit like men — but there is something sitting inside each of them that is not the same colour as the rest, and it does not fill the shape properly. It is like looking at a lamp behind a coat. Not demons. *Men*, with something in them, and the something is not fighting them.

They lift and set down, lift and set down, and neither of them has spoken because they do not appear to need to.

**One of them is small.**

Fourteen years old and about the size of a fourteen-year-old, and lit exactly the same wrong way as the man beside her, and she is carrying stone with him at the same unhurried pace and has been at it for some hours.

That is Bettan. She walked to the water beside a barefoot stranger and she is now working with him in the daylight and nobody has hold of her.

---

**And there is one that is not wrong at all.**

South-east of you. Close — a hundred and forty feet, no more.

**Up.**

In the tower-stub, three storeys, in the broken corner where you can see the floors inside like shelves — there is a single human light, and it is not lit wrong, and it is not working, and it is not moving.

It is very small. Not small as in young — small as in *pulled in*, gone right down into itself the way a thing does when it is hiding and has been hiding for a long time.

And it is **frightened**. You can read it off her from a hundred and forty feet like heat off a wall.

She has been in that stone since yesterday morning with no water, four hundred feet from two things that are looking for her, and she is still alive.

---

Corvin cannot see any of it. He is watching your face.

The two on the north side lift another stone and set it down.

Corvin has the boat off the weed before you are properly in it, and he rows like a man who has decided that the fastest way to stop being frightened is to work.

Behind you the hollow man comes down through the weed to the water's edge and does not stop there. He wades in to his chest, and then to his neck, still walking, still at the same pace — and then the bottom goes out from under him and he simply keeps going, under, with your rapier still in his hand.

He does not swim. He does not surface.

Corvin watches the place where he was for about four strokes and then stops watching it.

---

**And Bettan answers you.**

"Oh, I'm very well, thank you."

She says it into the thwart, face-down, with her wrists tied behind her and a man's knee in her back, in the bright unbothered voice of a child answering a neighbour.

"It's been a lovely day, actually. The weather's been kind and there's been a great deal to do. I do like having something to do." A pause. "Are you going to take these off? They're not hurting, I don't mind, only I can't be much use like this."

Sana has gone as far up the bow as the boat allows and has both hands over her mouth.

---

"How's your leg?" Bettan asks. "You want to get that seen to. Mistress Corliss keeps a good salve in the still-room, second shelf, in the brown jar — not the green one, the green one's for the chilblains and it stings something awful."

Then, without any change of tone at all:

"You've got Randall's face. That's confusing. There's two of you now, is there? Nobody said."

---

Sana makes a small noise.

"Hullo, Sana," says Bettan pleasantly. "Everyone's been ever so worried about you. Mistress Corliss dragged the channel and *cried*, and Ana Vell was horrid about it and said you'd gone off with a boy, which I said was unkind."

"You *saw* me," Sana says. Her voice is barely there. "You saw me on the island. You were walking with them—"

"I did see you, yes." Agreeable. Interested. "You were very quick. I said to him you'd gone up the tower and he said leave her, she'll come down when she's thirsty."

She thinks about it.

"You lasted a lot longer than he thought you would. I was quite proud."

---

Four hundred yards of open water. Corvin rowing hard. Nothing following.

The girl in the bottom of the boat is entirely comfortable and appears willing to discuss anything at all.

content.text:
"The stair," she says, as though you had asked about the weather.

"It's a lovely bit of work, actually. It's been under the weed for — oh, ages. Hundreds of years. It comes up out of the water on the north side and goes *down*, and there's carving on it that goes on down under the surface further than you'd think. We've had four days on it and we're nearly through."

"Through to what?"

"Through to it being *open*." She sounds mildly surprised at the question. "It's a door. It's been shut a very long time and somebody shut it deliberately, and we're taking the shut off it."

---

"A door to where?"

A pause. It is the first pause she has made.

"Down," she says. "It's — you'd not like it explained, I don't think. It's where the ones that stayed in the water go, when somebody finally takes them. There's a great many of them down there and most of them are very confused."

Then, brightly: "I wasn't one of those. Mine came off the *threshold*, not from down deep. There's a difference and he was quite particular about it."

---

"Who's he?"

"The quiet one." She says it the way you would say *the postman*. "I don't know his name. He doesn't give it and I've never thought to ask. He's not unkind. He's — precise. He likes things done properly and he doesn't shout when they're not, he just makes you do them again."

"Where is he now?"

"Away." She shifts her cheek against the thwart, comfortable. "He went off before dawn yesterday in the good boat and he's not back. He's fetching something and it's heavy and he won't put it in bad water, so he's taking his time about it."

Sana has stopped breathing properly.

---

"And why does the door have to be open *now*?"

And here she says the thing that goes through you like cold water.

"Because of the day after tomorrow," she says. "It has to be open while the water's **thin**. It goes thin on the day, you see — it's already started, it went a bit thin the day before yesterday round about noon and everyone got very excited about that. And on the day it'll go thin properly, all the way down the channel, and that's when you can move something through."

She sounds delighted for them.

"You can't do it any other time. He was very clear. It's the whole reason it's *now* and not next spring."

---

Corvin has stopped rowing.

The day after tomorrow is the Lake Lady's Tourney. Four minutes after noon two days ago, a channel went thin and a High Priestess rang a bell and a prince told her to be quiet.

And a fourteen-year-old girl tied over a thwart has just told you that this was the *small* one.
