content.text:
Corvin rows the whole channel and then the whole length of the Northern Isles reach without once easing off, and by the end of it he is grey and his hands are open blisters and he will not give the oars up.

Sana sits in the bow the entire way with her knees up, watching Bettan, and says nothing at all.

Bettan talks. Cheerfully. About the weather, and the tide, and a girl at the school called Ana Vell, and how nice it is to be out on the water. Nobody answers her. She does not appear to require it.

---

**Temple Isle, late afternoon, `d-2`.**

The two Swords on the colonnade take one look at the boat coming in and one of them runs.

---

Nerissa comes down the water-stair barefoot with her sleeves still pushed up, and she gets four steps and then she sees who is sitting in the bow.

She stops dead.

What happens then is not dignified and nobody who is there ever mentions it afterwards. She goes into the water up to her thighs to reach the boat, and gets hold of her sister's daughter with both hands, and does not say anything for quite a long time.

Sana starts crying about six seconds in — not before — and it is the loud, undignified, thirty-six-hours-of-terror kind, and Nerissa holds on to her in three feet of temple water and lets her do it in front of everybody.

Lilura turns the Swords round to face the other way with a single gesture.

---

Then Nerissa sees the girl tied over the middle thwart.

"That is Bettan Marrow," she says. "I have known that child since she was seven."

"Hullo, Mother," says Bettan.

Nerissa's face does something you would not want turned on you.

---

You give her all of it on the colonnade with your leg bleeding into her floor: the reed landing and the bare feet, the keel-drag pointing south-west, the working laid out cold on the north side in the same hand as the chalk at the Sylph's Embrace, the two wrong lights and the one that was not, and a hollow man who walked into deep water after you and did not come up.

And then the last of it.

**The stair is a door. It is nearly open. It has to be open while the water is thin — and it goes thin on the day of the Tourney.**

And the thing two days ago that cost her a bell and a prince's letter and a day and a half of standing in a tank was the *small* one.

---

Nerissa listens to all of it without moving.

At the end she says, very quietly:

"The day after tomorrow, at noon, I open the Lake Lady's Tourney. In front of the Governor, the council, every Guild in this city, and six thousand people."

She looks at the water going through her temple.

"And somebody has arranged for the Lady's own water to go thin underneath it."

**Right leg: 5 of 5. Whole.** You are unwounded for the first time since the ledge.

It is not gentle. Lilura kneels in the water with both hands round your thigh and something goes through the muscle like a hot wire pulled backwards, and the hole closes from the inside out, and she says "hold still" once in a tone that suggests she has said it to a great many people who did not.

Afterwards she sits back on her heels and looks about ten years older.

---

**On the blade**, Nerissa does not even let you finish being sheepish about it.

"You lost a sword getting my sister's daughter off a rock. Do not stand in my colonnade apologising for it."

The armoury is a stone room under the colonnade that smells of oil, and she unlocks it herself and stands back.

It is Swords of the Lake kit — blue-green over mail, maintained properly, and a good deal of it.

And you know exactly what you are looking for, because you learned it forty minutes ago with your own rapier in a dead man's fist: **you had the wrong weapon.** A rapier is a superb instrument for putting a hole in a man who minds about holes. You put eight inches into that thing's chest and it looked at your hand.

What is on the racks:

- **An arming sword** — a proper cut-and-thrust blade, one hand, 1d8, and it will take a limb off something that does not bleed.
- **A war axe**, single-handed, bearded — the thing that actually ended one of these on this island in another life.
- **A boar spear** with a crossbar behind the head, for stopping something that will not stop.
- **Javelins**, half a dozen.
- **Mail** and a **kettle helm**, if you want to be slower and harder to kill.
- And your buckler is still on your arm and undamaged.

---

**On going back with force**, Nerissa is already ahead of you and she is not sentimental about it.

"Yes. And not tonight."

She holds up a hand before you can argue.

"Listen to the shape of it. That door has to be open *the day after tomorrow*, and it is not open yet, and the man who is opening it is away fetching something heavy and has been for two days. Which means he is not there — and whatever we walk into tonight is two hollow labourers and a hole in the ground.

"You have just taken one of those apart and it cost you a sword and very nearly a leg, and you are the only person in this city who has seen what is on that rock with his own eyes."

She looks at the water.

"So we go with a dozen Swords, in daylight, with Hesper, and we go *tomorrow* — and in the meantime I send to Marisette tonight, because she has a twist of my niece's hair in her wrap and she does not yet know that any of this is about a door.

"And I am going to have to decide, before noon the day after tomorrow, whether I open the Lady's Tourney or stop it."

She turns to look at you.

"Which of those I do rather depends on what you find in that hole."

**Your 30 against 88. Her 42 against 24.** It is not close and it was never going to be.

You watch her try, and it is the single most uncomfortable thing you have witnessed today, on a day that included a man taking hold of your blade with his bare hand.

She opens her mouth to say something ordinary. You can see the sentence being assembled — *that is a great deal to have happened in a day* or something of that shape — and it does not survive the journey, and she closes her mouth again.

Then she stops trying.

---

"Which one of them is the carver," she says.

Not *who*. Not *what carver*. **Which one of them.**

She hears it as she says it. You see her hear it.

---

"Conall." She has not moved from the sand. "Sit down. There is a bench and you have been stabbed today."

"I'll stand."

"Yes." A breath. "Yes, all right."

---

"Ask me," she says. "Ask me directly, and I will answer it directly, and I want that noted — because I have had four years of not answering it and I have been extremely comfortable, and I would like the record to show that the reason it is ending is that you walked in here and told me you had a brother before I could decide to tell you first.

"Which is entirely my fault and I am not going to pretend otherwise."

She picks the bow back up off the sand, because her hands need something.

"Practice," she says, "is going badly. I have been standing in this yard since the second bell because I have entered an archery competition I do not care about, in a city I brought you to under an errand I did not explain, and this morning a boy came from the temple to tell me that the Order had taken a man off a ledge who looked exactly like the thief they were hunting.

"Here is the difficulty, and I am going to say it before I start rather than let you find out halfway through.

"**Baron Hanzo di Teufel.**

"Border lord out past the Ettinmarsh. He rules a march the size of a small kingdom and he rules it as a sorcerous tyrant — he enslaves, he exterminates elves wherever he finds them, he has burned settlements off the map and he has done every bit of it with enough deniability that the Crown has never once had to look at it.

"He is in this city now, being toasted by half the Governor's council, and he has entered a champion for the Single Combat that not one soul in Purewater has been permitted to look at.

"And the young man carving women on the Pearl with a face like yours is **his son.** Santo di Teufel. Twenty-two, and there is a name for him on the border that people hear and change the subject."

She does not pause and she does not soften her voice.

"And so are you."

---

The yard is very quiet. Somewhere beyond the wall the temple water is still going through its channel.

"That's what's going on," she says. "Now ask me the other half — **how do we stop it** — and I will tell you that I do not know, and that until an hour ago my entire plan was a bracer and a polite conversation with a prince.

You tell him first. In the passage, sitting on the floor beside him, before Marisette and before anybody else.

He listens to the whole thing without moving.

And when you finish, he does not ask about the Baron.

---

"What was her name?"

---

That is the first thing out of him, and his voice does not do anything clever with it.

"Your lady knight. Did she say her name?"

"She said your mother was a young elven mage. She said he seduced her and ruined her and she ran, and she came here, and she died here."

"But not her *name*."

"No."

Randall looks at the wall opposite for a while.

"Twenty-two years," he says. "Twenty-two years I have not asked one person in this city one question about that woman. Not Corliss. Not Marisette. Not Asphodel, and Asphodel would have told me anything I asked her at any hour of the day or night since I was nine years old."

He turns the untouched plate a quarter-turn on the floor with one finger, which is a gesture you have seen somebody else make today across a desk full of ledgers.

"And I could not tell you why. It was just a door, and I decided very early on that I wasn't going through it, and after a while not going through it was a thing I was rather good at."

He looks up at you.

"And then you came down a stair underground yesterday morning wearing my face and it went straight off its hinges."

---

Then he puts his hand out.

"Randall. No second name, and don't offer me one, I've been fine without."

He shakes properly, once.

"Conall. That's a good name. That's a name somebody *chose*." He hears it as he says it, and does not take it back. "Somebody chose that for you and gave it you and meant it, and that's — well."

A pause.

"Investigator."

"Investigator."

"Right." He almost smiles, and it is the first one you have seen off him. "Then here's the reputation, since you've heard about it: it's mostly true and it's smaller than people say. I steal. I'm very good at it and I'm better at knowing who to ask. I have never once in my life been through a window somebody wasn't paying me to be on the other side of."

He gets up off the floor, slowly, and he is stiffer than a twenty-two-year-old ought to be.

"And I've spent today sat on a board outside a door listening to a woman I've known since I was eleven not die, while everyone on this island had a lovely time deciding whether I'd cut her.

"So if there is a piece of work going that ends with somebody explaining themselves to me, I would very much like to be on it."

She does not comment on any of it.

"Hanzo di Teufel," she says. "Say the rest of it in here, both of you, and I'll send for wine, and somebody had better eat something."

"Some of them. And spares."

"Mm."

---

**Then you ask why Emmeralda has not been healed properly.**

The room goes very quiet.

Randall's head comes round from the window.

---

Marisette does not defend herself, which is the thing about her.

"Because I didn't send for one," she says.

"Why not?"

"Because at four o'clock yesterday morning I had a demon-worker's ritual on the floor of a house on my island and no idea who had done it, and the first thing I decided — before I got out of that chair — was that the word *demon* was not going to leave the Pearl until I chose who got to say it."

She turns a pen a quarter-turn on the desk.

"So I sent for Hesper. Who is mine, and who is the finest arcane practitioner in this quarter, and who is **not a healer.** He is a sorcerer. He has kept her breathing for a day and a half with a physician's bag and a great deal of skill and he has told me twice that she needs somebody who does the other thing, and both times I said *not yet*.

"And there are clerics of the Lake Lady forty minutes away across the water who could have been at that bed by six o'clock yesterday morning."

She looks up.

"I have been managing my island's reputation. That is the entire reason. There is not a better one underneath it."

---

Randall says, from the window, in a voice with nothing in it at all: "A day and a half."

"Yes."

"I sat outside that door all day."

"I know you did."

---

**And there is a second half to the answer**, and it is the part that is actually your business.

"There is also something *wrong* with the wound," Marisette says. "Hesper's words, not mine. It does not close properly and it does not go bad either — it simply sits there being open. He thought at first that meant something was in her, and he has been looking for it for thirty hours and there is nothing there.

"Which he says is worse, because it means the wound is like that on its own."

A barbed instrument, drawn slowly, in a seat that was chalked and stood in and abandoned half-finished.

Nobody in this room knows what an unfinished binding leaves behind in a body. You are the only person in it who has seen the figure and the break in the line.

---

Marisette is already writing.

"Right. Corliss's boy goes to Temple Isle tonight and asks the High Priestess for a cleric — properly, in my name, as a request from the Pearl, and he can tell her I should have asked yesterday.

"She'll send Lilura. She'll enjoy making me wait about four hours for her to do it, and she will be entitled to."

She blots it.

Here is where they actually are, run forward properly.

**Magda's dream sent her to the ford and she found Gardwen there** — that convergence is authored into both their entry points, and it happened on `d-3/dawn` while you were still on the Anminster road. She talked them past the water-gate and into the city the same morning.

And then she did the one thing she knows how to do in Purewater, which is go to the only person here she trusts: **Constantine.**

**Magda's Willpower, 20 against 63.** Tourney week, every room in the house spoken for, and an old woman leaned on a madame until there was a bed. They have had the top back room over the canal since `d-3`.

Which means they were **under this roof the night Emmeralda was carved**, three floors up.

They did not catch him. Nobody did — his escape roll was clean and he walked out of the water door unhurried while the house was still working out that anything had happened.

And you have not crossed them today because a grey wolf is not allowed in a working house, so a druid and a berserker have spent two days out on the island and the ledges with it, and they are due back.

---

Marisette is looking at you across the desk with her pen still in her hand.

"Two women in my house," she says slowly. "The old northerner and the wild one with the animal. Constantine took them in because the old one knew him twenty years ago and would not take no.

"And the wild one—"

She stops.

"Constantine said something at four o'clock yesterday morning that I have not thought about since, because I had a great deal else on. He said the young one went into that room before anybody and put her hands in the wound and prayed over it in a language nobody knew.

"And that it *closed*. And then opened again."

---

Randall is already at the door.

"She's a healer," he says. "There's been a healer in this house the whole time."

---

Down in the hall, the front door goes.

And a woman's voice you have not heard before — northern, unhurried, and entirely uninterested in whether anyone wants to hear it — says:

"Constantine. Where's the girl? We've been up and down that island all day and Gardwen says the water's gone wrong."

content.text:
You come out onto the landing above the hall.

There are two of them at the front door with Constantine, and the smell of the canal has come in with them.

---

**The one doing the talking is very old and very small.**

Seventy at least, in a cloak that has been rained on for three hundred miles, with a quarterstaff that is not a walking stick and has never once pretended to be, and a face that has been out in weather since before anyone else in this house was born. She has not taken her boots off and she is not going to.

**The other one is about twenty-one and she is soaked to the thigh.**

Woodland leathers, dark hair, and a stillness that does not belong on somebody that age. She is not looking at Constantine at all. She has one hand flat against the doorframe of a house she has lived in for two days as though she is listening to it, and her face is doing something unhappy.

Outside on the step, refusing the threshold, there is a grey wolf.

---

Magda looks up and sees you on the landing.

She takes you in — the sword, the boots, the state of the trousers — in one unhurried pass, the way a woman looks at a beast she is deciding whether to buy.

Then Randall comes out of the passage behind you.

---

She stops.

Her eyes go from one of you to the other and back, twice, and she does not do anything as undignified as being startled. What she does is go completely still, and then let out a short breath through her nose that might be a laugh.

"Well," she says. "That's new."

And to Constantine, without taking her eyes off the pair of you: "You never said there were two."

"There weren't," Constantine says, "until yesterday morning."

---

**Gardwen has not looked at either of you.**

She is still on the doorframe with her hand flat and her head slightly turned, and when she finally speaks it is not to anybody in the hall.

"Something's happened in this house."

"Aye, lass. Two nights back. We were three floors up when—"

"No." She takes her hand off the frame. "Not that. *Since.* Today." She looks up the stairs, and past you, at the green room door standing a hand's width open. "There's something in this building that isn't closing."

Then she does look at you, and her eyes are very direct and completely unbothered by your face.

"Are you the investigator? The old woman on the ledge said there was one and that he'd been arrested and let go."

---

Marisette has come out of the counting room behind you.

"Gardwen of the Ash Vale," she says — and she says it carefully, the way you say a name you have only just decided to take seriously. "You put your hands in that wound at four o'clock yesterday morning and closed it."

"I did."

"And it opened again."

"It did." Her jaw tightens. "And I have thought about nothing else for a day and a half, and I know what I did wrong, and nobody in this house has let me back in that room since."

content.text:
**69 against 72.** By three, and it is enough, because she has just handed you the half you were missing.

---

"Say that again," you tell her. "*There was nothing to fight.*"

"Nothing. I went in, I found the shape she's supposed to be, I leaned on it, and it *closed* — properly, all the way, I felt the flesh knit. And then it came apart again from the inside and there was nobody doing it."

And the two halves go together.

---

"It isn't a wound," you say.

Everyone in that hall stops.

"I knelt on those boards this morning. The figure on the floor is a **seat** — a thing you chalk to hold something in place while it is put somewhere. And the cut is not a cut. One long line, drawn slowly, with something *barbed* — and barbed for one reason only, which is so that it will not close behind him.

"He did not open her to hurt her. He opened her to have somewhere to put something. The channel is meant to stay open until the thing is seated, and the seating is what *shuts* it.

"He never seated anything. He got most of the way through, and it went wrong, and he stepped backwards out of his own figure and left the house."

You look at Gardwen.

"So there is nothing in her to fight, and the wound will not close, and both of those are the same fact. **She is a door that was propped open and never used.**"

---

Gardwen has gone quite white.

"That's why it came apart," she says. "I wasn't healing a body. I was closing a door somebody had wedged, and the wedge is still in it, and the moment I let go it swung back."

"Yes."

"Then it isn't a healing at all." She is talking fast now. "You'd have to take the *wedge* out. You'd have to undo the working, and I don't know one thing about workings, and I have been in this house for a day and a half trying to solve it with the only thing I've got."

---

**And Magda says the quiet part.**

She has not moved off the flagstones by the door. She has been listening to all of it with her hands on her staff and her boots still on.

"So there's a chair set out in that room," she says, "with nobody in it."

Nobody answers her.

"And somewhere in this city there's a lad with four more women's hair in his coat, who's short of a place to put something, and who has already been in this house once and knows the way to the water door."

She looks up the stairs at the green room.

"How many people are watching that girl tonight?"

content.text:
**97 against 50 — a bad failure.**

He does not work it out.

He knows he made a mess of it. He does not understand *what he left behind* — that a channel barbed to stay open and a seat that was never filled is a vessel already half-built, sitting in a room on the Pearl with nobody in it.

He thinks that one is spoiled. He thinks he has to start again.

So he is not coming here tonight.

**He is going somewhere quieter, with a fresh twist of hair, and he still has four of them.**

---

You do not know any of that, standing in Constantine's hall.

What you know is what Magda just said, and it is not wrong about the *risk* — it is only wrong about the man, and nobody in this house has any way to tell.

---

Marisette makes the call anyway, because that is what she does.

"Four on that room tonight. Two inside, two on the stair, and the water door barred and a man sitting against it. Nobody comes in or out of this house after the eighth bell — nobody, Constantine, including your regulars, and they can be angry at me in the morning and I will take it."

Then, to Gardwen: "And you go back in there. Tonight. Now, if you'll do it. Not to close it — he says you can't and I believe him. To sit with her, because you are the only person in this city who has had her hands inside that thing and you may notice something the rest of us can't."

Gardwen is already moving for the stairs.

"And the temple cleric's still coming," Marisette adds. "I have swallowed that particular frog and I'd rather not have to swallow it twice."

---

Magda has not moved off the flagstones.

**What he tells you, and it is true.**

"And there is a man he calls **the quiet one**. Not a name — nobody uses one. He came to the house when I was thirteen and my father speaks to him the way he speaks to nobody else, which is *carefully*. He does the actual work. Whatever the work is." A flat, ugly little laugh. "I asked once what he was. My father said *he is the man who knows where things are kept.*"

"He's been gone. Two days, three. He went off before dawn on a boat and he isn't back and my father has been checking the water since yesterday morning."

---

**And the thing you actually came for.**

"Where did you learn the form?"

He hesitates for the first time, and it is not calculation. It is shame.

"His **study**. Third shelf, behind the border rolls, in a case that locks and that he has never once thought to check, because it did not occur to him that I would.

"There are nine of them in there. Big folded sheets, older than the house, and the hand on them is—" he stops. "It's not his. He can't write it either. He can *read* it, some of it, and he keeps them because whoever wrote them is the point.

"I copied one. I copied it four times before I dared bring it out."

"Which one?"

"The one that looked like it did the most."

---

**And here is what the critical gives you on top, and it changes the night.**

He is not lying about any of that.

But he is **frightened of the quiet one in a way he is not frightened of his father**, and he has not said so, and it is sitting under every sentence.

And there is a specific hole in what he knows, and he does not know it is a hole — he thinks *noon on the day* is a plan. It is not. It is the *end* of a plan, and everything that actually matters has been arranged by somebody else, somewhere else, out of his sight, for a hundred years.

He has been given the date the way you tell a child which day is his birthday.

He was never part of it. He has spent nine years teaching himself to read a language out of a locked case in order to be included in something that was never going to include him — and he has just, in the last four minutes, worked that out in front of you.

---

He stops talking.

"He's not going to come for me," he says. "Is he."

It is not really a question, and it is the first time all night he has sounded twenty-two.

Three messages go out of that house inside ten minutes, and Crowbill does not send boys with any of them.

**To Marisette**, on the Pearl: one of his own, by water. *We have him. Alive. The Siren's Call. Nyssa is unhurt and Ravella has her.*

**To the High Priestess**, on Temple Isle: one of Ravella's, which is faster and does not use the surface for all of it, and which Crowbill watches go over the side with an expression he does not comment on.

**And to the Swords' barracks**, for Temerach Nebulo.

---

Ravella takes charge of Santo without anybody discussing it.

"Not your cellar," she tells Crowbill. "Yours is dry and it has a door onto a street and forty people know where it is."

"And yours?"

"Mine is under the water and it does not have a door at all." She says it without any particular relish, which is what makes it awful. "He will be dry, he will be fed, and he will be exactly where I put him. And when this is finished the Court will want to discuss what he took off our threshold, and *that* is a separate conversation and it is not yours."

Santo does not say anything. He has not said anything since *he's not going to come for me, is he.*

---

**And Temerach arrives at the Siren's Call in forty minutes, which is very fast from Temple Isle at night.**

She comes in off the water stair in blue-green with her bow cased and she does not look at Ravella or Crowbill or the room.

She looks at you.

"You have the Baron's son."

"We have him."

"Alive, unhurt, and in the private custody of a smuggler and a broker, in a pleasure house, with no warrant, no magistrate, and no charge."

"Yes."

---

She is quiet for a long moment.

"Four years," she says. "Letters that prove nothing. Witnesses who recant. Two dead informants, one of them nineteen years old. I have done all of it the correct way because the correct way is the only way that *sticks* — and you have had that boy on the floor of a room inside thirty hours."

Then, and it costs her something visible:

content.text:
**16 against 50.** Against a Hard grade, on a passion she has carried for four years — she makes it comfortably.

**She cannot put it down.** And she is honest enough to tell you so instead of pretending she is being strategic.

---

She listens to the whole argument without interrupting. When you finish she is quiet for a while, and then she says:

"You are right."

A beat.

"And I am going to be a problem about it anyway, and I want you to understand why, because if I dress it up as strategy you will believe me and you should not."

---

"Two years ago a girl called Sen carried a letter for me out of that man's march. Nineteen. She was clever and she was frightened and she did it because I told her it would *matter*, and they took her off a road eleven miles from safety, and what came back was not enough to bury properly.

"I have spent every day since telling myself that it will have been worth it when he stands in a room and answers for it. Not dies. *Answers.* In front of people, with his name read out, and the whole of it said aloud where it cannot be denied afterwards."

She looks at the floor.

"That is not a plan. That is a thing I need, and I have been calling it a plan for four years, and you have just held it up to a lamp."

---

"So here is where I actually am.

"You are right that the arrest is not the prize. You are right that a hundred years of work does not stop because one man is in a cell — it has a *quiet one* who does the work, and a case of nine sheets on a third shelf, and a date at noon, and none of that cares whether the Baron is arrested.

"And I will help you break it. All of it. Tonight, tomorrow, and on the field if it comes to that."

Her jaw sets.

"But I am not going to pretend I have let the other thing go, because I have not, and if it comes down to a moment where I can have the man or the *plan*—"

She stops.

"—I do not know what I will do. And I would rather you knew that about me now, in this room, than found it out at noon."

---

Crowbill, from the chair, without looking up:

"That's the most useful thing anybody's said all night."

---

**`d-2/night`. Thirty-four hours to noon.**

You have Santo under the water, Nyssa alive, Emmeralda closed, a fourteen-year-old in a temple cell, a watcher on a reed bank, and a name for the hand under the tracing that nobody can read.

And somewhere out past the sea road, a quiet man is still rowing something heavy home.

---

That is a hell of a place to break. Want to keep going, or bank it here?

content.text:
**30 against 65. Success.** You act in accordance with it, and the room is watching.

---

You do not say the thing.

That is what it looks like from outside, and Crowbill will describe it later as *the young one said nothing*, and he will be wrong.

What you do is cross the room while she is still looking at the floor, and stand in front of her, and say it in a perfectly ordinary voice, in front of a smuggler and a broker for something under the water and a boy who is being taken away down a stair.

---

"Sen."

Her head comes up.

"You've said her name once tonight and you said it to the floor. Say it to me."

"...Sen."

"Right." You hold her eye. "Then I've heard it, and Crowbill's heard it, and Ravella's heard it, and it's in a room now instead of in you. That's how it starts being *said aloud where it cannot be denied afterwards*. You've been waiting four years for a magistrate to do that and it turns out it only wanted somebody to be in the room."

---

She does not cry, because she does not, and it is much worse to watch than if she had.

"That is a *trick*," she says unsteadily.

"It isn't. And you know it isn't, because you cannot lie and you can't tell when other people are doing it either, and you have been checking my face for the last four seconds."

A shaky, appalling little laugh gets out of her.

"...That is true. That is annoyingly true."

---

**And then you do the part that costs you, and this is the passion actually driving you, and you will think about it later.**

"And when it comes to it," you tell her, "and you have to choose between the man and the plan — you're not going to be standing there on your own working it out.

"I'll be next to you. Whichever way you go."

---

She looks at you for a long moment.

"That is not a good promise," she says quietly. "That is not a promise an investigator makes. That is not even a promise a *soldier* makes — you have just told a woman who has admitted she may choose wrongly that you will go with her when she does."

"I know."

"Why?"

And there it is: the one question, at last, in a room full of people, with the exact opening you have wanted for three years.

---

**And you have already spent the roll.** You acted in accordance with it, and what it drove you to was *standing beside her*, not telling her.

"Because you pulled me out of a ditch," you say, "and taught me to read."

Which is true, and is not the answer, and she takes it — because she has no facility whatsoever for detecting the thing a man is not saying.

Crowbill, who has, looks very carefully at the ceiling.

---

**Recorded:** you are now bound to that. If it comes to a moment at noon where Temerach Nebulo chooses the man over the plan, your own passion will be rolled against you to see whether you can refuse to follow her.

That is what the roll bought, and what it cost.

**83 against 72 — you miss it by eleven.**

You do not get there. Not tonight, in a hot room at midnight, at the end of the longest day of your life, with a woman on a bed being wrapped in a blanket ten feet away.

Failure narrows; it does not delete. **Here is what you do assemble, and where it stops.**

---

You lay it out on the table with the cold jug on it, out loud, because that is how you think.

"A champion nobody has seen. Kept behind a wall, moved in a litter with the curtains laced, guards facing *inward* — you don't face inward to keep people out."

Temerach: "No. You face inward to keep something in."

"A hundred years and four generations of one house working at one thing. A locked case of nine sheets in a hand nobody in that family can write. A man who *knows where things are kept*, away three days on a boat, fetching something heavy and slow."

Ravella, very quietly: "And a threshold under Lost Isle that has been shut since before this city had a name, being dug open by men who do not bleed."

"And it only works while the water is thin. And the water goes thin at noon on the day of the Tourney."

---

**And you can see the shape of it.**

"It is not a swordsman. It has never been a swordsman. That thing in the litter is a *container* — a person with something kept inside him, and the family has been keeping it for a hundred years, and you cannot keep a thing like that in one vessel indefinitely.

"So on the day, while the channel is thin, they use the door. They take what is in him **out**."

---

**And that is where it stops, and you know it stops there, which is the maddening part.**

Because *out* is not an end. Nobody spends four generations and a hundred years to take something out of a boy and let it go.

Out **into what?** Into the door? Into something the quiet one is rowing home? Into somebody in a crowd of six thousand people?

And *why noon, in front of the whole city*, when the entire operation up to now has been conducted in laced litters and locked cases and rooms at the back of houses? A man who has hidden this for a century does not do the last step on a public field at midday unless the public field is *part of it* —

— and you cannot get any further, and you can feel yourself not getting there.

---

Temerach is watching you try.

"Stop," she says. "You have been awake since the causeway and you were stabbed this afternoon."

"It's *right there*."

"It is. And it will still be right there at six o'clock in the morning, and you will have slept, and Hesper will be in the room, and he has read nine tenths of the books you are trying to remember."

She picks up her bow case.

"Sleep. That is not a suggestion from your patron, it is one from somebody who has watched better investigators than you take a bad guess at midnight and spend the next day defending it."

---

**`d-2/night`, going on for the small hours. Thirty-three hours to noon.**

You have the shape and not the point.

Clean. **21 facts, 23 knowledge edges, no problems.**

---

You sleep at the Siren's Call, in a room Ravella gives you without discussion, and you sleep like something dropped.

**Magic points: 17 of 17.** Fatigue: Fresh. The leg is a pink pucker and an old woman's ache.

**Luck: 2 of 3** — those replenish per *session*, not per night, and this one has not ended.

---

**`d-1/dawn`. Thirty-one hours to noon.**

---

And while you slept, something happened that you were not there for, and it is the second time in two days that the answer has been somewhere in this city with nobody standing in the right place.

**At first light, aboard the DragonBarge at the Forge Quarter pier, they opened the champion in the same place they open him every morning, bled him, and quieted him.**

Nobody heard it. Nobody in this entire telling has been near that ship — not you, not Marisette's people, not Crowbill's. Nobody has counted the men on her deck, or spoken to whoever does her washing, or asked why a vessel that size is taking nothing aboard.

**That is where the piece you were missing at midnight has been sitting the whole time.**

*Out into what,* you asked, and *why noon, in front of six thousand people.*

The thing in that litter is not a swordsman. You worked that out. What you could not get to is what it *is* — and there is a boy on a cot on that ship who is opened every dawn to keep it quiet, and the two facts that would break the whole thing open are on that pier, out loud, once a day.

It happens again at first light tomorrow.

Which is the morning of the Lake Lady's Tourney, hours before noon.

---

Downstairs, Crowbill is already up, eating bread off a folded paper, with a man beside him who does the Forge Quarter runs.

**What do you want to do with today?**

content: Ask where the champion is? Where is the baron? Could Ravella capture the quiet man on the water?

message.content: Ask where the champion is? Where is the baron? Could Ravella capture the quiet man on the water?

content.text:
Crowbill does not answer any of it. He turns the paper round and pushes it at the man beside him.

"Tell him."

---

**The man's name is Renny and he has done the Forge Quarter run for nine years**, and he answers the first question in one word and then keeps going, because nobody has ever asked him about it and he has been wanting to tell somebody.

"She's at the private pier, east side of High Isle, seaward. Black hull, dragon on the prow, deep-water ship — no business being in a canal city at all."

"And?"

"And she *steams*." He says it flat, like a complaint. "Where the hull meets the water. All along her, all the time, day and night. Gulls won't go near her. There's a dead-water slick round her stern with things floating in it belly-up."

---

"Who's aboard?"

"Eight, most days. In scale, all of 'em, in this weather, on a moored ship. Nobody in shirtsleeves. Nobody idle. Nobody *talking*." He shakes his head. "No banner up neither, and every other hull in that harbour with anybody aboard has got colours flying."

"And the Baron?"

"Not on her. He's ashore — north-west round the point, one of the leased houses on High Isle proper, with the horses and the good clothes and the household. There's a ship's boat goes round from there twice a day with food, four men rowing, in under a canvas gangway where you can't see what comes off."

He wipes his mouth.

"That's the bit that's wrong, if you want the wrong bit. **Nothing goes aboard that ship off that yard.** Not a sack, not a crate, not a water butt. Two little boatloads a day, carried off the thwarts in armloads. That's not victualling for twenty-odd knights."

A pause.

"That's food for a handful."

---

**And then he gives you the thing.**

"Only one person off that yard gets anything from them at all, and it's the laundry woman. Yannick's wife — Ann. Does the rope-walk and the chandler, and now them.

"Bag down at the bollards, coin in her hand, off you go, and she's not allowed past the posts."

"How much laundry?"

He shrugs. "One bag. Every day."

Then he stops, and frowns, because he has not thought about it before and you have just made him.

"Rope-walk's forty men and they send out twice a week," he says slowly. "That ship sends out *every day* and it's one bag. And it's all the same thing — sheets, she reckons. Bedding."

He looks up.

"She won't talk about it, mind. Went right off about a fortnight back. Which is a shame, 'cause she'll talk about anything."

---

**The Baron.** Crowbill answers that one himself.

"High Isle, the leased house, and tonight he is at the Governor's brother's table with half the council, because it is the eve of the Tourney and there is a supper. He will be surrounded by the most respectable men in this city until well past midnight, and there is nothing you can do to him in that room."

---

**And Ravella, on the water.**

She has come down and heard the last of it standing on the stair.

"Take the quiet one on the water," she repeats. "Yes. She stops on the bottom step.

"...That is a better question than the one I was expecting."

She thinks about it properly, which she has not had to do about the water in front of a surface-dweller in a long time.

---

"Two things, and the first is smaller than you would like.

"**Out past the Mouth is not my water.** The Court is in the deep channels of *this city* — the cuts, the drowned streets, the old district under the Northern Isles. That is ours and we know every stone of it. The sea road is deep and cold and belongs to nobody, and I have four people who will go out there and they will not go far and they will not stay long.

"So while he is out on the sea road I can *watch* him. I cannot reach into it and take a thing off a boat."

---

"And the second is the one that matters, and it is why I said *let him land.*

"If he is cornered near the city and puts it over the side — yes. We would get it. It would take us an hour and we would find it, because a heavy thing on a hard bottom is not difficult.

"But he will not drop it just anywhere. He will drop it where he is going, because a man who has carried a thing for three days and gets caught two hundred yards short does the only thing left to him: **he gets it as close to the threshold as he can and lets the water take it the rest of the way.**

"And the threshold is *open.* Four days of digging and it is nearly through.

"So what you are proposing is that we chase him until he puts a hundred-year anchor into the water directly over an open door, uncontrolled, while the channel is already going thin."

She looks at you.

"I would rather have it in his hands on dry stone with my people round him than on the bottom of my own front hall with nobody's hands on it at all."

---

**But she takes the point, and the plan changes because you asked.**

"You are right that letting him reach the stair is too late. If he gets to the top of that stair he does not need to *do* anything clever — he only has to let go.

"So." She holds up two fingers. "Not the sea road, and not the stair.

"**In between.** He has to come off the sea road and through the city channels to get to the Northern Isles, and there is about a mile of that where he is in *my* water, in cuts he does not know, with weed on both sides — and it is shallow.

"Shallow is everything. If he drops it there, it is in four feet of mud and we have it in ten minutes and it is nowhere near the threshold."

She almost smiles.

"That is a considerably better plan than the one I came downstairs with, and I would not have got to it on my own, and I dislike admitting that."

---

Crowbill, without looking up: "She does. Enormously."

---

"So: my people hold the eastern approaches and the mile of cuts, and the moment he comes off the sea road we have him in shallow water with weed on both sides.

"And what he is carrying still comes to the Court." A beat. "That part does not change."

**GM ONLY.** The hidden architecture of the campaign.

**The scheme.** [[Baron Hanzo di Teufel]] is a fire-demonologist pursuing, ultimately, his own transformation into a Dragon King through the [[The Awake the Dragon Movement]]. His proof-of-concept is a possession ritual: years ago his Dragon Knights kidnapped a child during a border raid -- **[[Gardwen]]'s brother** -- and the Baron bound the spirit of the ancient dragon-knight **[[Thuban Eta]]** into him. That boy is now **[[Cailan]]**, the Baron's unbeaten champion, whom he means to field in the tourney's Single Combat to win political influence in Purewater.

**The binding.** Control is held by three things: **Thuban's bones** (the primary anchor, kept in the Baron's distant border tower, inaccessible during the adventure but essential to any permanent solution); a **binding locket** (a secondary component the Baron carries); and **daily ritual reinforcement**. Thuban is a reluctant, honorable captive -- betrayed and slain by his own comrades in the old Dragon army, now enslaved through the torment of that betrayal. He occasionally fights the Baron's will, surfacing as Cailan's moments of clarity. **Free him, and a betrayed knight may become an ally.**

**The twins.** [[Randall]] and [[Conall]] are identical twins and **both biological sons of Baron Hanzo**, born of an elven mage he seduced and broke long before his open descent into evil; she fled to the city and died when they were small. Separated, they grew up unaware of each other -- Randall in the Pearl' brothels, Conall adopted by a militiaman's family in Anminster and later trained by the [[The Order of the Blue Star]]. The Baron's legitimate, cruel heir **[[Santo di Teufel]]** is their half-brother -- which is why the Dragon Knight at the gate mistook Randall for "Lord Santo." [[Temerach Nebulo]] has known Conall's parentage for years; that is the real reason she brought him.

**The lever.** The campaign's resolution is **not** a frontal fight with the Baron but the dismantling of his ritual. The plot turns on the locket: [[Nus]] pickpockets it before the tourney on Conall's behalf; the Baron, discovering the theft, launches a purge to recover it and displays Nus's body as a warning -- "he would turn the entire city inside out to retrieve it." Hold the locket, and you have leverage; damage it and the bones, and the possession weakens. The emotional climax is Gardwen recognizing her brother across the tournament ground.

content.text:
Out of character, then. Here is the whole thing.

## The authored scenario

**Hanzo di Teufel is a fire-demonologist whose actual ambition is to become a Dragon King**, backed by a movement called *Awake the Dragon*. Everything else is proof-of-concept.

Years ago his knights raided a border steading, killed eight people and took one child — **Gardwen's brother**. Into that boy the Baron bound the spirit of **Thuban Eta**, an ancient dragon-knight. That boy is **Cailan**, seventeen, and he is the champion nobody has been allowed to see. Hanzo means to field him in the Single Combat to buy political weight in Purewater.

The binding rests on three things: **Thuban's bones** (primary anchor, kept in the border tower), a **binding locket** the Baron wears, and **daily ritual reinforcement** — the morning cut.

And Thuban is a *reluctant, honourable captive*. Betrayed and drowned by his own comrades, enslaved through the torment of that betrayal. He surfaces in Cailan's moments of clarity. **Free him and a betrayed knight becomes an ally** — that is the intended lever, not a fight.

You and Randall are Hanzo's bastard sons by the elven mage he broke. Santo is your half-brother. Temerach has always known.

**The authored resolution is not a duel.** It is dismantling the ritual — and the authored route runs through the **locket**: Nus the pickpocket lifts it before the Tourney, the Baron tears the city apart to get it back and displays Nus's body as a warning, and holding it gives you leverage. The emotional climax is Gardwen recognising her brother across the tournament ground.

## What you have done to it

Look at the beat list. You have bent it hard.

- **The recognition at the gate never happened** — Randall stayed invisible in the crowd, so no dragon-gold went on the street, and Hanzo still does not know you exist. *"A di Teufel who is not his" is still dormant.*
- **Santo's binding failed and his escape succeeded** — the inverse of last time. So no demon in Emmeralda to interrogate, and no soul-knife recovered. You had to reason the whole thing out of chalk instead.
- **You caught Santo four minutes early.** *"Santo goes again"* is preempted, *"Santo's tantrum"* cancelled. That entire branch is dead because you got there first.
- **Four beats still have no date on them** — *A price on the face*, *The houses close*, *Tat counts the cost*, *The purge* — they were all contingent on visibility you never gave the Baron.

## Your critique is correct

The laundress is a single thread and I let her stand in for the whole approach. That is thin, and it is thin because **nobody in this playthrough has gone near the ship at all** — so I have not had to build the approach out.

Here is what is actually available, and most of it is sitting unused:

| Route | What it gives |
|---|---|
| **Ann Yannick**, the laundress | The shape of the wound, the same place daily, the grey that will not boil out, the cut arming-points |
| **Renny / the waste-boys** | Nothing goes aboard; slops in the water; barrows of clinker; Renko walked off the pier |
| **The ship's boat** from the leased house | Two loads a day, food for a handful — the count of who is aboard |
| **Crowbill's canal routes** | The beat text names this explicitly as the way to get close enough to *hear* the morning reinforcement |
| **Ravella's water-folk** | Under the hull. Nobody has asked them what a steaming keel looks like from below |
| **Nus** | The authored locket-lift, and he is a Crowbill man you now have access to |
| **Hesper** | Has not been asked one question about the champion |
| **Santo** | In a cell under the water, and nobody has gone back to him with better questions |

**The two facts the whole thing turns on** — the champion is a *prisoner*, and the thing inside him *does not want to be there* — are deliverable by any of the top five, and are currently sitting on that pier unheard.

## Where it comes together

Noon tomorrow. The channel goes thin, the threshold under Lost Isle is open, and the quiet one is rowing the bones home. That is the removal — Thuban out of a worn-out boy and into something fresher, in front of six thousand people, on the Lady's own day, because the thin water only happens then.

**Your win condition is not killing anybody.** It is: hold the locket, control the bones, and reach Thuban rather than Cailan — and the man will help you.

---

Want me to build out the ship approach properly before we play tomorrow, or keep going and let you pick your route in the fiction?

Good catch, and the first half of it is a real seam — partly mine.

**The Lost Isle thread is not in the authored scenario.** I checked. The gm-secret names three things holding the binding: the bones in the border tower, the locket, and the daily reinforcement. No threshold, no drowned island, no thin water. All of that *emerged* in the previous playthrough and I carried it across into this one as established fact. So the collision you have spotted — champion on the sand at noon, extraction on an island at noon — is a tension I created by welding an emergent thread onto an authored one without checking the join.

But the answer to your second question is in the lore, and once you have it the first question stops being a problem. I had not joined it up either until you asked.

---

## Who is he putting him into

**Himself.**

The gm-secret is explicit and I read past it: *"Baron Hanzo di Teufel is a fire-demonologist pursuing, ultimately, **his own transformation into a Dragon King**… **His proof-of-concept** is a possession ritual."*

Cailan is not the project. Cailan is the **jar** — the demonstration that a Dragon King's spirit can be held in a living body for a decade without destroying it. Ten years of a boy being opened every morning is a hundred-year-old family working out the *engineering*.

Thuban Eta is a knight of the dragon wars. Hanzo does not want a champion. He wants what is *in* the champion, in himself, and he has spent four generations and one child proving it can be done.

## Which resolves the timing

The Single Combat is not the event. **The opening is.**

Noon is when the temple opens the Tourney and the channel goes thin — and it is the one moment in the year when the Governor, the council, every Guild in Purewater and six thousand people are all standing in one place looking at one thing.

A Dragon King is not made in a cellar. He is **acclaimed**. Doing it in the Lady's own water, on her own day, in front of the entire city, is not a risk he is running — it is the *point*, and it is why a man who has hidden this for a century is suddenly doing the last step in daylight.

The champion entry buys him three things: a reason to be in the Governor's box at noon, a reason for the city to be assembled, and a bout at the second hour that gives him two hours of everyone looking the wrong way.

**Cailan very probably never takes the sand.** *Injury in training.* The entry was never about fighting.

## Which means

- The Lost Isle threshold is where Thuban comes **out**. That is four miles from Temple Isle — so either Cailan is brought to the island, or the extraction is done at distance through the thinned channel that runs through *both*.
- Given the Lady's water connects the whole city and goes thin everywhere at once, I would make it the second: **the channel is the medium.** That is why it has to be her water, her day, her thin.
- Which makes Nerissa's decision the hinge of the campaign. If she does not open the Tourney at noon, the water does not get consecrated and thinned on schedule — and he loses his window.

That is the thing nobody in the fiction has worked out yet, and it is what your Arcane Knowledge roll missed by eleven last night.

Wrong on the join, right that it needed one. Do you want to keep playing from here, or shall I fix the Lost Isle thread properly in the beats and lore first so it stops fighting the authored spine?

- **Single Combat** -- a dueling tournament of one-on-one matches. Prizes of guild apprenticeships and contracts. **This is where the Baron means to field his possessed champion, [[Cailan]].**
- **The Harbor Run** -- an obstacle course unique to Purewater: swimming, climbing, and boat-hopping through the canals and over rooftops, testing agility, strength, and local knowledge. Cash and local fame for the winner -- and a covert recruiting ground for criminal and military interests.

**Timing:** arrivals and preparations begin three days before the main event; registration and the sizing-up of competitors two days before; then the events proper. The tourney's opening is the campaign's hinge -- the first public viewing of the Baron's champion, and the moment [[Gardwen]] recognizes her stolen brother.

The **Lake Lady's Tourney** is Purewater's most prestigious event: an annual sacred tournament honoring the goddess, older than the current political order, drawing competitors from across the realm. Because it is sacred, the Baron's plan to manipulate it is not mere politics but **desecration**.

**The events:**

- **Single Combat** -- a dueling tournament of one-on-one matches. Prizes of guild apprenticeships and contracts. **This is where the Baron means to field his possessed champion, [[Cailan]].**
- **The Harbor Run** -- an obstacle course unique to Purewater: swimming, climbing, and boat-hopping through the canals and over rooftops, testing agility, strength, and local knowledge. Cash and local fame for the winner -- and a covert recruiting ground for criminal and military interests.

**Timing:** arrivals and preparations begin three days before the main event; registration and the sizing-up of competitors two days before; then the events proper. The tourney's opening is the campaign's hinge -- the first public viewing of the Baron's champion, and the moment [[Gardwen]] recognizes her stolen brother.

entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

############ lore/gm-guide/gm-guide-running-the-living-world.md
---
id: "myth-lore-d5f2c24e1d31"
title: "GM Guide: Running the Living World"
category: "gm-guide"
visibility: "gm"
summary: "How the agenda/beat engine drives this campaign, and how to bend it"
created_at: "2026-09-05T12:00:00"
---

**GM ONLY.** How this campaign is built, and how to run it.

## There is no plot, there are clocks

The old version of this adventure was a timeline: on this day Santo attacks, on
that day the locket is stolen, then the purge, then the tourney. That works
exactly once, and only if the party stands where the script needs them.

This version is built out of **agendas** and **beats** instead.

- An **agenda** (`agendas/`) is what a character or faction *wants*, with a clock
  measuring how close they are. Santo wants to bind a demon and be seen as his
  father's son. The Baron wants to win the Tourney with a champion nobody has
  looked at. Marisette wants the name of whoever cut her girl.
- A **beat** (`beats/`) is the next concrete thing an agenda produces if nobody
  interferes -- placed in world time (`d-3/night`) or gated on a clock
  (`clock>=4`), with a location and a cast.

The tournament clock still runs from **d-3** (arrival) to **d0** (the Lake Lady's
Tourney), four watches to the day: `dawn`, `day`, `dusk`, `night`.

## The loop

```
list-agendas --campaign C --compact     # what is in motion
tick --campaign C --to "d-3/night"      # move time; see what came due
```

`tick` returns each due beat flagged **onscreen** or **offscreen**. That flag is
not your choice -- it is computed from where the PCs actually are. A beat is
onscreen when a PC is at its location or in its cast.

- **Onscreen** -> play it as a scene.
- **Offscreen** -> it happened anyway. Record it with
  `fire-beat --outcome narrated --log` so it enters the journal as a fact the
  party can *discover*: a rumour, a body, a closed door, a girl who was already
  bleeding when they got there.

This is the whole design. The same beat is a fight, an alibi, or a piece of news
depending only on where the players went.

## Adapt, don't adhere

Every beat file ends with notes on what to do when the players have made the
plan stale. Use them.

- `revise-beat` moves a beat's time, place, cast or framing.
- `add-agenda` mid-session when player action creates a new interest -- someone
  robbed wants restitution, someone saved owes a favour.
- `set-agenda-status --status thwarted` when they genuinely beat something, and
  then let the holder *react*. A thwarted agenda should produce a new one, not a
  quiet re-run of the old.
- `advance-agenda --by N` when the fiction earns it. Clocks are not timers.

The test of a beat is that it would happen without the PCs. If it only makes
sense when they are watching, it is a scene, not a beat -- write it as an
encounter instead.

## The one that fires on being seen

`agendas/hanzo-secures-the-bastard.md` starts **dormant** and activates the
moment the Baron or his people get a clear look at Randall's or Conall's face.
Once active it never goes dormant again and it drives the back half of the
campaign as a pursuit.

This is deliberate: it makes the players' own visibility the thing that raises
the stakes, rather than a GM decision about when to turn up the heat. Let them
walk into it or avoid it, and mean it either way.

## What the players should never be told

---

**GM reference.** Beyond the main cast (see `dramatis-personae`), the source names
a number of figures who shape the story from its edges. Those likely to appear in
Purewater have full sheets; the rest are recorded here.

**Present in Purewater (have sheets):**
- **[[Prince Emeric]]** -- the young, idealistic Governor of Purewater, the King's nephew; well-meaning and utterly out of his depth.
- **[[Hesper]]** -- publicly Marisette's arcane enforcer; secretly an agent of [[The Quiet Hand]], the hidden fellowship that works unseen for good. A potential secret patron.
- **[[Murgeroch]]** -- Temerach Nebulo's squire and go-between.
- **[[Ila]]** -- the young elven girl at the Sylph's Embrace, devoted to Emmeralda.
- **[[Mariarta]]** (Moriata) and **[[Asphodel]]** -- courtesans of the Promise of Heaven, Randall's informants.

############ lore/gm-guide/gm-guide-running-the-living-world.md
---
id: "myth-lore-d5f2c24e1d31"
title: "GM Guide: Running the Living World"
category: "gm-guide"
visibility: "gm"
summary: "How the agenda/beat engine drives this campaign, and how to bend it"
created_at: "2026-09-05T12:00:00"
---

**GM ONLY.** How this campaign is built, and how to run it.

## There is no plot, there are clocks

The old version of this adventure was a timeline: on this day Santo attacks, on
that day the locket is stolen, then the purge, then the tourney. That works
exactly once, and only if the party stands where the script needs them.

This version is built out of **agendas** and **beats** instead.

- An **agenda** (`agendas/`) is what a character or faction *wants*, with a clock
  measuring how close they are. Santo wants to bind a demon and be seen as his
  father's son. The Baron wants to win the Tourney with a champion nobody has
  looked at. Marisette wants the name of whoever cut her girl.
- A **beat** (`beats/`) is the next concrete thing an agenda produces if nobody
  interferes -- placed in world time (`d-3/night`) or gated on a clock
  (`clock>=4`), with a location and a cast.

The tournament clock still runs from **d-3** (arrival) to **d0** (the Lake Lady's
Tourney), four watches to the day: `dawn`, `day`, `dusk`, `night`.

## The loop

```
list-agendas --campaign C --compact     # what is in motion
tick --campaign C --to "d-3/night"      # move time; see what came due
```

`tick` returns each due beat flagged **onscreen** or **offscreen**. That flag is
not your choice -- it is computed from where the PCs actually are. A beat is
onscreen when a PC is at its location or in its cast.

- **Onscreen** -> play it as a scene.
- **Offscreen** -> it happened anyway. Record it with
  `fire-beat --outcome narrated --log` so it enters the journal as a fact the
  party can *discover*: a rumour, a body, a closed door, a girl who was already
  bleeding when they got there.

This is the whole design. The same beat is a fight, an alibi, or a piece of news
depending only on where the players went.

## Adapt, don't adhere

Every beat file ends with notes on what to do when the players have made the
plan stale. Use them.

- `revise-beat` moves a beat's time, place, cast or framing.
- `add-agenda` mid-session when player action creates a new interest -- someone
  robbed wants restitution, someone saved owes a favour.
- `set-agenda-status --status thwarted` when they genuinely beat something, and
  then let the holder *react*. A thwarted agenda should produce a new one, not a
  quiet re-run of the old.
- `advance-agenda --by N` when the fiction earns it. Clocks are not timers.

The test of a beat is that it would happen without the PCs. If it only makes
sense when they are watching, it is a scene, not a beat -- write it as an
encounter instead.

## The one that fires on being seen

`agendas/hanzo-secures-the-bastard.md` starts **dormant** and activates the
moment the Baron or his people get a clear look at Randall's or Conall's face.
Once active it never goes dormant again and it drives the back half of the
campaign as a pursuit.

This is deliberate: it makes the players' own visibility the thing that raises
the stakes, rather than a GM decision about when to turn up the heat. Let them
walk into it or avoid it, and mean it either way.

**What he wants.** Influence in Purewater, and past that something far
larger -- the Awake the Dragon Movement's promise that a man can be made into a
Dragon King. Cailan is the proof of concept: a boy taken in a border raid with
the spirit of the dragon-knight Thuban Eta bound inside him. Win the Single
Combat, and the Baron becomes a man the city's powers must deal with.

**How he pursues it.** Money, protocol, and patience. He arrives with a retinue
and a tournament entry, keeps the champion behind his own walls, and reinforces
the binding by ritual every night. He does not brawl in the street; he has Blau
and Tat Atarer for that.

**What changes his mind.** Nothing short of the binding failing in public. He is
not deterred by cost or by scandal -- both are survivable. He is deterred by
losing the locket, because without it the daily reinforcement gets harder and
Thuban gets louder.

**Pressure points.** The locket he carries; the bones in his border tower
(out of reach this adventure); and Thuban's own reluctance.

content.text: I have the full shape of the artefacts now. Three decisions genuinely change the structure of the rewrite, and they are yours.

questions.question: The Lost Isle threshold — a swept stair under a drowned island, dug open over four days, usable only while the channel runs thin at noon — is not in the authored scenario. It emerged in the Magda playthrough and I carried it into this one as established fact. What should it be in the rewrite?

options.label: The mechanism
options.description: Keep it. A living-to-living transfer needs the door open and the water thin; the quiet one works it at the stair with Thuban's bones while the Baron is in the closed room with Emeric. Explains why noon, why the Lady's day, why a hundred years of waiting.
options.preview:
WHY NOON?
  channel goes thin  ->  door opens  ->  transfer possible
  Tourney opens at noon  ->  the thin water IS the sacred rite

Hanzo needs BOTH:
  the room (won by the champion)
  the door (opened by the quiet one)

-> two separable targets, party can break either

options.label: Demote to a side-plot
options.description: The bones alone are the anchor, as authored. The digging is the quiet one's own project — a second, deeper conspiracy behind Hanzo — and stopping it does not stop the Tourney plan.
options.preview:
MAIN LINE:   bones + locket + daily rite
             -> champion wins -> the room -> Emeric

SIDE LINE:   the quiet one, the threshold,
             something older than Hanzo
             -> sequel hook, not this week's problem

options.label: Cut it from canon
options.description: Treat it as local colour from the Magda run. The rewrite goes back to the authored three-part binding — bones, locket, daily reinforcement — and nothing under the island matters.
options.preview:
BINDING = bones (border tower)
        + locket (on Hanzo)
        + daily reinforcement

no threshold, no thin water,
noon is just when the Tourney opens

questions.question: For the champion to be beaten, somebody has to beat him — or the bout has to be stopped. Should entering the Single Combat be a supported route for the party?

options.label: Yes — build the bracket
options.description: Write a real Single Combat: named entrants, rounds, a bracket the party can put someone into. Beating Thuban on the sand becomes a genuine option with a genuine cost, and the fight is a real fight.
options.preview:
ROUND 1  8 entrants, named
ROUND 2  4
FINAL    the masked champion vs ?

Party options:
  enter Conall (Fighter 82)
  enter a hired blade
  bribe/injure an entrant to take a slot

options.label: No — the bout is unwinnable
options.description: Thuban is a dragon-knight and cannot be beaten by anyone in the city. The only routes are stopping the Tourney, keeping Hanzo out of the room, or reaching Thuban and asking him to throw it.
options.preview:
He wins. Always.

Routes:
  Nerissa stops the Tourney
  keep Hanzo from the audience
  reach THUBAN and ask him
     to lose on purpose

options.label: Both — but only Thuban can throw it
options.description: The bracket is real and the party can enter, and they will still lose on the sand. The fight is there so the party learns the hard way that the answer is the man inside, not the blade.
options.preview:
Enter anyone you like.
You will be beaten, honourably,
by someone trying not to hurt you.

And THAT is the clue:
  he is pulling his blows
  he does not want to be there

questions.question: When does Gardwen get her look at his face? This is the emotional hinge, and its timing decides whether it is a call to action or a tragedy.

options.label: Between rounds
options.description: She sees him early — a helm off for water, a visor raised — with bouts still to come. The party then has hours and a reason, and the climax is a rescue they choose to attempt.
options.preview:
ROUND 2 ends -> helm comes off for water
  Gardwen, 40 yards, in the crowd

-> hours of clock left
-> the party ACTS

options.label: At the moment of victory
options.description: He wins, the helm comes off for the acclamation, and she sees him as he is being walked away to the private audience. Maximum pressure, minutes to act, and the audience is already happening.
options.preview:
HE WINS -> helm off -> the ground roars
  Gardwen sees him
  he is already being walked
  toward the door

-> minutes. no plan survives.

options.label: She does not see him — Conall does
options.description: Gardwen is not on the ground. Someone else recognises the face from the ship or from Sana's account, and the tragedy is that the one person who would have known him is somewhere else.
options.preview:
Gardwen is elsewhere (her choice, earlier)

The recognition falls to whoever
put the pieces together

-> and she finds out afterwards

=== magic.md head ===
# Mythras Imperative — Magic & Powers Reference

Distilled from the Mythras Imperative SRD chapter "Magic and Powers."
Two separate frameworks: **Magic** (spells, for magicians) and
**Superpowers** (core powers + Boosts + Limits, for super-beings).
Settings rename and re-flavor these (e.g. the Veilwrack campaign's
Windworking is the Magic system verbatim — see that campaign's lore).

## Magic

**Skill:** Magic (POW+CHA), a Professional skill. No skill, no magic.
**Pool:** Magic Points = POW. Recovery: Healing Rate per hour of full rest.

**Casting:** one Action + a Magic skill roll:

| Roll | MP cost | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | 0 | spell works |
| Success | 1 | spell works |
| Failure | 1 | spell fails |
| Fumble | 1d3 | spell fails (GM may add a mishap) |

All spells are Intensity/Magnitude 1 (petty magic). Duration: the scene,
unless the spell is *Instant*, *Concentration*, or has a special duration.

**Traits:**
- *Instant* — happens immediately, no duration
- *Concentration* — lasts while the caster concentrates undisturbed
- *Ranged* — up to Magic skill score in metres; unseen targets = one grade harder
- *Touch* — physical contact required (unwilling targets generally need Grip/surprise)
- *Resist (Endurance/Evade/Willpower)* — opposed roll vs the casting result;
  Evade resists cost the target an Action Point

**Starting spells:** 1d4+1. **Learning:** 3 Experience Rolls + one week +
a teacher or reliable source.

**Counter-magic in combat:** Avert (or setting equivalent) via the Counter
Spell reactive action; held spells use the Hold Magic action.

_Concentration, Ranged, Resist (Special)._ Find has many variations, each specific and learned as a separate spell. It attunes to the natural emanations of a creature or thing, alerting the caster to its presence within range. Find can be blocked by dense materials such as metal, or earth and stone at least one metre thick, and cannot discern emotions or thoughts. Common examples:

- _Find Arrows_: locates ammunition shot by hunters that missed their target.
- _Find Flaw_: identifies flaws in an object, such as hidden imperfections or physical damage.
- _Find Livestock_: locates a particular type of animal. Resisted with Willpower.
- _Find Loot_: locates precious metals and gems.
- _Find Object_: locates a lost personal possession.
- _Find Sickness_: identifies the existence of disease and illness, magical or mundane.
